cv06.evidence: Scientific studies have shown that while COVID-19 vaccines significantly reduce the risk of severe illness and death, breakthrough infections can occur, especially with variants like Delta. The CDC reported that in a Massachusetts outbreak, approximately 74% of cases were among fully vaccinated individuals, indicating that vaccinated people could still transmit the virus. This led to updated mask recommendations for vaccinated individuals in certain settings. Regarding myocarditis, the CDC acknowledged reports of increased cases among young males following mRNA vaccination and updated vaccine information to reflect this risk. These instances demonstrate the dynamic nature of scientific understanding and the necessity for ongoing research and data analysis.
cv06.happened: During the COVID-19 pandemic from 2021 to 2026, several health guidelines and statements were revised as new information emerged. Initially, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) stated that vaccinated individuals did not carry the virus. However, by July 2021, data indicated that vaccinated people infected with the Delta variant could carry high viral loads and potentially transmit the virus to others. This led the CDC to update its guidance, recommending that vaccinated individuals wear masks indoors in areas of substantial or high transmission. Additionally, the six-foot social distancing rule, widely promoted to reduce virus spread, was later acknowledged to lack a firm empirical basis. The emphasis on extensive surface disinfection was also reconsidered, as evidence suggested that COVID-19 primarily spreads through respiratory droplets rather than contaminated surfaces. Furthermore, cases of myocarditis, particularly in young males following mRNA vaccination, were initially downplayed but were subsequently confirmed and added to vaccine labeling. The origin of the virus also remained a topic of debate. Early in the pandemic, the lab-leak hypothesis was dismissed by many experts. However, by 2023, agencies like the CIA, FBI, and Department of Energy considered a research-related origin plausible, though with varying degrees of confidence. In July 2026, Senator Rand Paul released over 1,000 pages of Dr. Anthony Fauci's daily journals. When questioned about them, Dr. Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment, choosing not to answer.
cv06.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of seeking knowledge and wisdom. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, it states, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith." This encourages individuals to pursue both secular and spiritual understanding. Additionally, Moroni 10:4-5 invites believers to ask God for truth, emphasizing personal revelation as a means to discern right from wrong.
cv06.background: The COVID-19 pandemic, which began in late 2019, led to unprecedented global health challenges. Governments and health organizations worldwide implemented various measures to curb the virus's spread, including lockdowns, mask mandates, and social distancing guidelines. Vaccines were developed at an accelerated pace, with mRNA vaccines like Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna receiving emergency use authorization in late 2020. As the pandemic progressed, new variants of the virus emerged, such as the Delta variant, which was more transmissible and led to increased cases even among vaccinated individuals. The rapid evolution of the virus and the urgency to provide public guidance meant that health recommendations were frequently updated as new data became available.

fa01.talk: Why do you think God keeps telling families His promises, instead of just one person?
fa01.child: A long time ago, Heavenly Father made big promises to Abraham and his family. They trusted God, even when things were hard. Because of them, we have many stories and blessings, too.
fa01.learn: We can learn that being faithful, even when it’s hard or unpopular, can bless families and many others, just like Abraham’s family did. Technology, like scripture apps or family history tools, can help us remember and share our own family covenants and stories. Understanding Judaism reminds us that God keeps His promises and that every family is important in His plan.
fa01.matters: Judaism matters because it introduced the powerful idea that all people are children of one loving God who makes promises and calls people to live righteous lives. For families of faith, every story in the Old Testament is part of this history. Christianity comes from these same roots, believing Jesus is the fulfillment of God's promises to Abraham. Learning about Judaism helps us understand our own spiritual family tree, to respect others' faiths, and to see how God's work can move across centuries and cultures. It also teaches about staying true to beliefs even when living among those who believe differently.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Judaism
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum – Jewish History and Community
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Abrahamic Covenant

fa01.evidence: Most historians agree that the stories of Abraham and the earliest patriarchs were passed down by word of mouth for many generations before being written. Archaeologists have found evidence of towns and practices in ancient Canaan that fit what the Bible describes. However, there is no direct archaeological proof for Abraham himself. Later figures, like King David and the existence of ancient Israel, have strong evidence, including inscriptions and buildings. The Jewish people's survival and traditions, even after thousands of years of being scattered and sometimes persecuted, are a testament to their deep faith and commitment. While the story's details are debated, Judaism’s ancient roots and influence are well supported historically.
fa01.happened: Judaism began about 4,000 years ago, around the time of Abraham, in a land called Canaan, which is now mostly Israel and nearby places. According to Jewish tradition and the Bible, Heavenly Father made a sacred promise called a covenant with Abraham and his family. The Lord promised to bless Abraham, give him many descendants, and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abraham, his son Isaac, and his grandson Jacob are often called the patriarchs of Judaism. Over centuries, their families grew and became a people—later called Israelites—who believed in one God and followed His teachings. God gave them special laws and commandments, most famously through Moses, including the Ten Commandments. Life was not easy: they were sometimes slaves, sometimes wanderers, sometimes kings and then exiles. Even when scattered across many lands, Jews kept their faith, traditions, and hope in God's promises. Judaism remains a living faith, practiced by families all over the world, sharing many stories also found in the Christian Old Testament.
fa01.scripture: Many scriptures speak of the covenant the Lord made with Abraham. Genesis 12:1-3 describes God calling Abraham and promising to bless all nations through him. Galatians 3:8-9 in the New Testament teaches that this covenant found its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon often refers to the house of Israel and the promises given to Abraham and his children (see 1 Nephi 15:18, 3 Nephi 20:25-27). Doctrine and Covenants 110:11 mentions the return of the keys of the gathering of Israel, further connecting this ancient promise to the latter days.
fa01.background: Before Judaism, most people in the world worshipped many gods and followed the customs of their tribe or city. Canaan, where Abraham traveled, was filled with small villages and towns, each with their own idols and ways of life. Families lived in tents or small houses, raised animals like sheep, and grew crops. Society was organized around clans and families, and traditions were passed down by word of mouth. The idea of one God who cared for all people was very different from the beliefs of their neighbors. Since there were no written scriptures yet, stories of Abraham and his family were shared by telling and retelling them, especially as they traveled and moved to new places. Over time, these stories were written down and became the Jewish scriptures.

fa02.talk: What is one way we can show kindness or help someone who is having a hard time?
fa02.child: A long time ago, a man named the Buddha taught people how to be kind and wise so they could be happy and help others. Even today, many people try to follow his example and make the world a kinder place. Loving and helping others is something Jesus taught too.
fa02.learn: Buddhism teaches us that seeking peace and compassion is good for everyone. We learn that every person struggles, and that being gentle and understanding—rather than judging or ignoring others' pain—can help heal hearts. For Latter-day Saint families, seeing what is good and true in other religions helps us respect our neighbors and recognize God’s hand across the world. It reminds us to act with love, just as Christ would.
fa02.matters: Buddhism’s way of teaching compassion and wisdom has influenced how entire cultures think about respect, peace, and kindness for thousands of years. For families of faith, it offers a view of God’s love at work, planting seeds of truth in many places. Even though most Buddhists do not speak of Heavenly Father in the ways Christians do, their focus on kindness echoes what Jesus taught: to love others and care for those who suffer. Learning about Buddhism helps children see how Heavenly Father’s light can be found in every nation and culture, preparing people to receive more truth.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Buddhism
BBC – The Story of Siddhartha Gautama
Smithsonian Magazine – Who Was the Buddha?
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Principles of Compassion

fa02.evidence: Most historians agree that Siddhartha Gautama, later known as the Buddha, was a real person who lived in northern India and taught the ideas that we now call Buddhism. Ancient texts, such as the Pali Canon, were written down several hundred years after his life, preserving his teachings. Archaeological sites like Bodh Gaya, where he is said to have reached enlightenment, are visited by pilgrims to this day. Artifacts, such as ancient sculptures and carvings, show how early followers honored his memory. While the exact dates and some details of his life are still debated, scholars generally believe he lived in the sixth century BC and shaped world religion through his teachings.
fa02.happened: Around 563 BC, in a place called Bodh Gaya in India, a young prince named Siddhartha Gautama lived in a palace with every luxury. Yet, he was troubled by suffering he saw in the world—pain, old age, and death. Leaving behind his royal life, he traveled and sought answers through deep thinking and meditation under a tree known now as the Bodhi Tree. After much effort and reflection, Siddhartha gained insight, or 'enlightenment,' understanding the causes of suffering and how to overcome them. He became known as the Buddha, meaning 'The Awakened One.' The Buddha spent the rest of his life teaching others a path called the Dharma, which centers on living with wisdom, compassion, and moderation to end suffering and find true peace. His teachings spread widely, and today, millions follow this way of life, called Buddhism, striving to be kind and mindful wherever they live.
fa02.scripture: While the scriptures of the Church do not talk directly about the Buddha, several teachings from the Bible and Book of Mormon relate to the Buddhist focus on compassion and ending suffering. The Savior taught, "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Matthew 5:7) and commanded, "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39). In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 invites believers to "bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light" and to "mourn with those that mourn." These principles encourage us to feel and show compassion, just as Buddhism teaches.
fa02.background: India in the sixth century BC was a land of many kingdoms, each with its own rulers, customs, and beliefs. Most people lived in small villages, farming the land or trading goods in busy town markets. Society was divided into castes, or social classes, with strict rules about one’s place and duties. Religion was important, centered largely on many gods, rituals, and sacrifices led by priests. It was also a time of great questioning, as some people started to wonder about deeper meaning beyond everyday struggles. The Buddha grew up during this period, surrounded by both great wealth and the stark realities of suffering, which made him wonder if there was a better way to live. He was not the only philosopher of his age; in other parts of the world, teachers like Confucius and Pythagoras were asking big questions, too.

fa03.talk: What can we learn from other people's beliefs that helps us be better friends and neighbors?
fa03.child: Long ago, a man named Muhammad received messages from God, teaching people to be kind and fair. These teachings grew into the religion of Islam, which many people follow today.
fa03.learn: Studying the founding of Islam teaches us the power of faith to inspire societal transformation. It highlights the importance of compassion, justice, and community in addressing social inequalities. Recognizing the shared values among different faiths encourages mutual respect and understanding. This knowledge empowers families to engage in meaningful dialogues with people of diverse backgrounds, fostering a more inclusive and harmonious world.
fa03.matters: The founding of Islam has had a profound impact on world history, shaping cultures, laws, and societies across continents. For families of faith, understanding Islam's origins offers insights into the shared values and teachings among Abrahamic religions. Islam's emphasis on monotheism, compassion, and social justice resonates with principles found in other faith traditions. Recognizing these commonalities fosters mutual respect and understanding among diverse religious communities. Additionally, Islam's reverence for figures like Jesus and Mary highlights the interconnectedness of religious narratives, encouraging families to appreciate the rich tapestry of global faiths.

fa03.evidence: Historical records provide a detailed account of Muhammad's life and the early development of Islam. Islamic tradition, preserved through oral and written histories, offers insights into his experiences and the societal changes he initiated. Archaeological findings, such as early Quranic manuscripts, support the textual preservation of the Quran. The rapid expansion of Islam after Muhammad's death is documented through various historical sources, illustrating its significant influence on subsequent civilizations. While some aspects of early Islamic history are debated among scholars, the core events surrounding Muhammad's life and the establishment of Islam are well-documented and widely accepted.
fa03.happened: In the early 7th century, a man named Muhammad lived in Mecca, a bustling city in present-day Saudi Arabia. Around the year 610 AD, during a period of deep reflection in a cave called Hira, Muhammad experienced a profound event. He reported that the angel Gabriel appeared to him, delivering messages from God. These messages, emphasizing the oneness of God and calling for moral and social reform, were later compiled into the Quran, the holy book of Islam. Initially, Muhammad shared these revelations privately, but as he began to preach publicly, he and his followers faced increasing opposition from Meccan leaders who felt threatened by his teachings. In 622 AD, to escape persecution, Muhammad and his followers migrated to the city of Yathrib, later known as Medina. This migration, called the Hijra, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina, Muhammad established a community based on the principles revealed to him, uniting various tribes under the new faith. Over the next decade, Islam spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula. By 632 AD, when Muhammad passed away, Islam had become a significant religious and social force in the region.
fa03.scripture: While the scriptures of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints do not directly reference the founding of Islam, they emphasize principles of seeking truth and understanding among all people. The Book of Mormon teaches, "All are alike unto God" (2 Nephi 26:33), underscoring the importance of recognizing the worth and contributions of diverse cultures and beliefs. Doctrine and Covenants encourages believers to "seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom" (D&C 88:118), promoting the pursuit of knowledge and understanding from various sources. These teachings inspire an attitude of respect and learning towards all of God's children, including those of different faith traditions.
fa03.background: Before Islam's emergence, the Arabian Peninsula was a land of diverse tribes and cultures. Mecca, Muhammad's birthplace, was a significant trade hub, attracting merchants and travelers from various regions. The city was also home to the Kaaba, a sacred sanctuary housing numerous idols worshiped by different tribes. Society was predominantly tribal, with loyalty to one's clan being paramount. While some communities practiced monotheistic beliefs, such as Judaism and Christianity, polytheism was widespread. The region lacked a centralized political authority, leading to frequent inter-tribal conflicts. Economically, the area relied heavily on trade, with caravans transporting goods like spices, textiles, and incense across vast deserts. Socially, there were stark inequalities, with a clear divide between the wealthy elite and the impoverished. Practices like infanticide, especially of female infants, and the marginalization of certain groups were common. This was the world into which Muhammad was born, a society ripe for the transformative messages he would later convey.

fp07.talk: What have you ever worked really hard to learn, and why was it worth it?
fp07.child: Fa Xian was a monk who walked thousands of miles to find holy books for his people. He made friends far away and helped everyone learn. He chose the hard road to do something good and important.
fp07.learn: Fa Xian’s life teaches that searching for truth is worthwhile, even when it is hard. He showed courage, faith, and patience, spending many years away from home so that others might have knowledge and understanding. Families can be inspired by his example to treasure the scriptures and to value learning, even when answers are not easy to find. Like Fa Xian, anyone with faith, curiosity, and kindness can help bring light and truth to the world.
fp07.matters: Fa Xian’s journey still matters because it is one of the earliest, most detailed descriptions of ancient societies and religions across Asia. His writings helped people in China understand more about Buddhism and inspired later travelers and seekers of knowledge. For families of faith, his story is an example of what it means to love truth and go to great effort, even hardship, to find and preserve the word of God. His mission to bring home sacred writings echoes the scriptural principle of searching, studying, and treasuring up the words of life.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica - Faxian
Asia Society - Pilgrimage of Faxian
World History Encyclopedia - Faxian

fp07.evidence: Historians are confident that Fa Xian lived and made this journey because his own detailed written account survives and matches evidence from other ancient sources. His book describes the geography, towns, climates, and customs he saw; modern scholars find that many of his details about India and Central Asia fit what archaeology and later records confirm about those places in his day. Translations of Buddhist scriptures that he brought back still exist. While some older details are hard to check exactly, the main facts—his travels, his work translating scripture, and his influence on Chinese society—are agreed upon by experts. His story is valued in universities and libraries as a real and reliable source for learning about the ancient world.
fp07.happened: Fa Xian was a Chinese Buddhist monk who made one of the most remarkable journeys of the ancient world. Around the year 399 AD, he left his home in China and set out on foot for India, traveling with a small group of monks. Over fifteen years, Fa Xian walked more than 10,000 miles across dangerous deserts, high mountains, and bustling cities. His main purpose was to find ancient Buddhist scriptures that were not available in China and to bring back teachings that could help his people better understand their faith. Traveling through places now called Uzbekistan, Pakistan, India, and Sri Lanka, he carefully noted everything he saw—from kings and holy places to how people lived and worshipped. Along the way, he copied important Buddhist texts and learned from teachers in monasteries. When he finally returned to China by sea in 412 AD, he spent the rest of his life translating the sacred writings he had collected, making them available to countless people who had never read them before. His record of the journey, called 'A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms,' is still read today for the way it opens a window into a world long gone.
fp07.scripture: No specific Book of Mormon, Bible, or Doctrine and Covenants passage directly tells a story like Fa Xian's, but scripture honors those who seek after truth with all their heart. Proverbs 2:4-5 says, 'If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God.' The Book of Mormon teaches in 2 Nephi 32:3 to 'feast upon the words of Christ'. Fa Xian’s journey is a powerful example of searching and feasting upon sacred words, reminding us that truth can require effort, sacrifice, and real seeking.
fp07.background: Fa Xian lived during the Jin Dynasty in China, a time when many people were searching for meaning and stability after periods of war and change. Buddhism was growing, but much of its original scripture, written in Sanskrit, was missing in China, and what people knew had sometimes been misunderstood or was incomplete. In those days, travel across Asia was slow and dangerous, with no easy roads or border crossings. Caravans crossed deserts facing thirst and robbers, and travelers who climbed the Himalayas had to brave snow and thin air. Daily life in both China and India was full of hard work, farming, and family duties, but was also shaped by devotion, learning, and a respect for holy texts. Monks like Fa Xian often relied on the kindness of strangers, eating simple food and living by faith.

fp08.talk: If you were very powerful, what would you do to help people feel safe and cared for?
fp08.child: Genghis Khan helped many groups in Asia work together and made it safer to travel far away. But he also fought many wars, and lots of people were hurt or killed because of his choices. We can learn to be leaders who help and protect others.
fp08.learn: From Genghis Khan, we learn that leadership brings great responsibility. He could unite fighting people and bring peace to a troubled land, but when power is used without compassion, the results can be tragic. We can be inspired by his big vision and organization, but also remember to build and strengthen others instead of causing pain. Our choices matter, and with God’s help, we can use our gifts for good.
fp08.matters: Genghis Khan’s story matters because he shows how one person’s choices can deeply shape the world, both for good and for harm. Under his rule, the world became more connected, with safe roads stretching across Asia so people could trade, share ideas, and learn new things. In many ways, he helped open the door between the East and the West, laying the groundwork for future ages. For a family of faith, Genghis Khan’s life is a reminder that the gifts of organization, courage, and vision can be used to bless or hurt others. We must choose to use our influence wisely, and recognize that our actions—especially in times of power or struggle—leave lasting marks on others.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Genghis Khan
Smithsonian Magazine: Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire
National Geographic: Genghis Khan’s Army

fp08.evidence: Historians have pieced together Genghis Khan’s life from Mongol stories, Chinese records, Persian chronicles, and more recently, archaeological evidence. The “Secret History of the Mongols,” written soon after his death, gives a Mongolian view, while accounts by travelers and traders like Marco Polo help fill in the picture. Archaeologists have found remains of Mongol camps, weapons, and bones in the lands that he conquered. Genetic studies show the Mongol impact stretched across Asia. However, exact details—such as the true number of lives lost—are often estimates, sometimes based on records written by enemies of the Mongols. Still, the basic facts of his rule, laws, and conquests are well supported and researched by modern scholars.
fp08.happened: Genghis Khan was born around 1162 in what is now Mongolia. At first, his name was Temüjin. He grew up in a world where families and tribes fought over land, animals, and respect. Through great hardship, betrayal, and courage, Temüjin became a skilled leader. By uniting the scattered Mongol tribes, he was chosen as their Great Khan, taking the name Genghis Khan, which means “Universal Ruler.” He led his people to create the Mongol Empire, which stretched from China to Eastern Europe. Genghis Khan built new ways for people to communicate, such as the first international mail system, and made sure laws were followed by all, not just the powerful. Trade and travel became much safer because of his leadership, but his conquests were also incredibly brutal. Many cities that resisted the Mongols were destroyed, and whole populations lost their lives. By the time he died in 1227, Genghis Khan had changed the world forever, leaving behind both a mighty empire and a legacy marked by both progress and terrible suffering.
fp08.scripture: No scripture directly mentions Genghis Khan or the Mongol Empire, but the principle of agency—our power to choose—runs through all scripture. In the Book of Mormon, for example, 2 Nephi 2:27 teaches that “men are free according to the flesh; ... they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, ... or to choose captivity and death.” Genghis Khan used his agency to unite and build, but also to destroy. Scriptures urge us to seek peace, use power with care, and remember that all people are children of God. Proverbs 16:32 in the Bible says, “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.”
fp08.background: Before Genghis Khan, the people of the Central Asian steppes lived mainly in small tribes. Life was hard, with families moving with the seasons to care for their herds of horses, sheep, and goats. Tribes often fought over grazing land and water. There were no big cities, and few people could read or write. Neighboring civilizations, like the powerful Chinese dynasties and Muslim empires to the west, often saw the Mongols as wild outsiders. But the steppe people had their own ways and strengths, such as horse riding, archery, and strong family ties. Into this world came Genghis Khan, whose ability to unite people changed everything. The Mongols soon became the most feared force in the world, reshaping how people lived for thousands of miles in every direction.

fp09.talk: How can we find joy in simple things we do every day?
fp09.child: Long ago in Japan, a man named Sen no Rikyū taught people how to make and enjoy tea in a special way. He believed that simple things could be very beautiful and that sharing tea could bring people closer together.
fp09.learn: From Sen no Rikyū's life and teachings, we learn the value of simplicity and mindfulness in our daily practices. Embracing the beauty in imperfection can lead to a deeper appreciation for the world around us and the people we share it with. His example encourages us to find sacredness in everyday moments and to approach life with humility and grace.
fp09.matters: Sen no Rikyū's contributions to the tea ceremony have had a lasting impact on Japanese culture and beyond. By emphasizing wabi-sabi—the appreciation of beauty in imperfection and transience—he influenced various art forms, architecture, and philosophical thought. For families of faith, Rikyū's teachings resonate with gospel principles that value humility, mindfulness, and the recognition of divine beauty in everyday moments. His approach encourages individuals to find joy and meaning in simple acts, fostering a deeper connection with others and with Heavenly Father.

sources.name: Sen no Rikyū - Wikipedia
Japanese tea ceremony - Wikipedia
Sen no Rikyū: Appreciation of Nature Fused with Aesthetic Sense | Nippon.com

fp09.evidence: Historical records and artifacts provide substantial evidence of Sen no Rikyū's life and influence. His designs for tea rooms, such as the Taian, are preserved and recognized as national treasures in Japan. Writings from his disciples and contemporaries document his teachings and the philosophical underpinnings of his approach to the tea ceremony. The continued practice and reverence of his methods in modern tea schools further attest to his enduring legacy. While some details of his life are subject to interpretation, the core aspects of his contributions are well-documented and widely accepted.
fp09.happened: In 1543, Sen no Rikyū, a young man from the merchant city of Sakai, Japan, began his journey into the world of tea. Under the guidance of tea master Takeno Jōō, Rikyū immersed himself in the practice and philosophy of the tea ceremony. He embraced the wabi-cha style, which emphasized simplicity and the beauty found in imperfection. Over time, Rikyū's deep understanding and innovative approach to tea elevated the ceremony from a mere social activity to a profound spiritual and aesthetic practice. His influence was so profound that he became the tea master for prominent leaders like Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Rikyū's teachings and designs, including the creation of intimate tea rooms and the use of rustic utensils, laid the foundation for the Japanese tea ceremony as it is known today.
fp09.scripture: The principles embodied in Sen no Rikyū's tea ceremony align with scriptural teachings on humility and mindfulness. In the Book of Mormon, Alma counsels his son Shiblon: 'See that ye are not lifted up unto pride; yea, see that ye do not boast in your own wisdom, nor of your much strength' (Alma 38:11). This admonition mirrors the wabi-sabi aesthetic, which values simplicity and the humble acceptance of imperfection. Additionally, the Savior taught, 'Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin' (Matthew 6:28), encouraging us to find beauty and trust in the simple, natural aspects of life.
fp09.background: During the 16th century, Japan was undergoing significant political and social changes. The Sengoku period, marked by constant military conflict and the rise of powerful warlords, was in full swing. Amidst this turmoil, the city of Sakai emerged as a prosperous hub of commerce and culture. Merchants in Sakai engaged in trade with China and other regions, bringing diverse influences to the city. The practice of drinking powdered green tea, introduced from China, had become popular among the samurai and merchant classes. Tea gatherings evolved from lively social events to more subdued and contemplative ceremonies, reflecting a growing appreciation for simplicity and mindfulness in daily life.

fp10.talk: What do you think it means to use our talents to help others, like Ibn Sina did?
fp10.child: Ibn Sina was a wise man who lived a long time ago. He wrote a big book about medicine that helped doctors for hundreds of years. His work shows us how learning and helping others can make a big difference.
fp10.learn: From Ibn Sina's life and work, we learn the value of diligent study, the integration of knowledge across disciplines, and the importance of sharing wisdom to benefit others. His example teaches us that the pursuit of understanding, when coupled with a desire to serve, can lead to lasting contributions that transcend time and culture.
fp10.matters: Ibn Sina's work matters because it bridged ancient medical traditions with future advancements, creating a foundation that influenced medical practice for centuries. His Canon of Medicine not only compiled existing knowledge but also introduced systematic methods for diagnosis and treatment, emphasizing the importance of observation and experimentation. For families of faith, his contributions exemplify how the pursuit of knowledge and the application of one's talents can lead to significant advancements that benefit humanity. Ibn Sina's dedication to learning and sharing knowledge reflects the principle of seeking wisdom and using it to serve others, aligning with the belief that our abilities are gifts meant to be developed and utilized for the greater good.

sources.name: Historia Medica - The Canon of Medicine
Library of Congress - The Canon of Medicine
PMC - Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine: 11th century rules for assessing the effects of drugs

fp10.evidence: Historical records and manuscripts provide substantial evidence of Ibn Sina's life and works. Numerous copies of "The Canon of Medicine" exist, some dating back to the 12th century, indicating its widespread use and influence. Translations into Latin and other languages facilitated its integration into European medical curricula. Additionally, references to Ibn Sina's works by subsequent scholars and the preservation of his writings in libraries worldwide attest to his enduring impact. Archaeological findings, such as ancient medical instruments and texts, further corroborate the medical practices and theories he described, aligning with the historical context of his contributions.
fp10.happened: Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, was a Persian polymath born in 980 AD near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan. By the age of sixteen, he had already begun studying medicine, quickly surpassing his teachers in knowledge. His most renowned work, "The Canon of Medicine" (Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb), was a comprehensive medical encyclopedia that he started in Gorgan and completed in Hamadan around 1025 AD. This five-volume work systematically organized medical knowledge of the time, covering general medical principles, simple and compound drugs, diseases affecting specific organs, and general diseases. The Canon became the standard medical text in both the Islamic world and Europe, remaining a primary reference in European medical education until the late 17th century. Ibn Sina's contributions extended beyond medicine; he wrote extensively on philosophy, astronomy, and poetry, leaving a legacy that influenced various fields for centuries.
fp10.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention Ibn Sina, they emphasize the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom. Proverbs 4:7 states, "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." Similarly, Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 encourages, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith." These passages highlight the importance of acquiring knowledge and understanding, principles that Ibn Sina embodied through his extensive studies and contributions to various fields.
fp10.background: During Ibn Sina's lifetime, the Islamic Golden Age was at its peak, characterized by significant advancements in science, medicine, and philosophy. Scholars in the Islamic world had access to and were translating Greek, Roman, and Persian texts, preserving and expanding upon ancient knowledge. Daily life in the region was marked by a rich cultural and intellectual environment, with cities like Bukhara and Baghdad serving as centers of learning. The medical field was evolving, with physicians building upon the works of predecessors like Hippocrates and Galen, integrating their teachings with new discoveries. In this context, Ibn Sina's systematic approach to medicine provided a structured framework that synthesized existing knowledge and introduced innovative concepts, setting a new standard for medical practice and education.

fp11.talk: What would it be like to look at the stars or bugs up close if no one had figured out how light and eyes work?
fp11.child: A long time ago, Ibn al-Haytham wanted to know how we see. He learned that light from the world comes into our eyes, and his discoveries helped people make glasses, telescopes, and cameras. Because he loved learning, we can see and remember more today.
fp11.learn: We learn from Ibn al-Haytham’s story that asking honest questions, being humble enough to test our ideas, and sharing what we discover help everyone grow. When we use the gifts Heavenly Father gives us with curiosity and care, we can find answers that bless our families and even the whole world. Faith and reason can go hand in hand, helping us become better learners and helpers.
fp11.matters: Ibn al-Haytham’s discoveries made it possible to invent eyeglasses for clearer vision, the telescope for looking into space, the microscope for seeing tiny life, and cameras for preserving memories—things that bless families and communities even today. For families who see God as the giver of all light and truth, Ibn al-Haytham’s work can be viewed as uncovering more of Heavenly Father’s marvelous creation. His search for truth, humility in testing his own ideas, and use of God’s gifts remind us that technology and learning can help us see the wonders of the world and honor our Creator.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn al-Haytham
Khan Academy: The Golden Age of Islam
The British Library: Ibn al-Haytham

fp11.evidence: Historians have preserved Ibn al-Haytham’s writings, including early copies of his Book of Optics, and many later scientists—like Roger Bacon, Kepler, and Newton—quoted his work and built on his discoveries. Museums and universities around the world recognize his experiments as the start of modern optics and scientific method. Archaeological evidence and manuscripts confirm his life and teaching role. The influence of his methods and models can be seen directly in the history of science and the technology we use for vision and photography today.
fp11.happened: Ibn al-Haytham was born in the year 965 in what is now Iraq, at a time when the Islamic world was a center for learning and discovery. He was very curious about the world and wanted to understand how things worked, especially light and vision. People used to think that seeing happened because something came out of our eyes and touched objects. Ibn al-Haytham thought differently. He carefully observed, asked questions, and experimented with light and lenses. He wrote a great book called the Book of Optics, where he explained that we see because light reflects off objects and enters our eyes. He showed how lenses could bend light and help us see better, which was a brand-new idea. His careful experiments set new scientific standards for using evidence and testing ideas, something scientists and inventors built on for hundreds of years after.
fp11.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention Ibn al-Haytham or optics directly, they teach that all light and knowledge come from God, who gives us curiosity and intelligence to learn and serve others. Doctrine and Covenants 88:11–12 speaks of God giving light that enlightens our eyes and understanding, and James 1:5 encourages seeking wisdom from God. These principles celebrate faithful seeking and the discipline of learning for good purposes.
fp11.background: The world Ibn al-Haytham lived in was full of scholars, tradespeople, and families living in thriving cities like Baghdad and Basra. It was a golden age for science and learning in the Islamic world. Scholars studied ancient Greek, Roman, and Persian texts and built libraries filled with knowledge. People went about their daily lives with markets, mosques, and schools threading together busy communities. Few people had books in their homes, and the tools of science were rare and handmade. Still, universities and libraries were centers where discoveries flourished, and scholars from different lands met to share ideas and solve everyday problems, often using the talents and gifts they believed came from God.

fp12.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to ask questions about the world and about life?
fp12.child: Omar Khayyam was a man who loved numbers and stars, and he also liked writing poems about life. He made a very accurate calendar and wrote questions about the meaning of life that people still read today. His work teaches us it’s good to ask questions and look for answers.
fp12.learn: From Omar Khayyam, we learn that it’s possible to love science, math, and poetry at the same time, and that asking big questions is part of being human. His life shows that each person’s curiosity is a gift that can help others and bring more beauty and understanding into the world. As families, we can remember that seeking answers—whether in faith or in science—can help us grow closer to Heavenly Father and to each other.
fp12.matters: Omar Khayyam’s work matters to the world because he showed that a person can seek truth in many ways—in numbers, in the stars, and in poetry. His precise calendar made it easier for people to grow food at the right times and celebrate holy days in the right season. For families of faith, his poetry reminds us that the desire to understand life’s purpose is shared across generations and cultures. Seeking knowledge, as Khayyam did, can be a way to honor Heavenly Father’s gift of curiosity and reason, and reminds us to look for meaning in both the works of creation and the words of wise people.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Omar Khayyam
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Omar Khayyam
Smithsonian Magazine: Omar Khayyam's Calendar

fp12.evidence: Historians have well-documented records of Khayyam’s mathematical manuscripts and the calendar reforms he and his colleagues enacted. The Jalali calendar’s calculations still impress scientists and are recognized for their accuracy. Many of Khayyam’s poems survive as handwritten manuscripts, with copies dating back hundreds of years, showing how widely they were shared and treasured. Some details about his life are based on early biographies from near his own lifetime, though some stories about him have grown legendary over the centuries. Scholars can directly study the mathematics he wrote, the calendar he reformed, and the poems he left behind. Both the impact and reach of his work are confirmed by physical records and modern mathematical validation.
fp12.happened: Omar Khayyam was born in 1048 in Persia, which is now Iran. He grew up to become one of the most remarkable minds of his time, deeply interested in numbers, the stars, and the mysteries of life itself. As a mathematician, Khayyam found new ways to solve cubic equations, which are more complex than most children see in school and were a puzzle that had been worked on for centuries. In addition to his math, Khayyam was asked by the rulers of Persia to improve the calendar people used, because the one they had was not very accurate. He and his team made a solar calendar—the Jalali calendar—which was incredibly precise: it was accurate to within one day over almost four thousand years. Khayyam is also famous for his poetry, especially a book of four-line poems called the 'Rubaiyat.' These poems were written in Persian and talk about life, love, wonder, and the questions people ask about why we are here. Today, the Rubaiyat is read all around the world, in many languages, and his mathematical ideas helped shape future science and learning. Even after nearly a thousand years, people still study his work and wonder about the same mysteries Khayyam wrote about.
fp12.scripture: The scriptures teach that 'the glory of God is intelligence' (Doctrine and Covenants 93:36) and encourage all to seek wisdom wherever it may be found. Khayyam’s story echoes the Book of Mormon’s message that God invites everyone, everywhere, to learn and ponder (2 Nephi 29:7). In Proverbs 2:2-6, we are told to 'incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding,' showing that seeking truth and understanding, as Khayyam did, is a noble and godly pursuit, even when answers come in ways we do not expect.
fp12.background: During Khayyam’s time, Persia was a center of learning and culture, part of a golden age for the Islamic world. Mathematics, philosophy, medicine, and astronomy thrived in great cities like Nishapur, where Khayyam was born. Many of the books and discoveries that survived from ancient Greece, Rome, India, and earlier Persian periods were studied and improved by scholars. Ordinary people in his time lived by farming the land, weaving, trading in busy markets, and attending religious gatherings. Most learning was done in schools attached to mosques or in private homes of wealthy families, where sons—like Khayyam—were often taught to read and write, which was a rare skill for most children in that age.

fp13.talk: Why do you think Socrates kept asking questions, even when it was hard or others were upset with him?
fp13.child: Socrates was a wise, cheerful teacher who taught people by asking questions. He wanted everyone to think for themselves and find out what is really true. Some people didn’t like that, and he got in trouble, but his ideas are remembered all over the world.
fp13.learn: We can learn from Socrates that asking good, honest questions is one of the best ways to grow in wisdom and faith. It is not enough to accept things just because they are tradition or authority says so. Heavenly Father wants each of us to seek truth quietly and bravely, whether we are learning about history, science, or the gospel. We can encourage each other to think deeply and not fear doubt, trusting that light and answers will come.
fp13.matters: Socrates’s way of seeking truth by asking questions has shaped how people learn and discover right from wrong. His belief that understanding goodness and truth comes from honest, open questions rather than just believing what we’re told is important in schools, science, and even at home. For families of faith, Socrates’s life reminds us that seeking truth can be hard or even risky, but it is also sacred and powerful. In the restored gospel, we are taught to seek truth through study and prayer, trusting that, like Socrates, we can find answers if we search with real intent and humility.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Socrates
The Met: Life in Ancient Athens
Church of Jesus Christ: Seeking and Receiving Answers to Prayers

fp13.evidence: Most of what we know about Socrates comes from the writings of his students, especially Plato and Xenophon. Socrates himself left no writings, so historians must rely on these sources to piece together his life and ideas. Plato’s dialogues describe many conversations Socrates had with Athenians and his famous trial. These works are considered reliable, but they sometimes blend fact with philosophical ideas, so it is challenging to know exactly what Socrates said versus what his students later believed. Archaeological discoveries confirm details about daily life in Athens, the practice of public trials, and even the use of hemlock as a method of execution, lending support to the main events of Socrates’s story.
fp13.happened: Socrates lived in Athens, Greece, over 2,400 years ago, at a time when the city was famous for its art, politics, and ways of thinking. Instead of writing books or giving big speeches, Socrates spent his days talking with people in the city’s markets, asking them questions to help them think deeply about life, goodness, and truth. He wanted people to examine their beliefs and not just accept what they had been told. His way of teaching, called the Socratic method, involved lots of asking and answering, helping others discover truth for themselves. Some people loved how Socrates made them think, but others in Athens worried that he was influencing the young people to question traditional ways too much. Some leaders accused him of corrupting the youth and not respecting their gods. After a trial in 399 BC, Socrates was found guilty by a jury of Athenian citizens and sentenced to die by drinking poison. Socrates accepted his sentence calmly, saying he would rather die than stop seeking and sharing truth. His student Plato wrote down many of these teachings, so they would not be forgotten.
fp13.scripture: The scriptures teach the value of seeking, asking, and knocking to find truth, even when it may be difficult or unpopular. James 1:5 encourages anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, with the promise that answers will come. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 32 teaches that faith begins with a desire to believe and grows as we test and nourish the word, similar to how Socrates urged his students to examine and test ideas. Doctrine and Covenants 9:8-9 speaks of studying things out in our mind and then seeking confirmation from God, echoing Socratic inquiry coupled with revelation. The deeper principle is that God values honest searching and welcomes our sincere questions.
fp13.background: Athens during Socrates’s life was a place where many new ideas were discussed. It was a democracy, which meant citizens gathered to make decisions about their city. Many people were busy with trade, crafts, and government. Children learned reading, writing, and sometimes philosophy if their families could afford teachers. Before Socrates, philosophers called the Sophists taught people how to speak well and persuade others, but they often cared more about winning arguments than finding truth. Socrates was different because he cared deeply about what was truly good, right, and wise. He came from a humble family—his father was a sculptor and his mother a midwife. This simple background helped him speak to all sorts of people, from the rich and powerful to ordinary workers in the marketplace.

fp14.talk: What kind of questions do you think Plato asked his friends, and what big questions do you wonder about?
fp14.child: Plato was a thoughtful man who loved to ask questions about the world and what is true. He started a school where people came to talk and learn together. He believed our souls live on after this life, and that there are things more real than what we see.
fp14.learn: Studying Plato helps us see the value of asking big questions, listening before answering, and searching for truth together. His example encourages families to talk honestly about what is right and what is eternal. We can also learn from Plato’s belief that learning should be shared among friends, and that ideas are not just for scholars—they are for everyone willing to seek and ponder. His life gently reminds us that wisdom is a journey, not just a lesson.
fp14.matters: Plato matters because he changed forever how people search for truth. He founded the Academy, which became the model for all later universities—a place where questioning and discussion are welcome. He also showed that ideas like justice, goodness, and the soul deserve careful thought, not just quick answers. For families of faith, Plato’s belief in a reality beyond the visible world helped prepare people’s minds for the teachings of Jesus Christ. He helped shape Christian, Jewish, and Islamic thought, and his questions about eternal truth connect strongly with teachings about life before and after this mortal journey.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Plato

fp14.evidence: Many of Plato’s works have survived over two thousand years as handwritten manuscripts passed from one generation to the next. Scholars have preserved his dialogues in many languages and found early copies in Greek, dating back well over a thousand years. Ancient histories, like those by Diogenes Laertius, and archaeological finds in Athens support the existence of Plato’s Academy and his role in founding Western philosophy. However, the exact details of Plato’s daily life are less certain, since most information comes from later writers or his own philosophical stories. Historians agree on his impact and his main ideas, even when the details of his life are less clear. The fragments and copies we have today let us piece together much of what he taught.
fp14.happened: Around 2,400 years ago in ancient Greece, a boy named Plato was born into a noble family in the city of Athens. As he grew, he became a student of Socrates, a famous thinker who asked big questions about goodness, right and wrong, and how to live well. Socrates never wrote anything down, but Plato listened closely and later used what he learned to write many stories called dialogues. In these writings, Plato imagined conversations between thinkers who explored ideas about truth, justice, love, and the soul. After Socrates died, Plato traveled, studied, and returned to Athens, where he started a school called the Academy. This was the first institution of higher learning in Western history, where students could gather to learn and debate. At the Academy, Plato taught another bright student, Aristotle, who would also become one of history’s great thinkers. Through his teaching and writing, Plato laid stones for much of Western philosophy—the study of wisdom and the questions that shape our lives. He believed there was more to life than what we see, that beyond the world is a place of perfect Forms—truths and ideals that never change.
fp14.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention Plato by name, many scriptural teachings touch on ideas he pondered. In the Bible, Ecclesiastes 3:11 speaks of eternity being set in the heart, suggesting that people have a longing for something beyond this life. Alma 40:11-14 in the Book of Mormon describes the soul’s journey after death, teaching the reality of life before and after this earth. Doctrine and Covenants 93:29 teaches that “man was also in the beginning with God,” echoing Plato’s idea of immortal souls. These passages show that the hunger for truth and the hope of immortality are part of God’s plan, and that philosophy and faith can work together to help us seek answers.
fp14.background: Greece in Plato’s time was a tapestry of city-states, with Athens as a center for arts, politics, and learning. Most people lived simple lives, farming or trading, gathering at the marketplace to talk and share news. The gods and myths of Greek religion shaped their everyday customs, and stories about heroes and thinkers were part of daily conversation. Before Plato, thinkers known as pre-Socratic philosophers tried to explain the world by looking for patterns in nature, but it was Socrates who made the question of how to live well the heart of philosophy. Education mostly happened at home, unless a family was wealthy enough to afford tutors. Debates and learning took place in open spaces, and writing things down was becoming more common, even though most people could not read. This world was just beginning to value organized schools and recorded ideas, setting the stage for Plato’s Academy.

fp15.talk: What is something you wonder about, and how could we find answers together?
fp15.child: Aristotle was a smart man from Greece who loved to ask questions and figure out how things worked. He helped people learn how to think carefully about what is true. His ideas are still used in science and school today.
fp15.learn: From Aristotle, we learn that the desire to understand the world, use reason, and ask thoughtful questions is a holy pursuit when done humbly. We can learn to balance faith and reason, trust in the value of careful study, and appreciate that technology and learning can bring us closer to truth, service, and understanding the world Heavenly Father made. As we learn and grow, we can remember that wisdom is a treasure and a responsibility.
fp15.matters: Aristotle’s careful system of logical thinking became the bedrock for almost all later science and philosophy in Europe, the Middle East, and beyond. For families of faith, his way of asking questions and seeking evidence encourages us to use our minds as a gift from God, trusting that learning and faith can work together. His influence made it possible for Christian, Jewish, and Muslim thinkers in the Middle Ages to explore both scripture and the natural world respectfully. Even today, when we reason things out step by step, or classify animals, plants, or ideas, we often trace those habits back to Aristotle’s teachings.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Aristotle
BBC – Aristotle: Father of Philosophy
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Aristotle

fp15.evidence: Surviving ancient manuscripts and references by later thinkers provide strong evidence that Aristotle lived, taught, and wrote extensively between 384 and 322 BC. Many of his texts, including works on logic (like the Organon), ethics (Nicomachean Ethics), biology, and politics, have been preserved, copied, and translated over centuries. Archaeologists have found records of his travels and work, such as at the Lyceum, his school in Athens. Historians also agree that he tutored Alexander the Great, based on writings from both Greek and Roman historians. While some details of his life may be lost, there is no serious doubt about his major role in shaping Western thought.
fp15.happened: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in the ancient city of Stagira, in what is now part of Greece. He was the son of a royal doctor, which gave him an early taste of both science and thoughtful study. When he was a young man, he traveled to Athens and became a student at Plato's Academy, the most famous school in the world at that time. After Plato died, Aristotle went on his own way, studying the world around him with a careful and curious eye. Later, he was called to tutor a young prince named Alexander, who would become Alexander the Great. Aristotle wrote many books covering nearly every area of knowledge, including animals and plants, the way the world works, how people should live together, how to make good decisions, and how stories are told. His greatest gift may have been his way of teaching others how to think very carefully and logically, weighing evidence and drawing wise conclusions. Because of this, scholars many centuries later called him simply “The Philosopher.”
fp15.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention Aristotle by name, they remind us that wisdom and learning are gifts from God and that we should seek knowledge by study and by faith. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches, “Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” Proverbs 4:7 says, "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." These verses encourage us to value both careful thinking and spiritual insight, much like Aristotle’s work encouraged clear reasoning alongside wonder.
fp15.background: During Aristotle’s time, Greece was a collection of small cities and lands, each with its own government and traditions, but they shared a love of debate, theater, and learning. Most everyday people farmed the land, but some cities like Athens grew wealthy and supported many teachers and artists. Before Aristotle, thinkers like Socrates and Plato tried to answer big questions about goodness, truth, and the universe. Education was done face-to-face, with students gathering around wise speakers. Instead of books for everyone, ideas were shared through speech and, for the privileged few, through handwritten scrolls. There were no microscopes or telescopes; Aristotle looked at nature with his good eyes and sharp mind, searching for patterns God had placed in His creation.

fp16.talk: How do you think learning new things can help you understand Heavenly Father better?
fp16.child: Thomas Aquinas was a wise man who loved learning about God and everything else. He taught that using our minds helps us get closer to Heavenly Father. He believed we can use both faith and good thinking to find truth.
fp16.learn: From Thomas Aquinas, we can learn that it is good to think deeply and study carefully, even about our faith. Heavenly Father wants us to use both our hearts and our minds. We do not have to be afraid to ask hard questions or to learn from the world around us, because all truth belongs to God. Like Aquinas, we can find ways to bring faith and honest study together.
fp16.matters: Thomas Aquinas matters greatly because he helped Christians of many ages understand that we do not have to choose between believing in God and using our minds. For families of faith, his life reminds us that Heavenly Father values our honest searching, our studying, and our efforts to understand the world and His plan. Parents can teach their children that faith grows stronger when we use both prayer and careful thinking, and that real truth will fit together in time. Aquinas’s work still shapes how millions of people think about God and learning today.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas
Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Thomas Aquinas
Encyclopædia Britannica: St. Thomas Aquinas

fp16.evidence: Historians agree that Thomas Aquinas lived from about 1225 to 1274. We still have many of his books, letters, and records from students and church officials who knew him. His writings are carefully preserved in libraries and have been studied for centuries. Over time, scholars have confirmed that his big ideas deeply influenced not just theology, but education and philosophy in Europe and beyond. The places where he studied, taught, and lived—like the University of Paris—still keep records about him. No major part of his life story is seriously doubted by historians today.
fp16.happened: In the year 1267, Thomas Aquinas was hard at work teaching, writing, and serving as a Dominican friar in Italy. At this time, he was already known as a great thinker and faithful follower of Jesus Christ. Thomas believed that learning about the world—science, philosophy, and truth—could help people draw closer to God. He spent years writing and teaching, most famously in his huge work called the Summa Theologica. This book gathered nearly everything he knew about God, goodness, and how we find truth. Aquinas did something new and brave for his time: he used the ideas of an old Greek thinker, Aristotle, and showed Christians that thinking deeply, even outside of scripture, could strengthen faith. He explained that faith (what we trust God to reveal) and reason (what we discover through careful thought) can both lead to truth, because both ultimately come from God. Many of his students and readers felt their beliefs grow stronger because Aquinas showed them a way to love God with both heart and mind.
fp16.scripture: The scriptures teach that loving God involves our whole selves, including our minds. Jesus teaches in Mark 12:30 to "love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind." In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we are told to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." These verses show the same principle that Aquinas taught: faith and reason are both gifts from Heavenly Father to help us learn truth.
fp16.background: In the 1200s, most Europeans belonged to the Catholic Church, and learning happened mainly in monasteries, churches, and growing universities. The world was changing—books from old Greece and the Muslim world were finding their way to Europe, and cities were growing, bringing new jobs and ideas. Thomas Aquinas grew up in a wealthy family in Italy, but instead of living as a nobleman, he chose to become a Dominican friar, giving up great comfort for a life of study, teaching, and prayer. The Middle Ages were a time of faith, but also of questions—people wondered how ancient learning and new discoveries fit with their beliefs.

fp17.talk: If you could invent or draw anything to help people in the future, what would it be?
fp17.child: Leonardo was a smart and curious man who loved to paint, invent, and learn about everything. He made the famous picture of Jesus and His friends at dinner, and he drew ideas for flying machines hundreds of years ago. He used the talents God gave him to help others see things in new ways.
fp17.learn: Leonardo da Vinci’s life teaches that Heavenly Father blesses each of us with unique talents, and when we use them to learn, create, or help others, we honor Him and build up His world. We can appreciate the wonders around us—whether drawing, building, solving problems, or singing—and see that faith and learning grow stronger together. When we study the lives of great people from the past, we learn that curiosity, kindness, and a love for truth never go out of style.
fp17.matters: Leonardo’s example reminds us of the vast power of human curiosity and the gifts God gives to each person. For families of faith, his painting The Last Supper is especially important because it helped many people imagine and remember the story of Jesus with His apostles—a story that Christians hold sacred. His detailed studies of how creation works, from plants to the stars, show how science and faith can work together to bring light to the world. Leonardo's life inspires us to learn, create, and serve with all the talents God has given us. His work continues to open eyes in both museums and books, making him important in art, history, and science.

sources.name: Leonardo da Vinci – Britannica
The Last Supper – The National Gallery
Leonardo da Vinci – The Metropolitan Museum of Art
Gospel Topics: Talent – churchofjesuschrist.org

fp17.evidence: Historians have carefully preserved Leonardo’s original notebooks, sketches, and paintings. Museums today hold many of his works, allowing people to study his handwriting, sketches of inventions, and the unique style of his brushstrokes. Scientific studies have confirmed that he dissected human bodies and animals to learn about anatomy, and comparisons of his drawings with modern scans show they were remarkably accurate for his time. Analysis of The Last Supper, painted between 1495 and 1498, shows both the skill and difficulty—much of the original paint has faded, but experts have found ways to recover what he created. There is no doubt Leonardo invented and drew many things before anyone else. He signed many papers and letters, and his life is well recorded in Italian records and letters from people who knew him.
fp17.happened: Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 in a small town in Italy, and he grew to become one of the most gifted and curious people in history. He is often called the ultimate “Renaissance man” because he excelled in so many different fields at once. Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa, a portrait that became world-famous for her mysterious smile, and The Last Supper, showing Jesus with his disciples at their final meal together. But Leonardo didn’t just paint—he filled many notebooks with sketches and ideas far ahead of his time, including designs for flying machines, tanks, and even a kind of solar power collector. He also studied the human body carefully, making some of the most accurate medical drawings the world had ever seen, impacting how doctors understood anatomy. Leonardo’s blend of art and science, meant his work was both beautiful and useful. Even today, people visit museums to see his paintings and drawings, and scientists still study how he saw the world. His life, from 1452 to 1519, helped shape how we think about both science and art, and his greatest works remain among the most recognized in the world.
fp17.scripture: Though Leonardo da Vinci and his paintings are not directly mentioned in the scriptures, his desire to use his gifts for good echoes scripture teachings about talents and seeking knowledge. In Matthew 25:14-30 (the Parable of the Talents), Jesus teaches about using God-given talents to bless others. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, the Lord instructs us to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." Leonardo’s careful study of creation—whether painting Christ or drawing the workings of a bird’s wing—shows how learning can help us understand and appreciate God’s world.
fp17.background: Leonardo lived in Italy during the Renaissance, a time about 500 years ago when people across Europe became very interested in art, sciences, and learning. Cities were growing, new ideas about nature, the earth, and how to represent people and stories in art were spreading quickly. In Leonardo’s time, people traveled mainly on foot or by horse, families made their own clothes, and most work was done by hand. Books were rare and precious, often written by hand, though the printing press was just starting to change that. Artists, inventors, and thinkers gathered in cities like Florence, Milan, and Venice to share ideas. Religion was a central part of daily life, and magnificent churches and paintings were created to honor God and help people understand important stories from the Bible.

fp18.talk: Why do you think it's important to learn new things, even if they challenge what we already believe?
fp18.child: Long ago, people thought the sun moved around the earth. But a man named Copernicus discovered that the earth actually moves around the sun. This helped us understand more about the stars and planets.
fp18.learn: From Copernicus's experience, we learn the importance of seeking truth, even when it challenges prevailing beliefs. His dedication to observation and careful reasoning exemplifies the value of scientific inquiry. For families, his story teaches us to encourage curiosity and critical thinking in our children, fostering a love for learning and a willingness to explore new ideas. It also reminds us that understanding the natural world can deepen our appreciation for the Creator's handiwork.
fp18.matters: Copernicus's heliocentric model was a catalyst for the Scientific Revolution, fundamentally altering humanity's understanding of the cosmos. By displacing the earth from the center of the universe, it encouraged a shift towards observation and inquiry, paving the way for future scientists like Galileo and Kepler. For families of faith, this discovery underscores the vastness and order of Heavenly Father's creation. It reminds us that while the universe is immense beyond our comprehension, it operates according to discoverable laws, reflecting a Creator of extraordinary order and intelligence. This perspective can deepen our appreciation for the divine craftsmanship evident in the natural world.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nicolaus Copernicus
National Geographic: How Copernicus put the sun at the center of the cosmos
History.com: Copernicus: Facts, Model & Heliocentric Theory
Khan Academy: The heliocentric model theory

fp18.evidence: Historical records confirm that Copernicus developed his heliocentric theory over several decades, culminating in the publication of "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" in 1543. This work meticulously detailed his observations and mathematical calculations supporting the sun-centered model. Archaeological findings, such as the heliograph he created at Olsztyn Castle, further demonstrate his dedication to precise astronomical measurements. While his model was not immediately accepted and faced opposition, it eventually gained traction, especially after Galileo's telescopic observations provided additional evidence. Today, the heliocentric model is a fundamental principle of astronomy, supported by extensive scientific evidence.
fp18.happened: In the early 16th century, Nicolaus Copernicus, a Polish mathematician and astronomer, proposed a groundbreaking idea: the sun, not the earth, is at the center of the universe. This heliocentric model suggested that the earth and other planets revolve around the sun. Copernicus developed this theory over many years, carefully observing the heavens and performing detailed calculations. He first shared his ideas in a brief manuscript called the "Commentariolus" around 1514, which circulated among a small group of scholars. However, he hesitated to publish his full work due to potential backlash from the prevailing geocentric beliefs, which held that the earth was the center of the universe. It wasn't until 1543, the year of his death, that his seminal work, "De revolutionibus orbium coelestium" (On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres), was published. This publication marked a pivotal moment in scientific history, challenging long-held views and laying the foundation for modern astronomy.
fp18.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the majesty and order of God's creations. In the Book of Moses, we read: "And worlds without number have I created; and I also created them for mine own purpose" (Moses 1:33). This passage highlights the vastness of God's creations, aligning with the understanding that the universe is expansive and orderly. Additionally, in the Doctrine and Covenants, it states: "All things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that are upon the face of it" (D&C 88:47). These scriptures encourage us to seek knowledge and understanding of the natural world, recognizing it as a testament to God's power and glory.
fp18.background: Before Copernicus, the widely accepted view of the universe was the geocentric model, primarily based on the teachings of the ancient astronomer Ptolemy. This model placed the earth at the center, with the sun, moon, planets, and stars orbiting around it. This perspective aligned with the philosophical and religious beliefs of the time, emphasizing humanity's central place in creation. Daily life in the 15th and 16th centuries was deeply intertwined with these beliefs, and the idea of an earth-centered universe was rarely questioned. The church held significant influence over intellectual thought, and deviations from established doctrines were often met with suspicion or condemnation. In this context, proposing a sun-centered universe was not only scientifically revolutionary but also a bold challenge to the societal norms of the era.

fp19.talk: How do you think stories help us feel closer to each other or to Heavenly Father?
fp19.child: William Shakespeare wrote lots of plays and poems a long time ago, and people still act them out today. He made up words that we use every day and told stories that help us understand how people feel and change. His plays feel real because they show both happy and sad parts of life.
fp19.learn: We learn that the words we choose can shape the world for centuries. Even one person, using the gifts Heavenly Father gives, can brighten minds and hearts far beyond their own time. Shakespeare’s example shows that exploring big questions and feelings through art or writing can prepare us to understand God’s love and our purpose. Creativity is a precious tool and a blessing for families and for all of Heavenly Father’s children.
fp19.matters: Shakespeare matters because he shows what language can do: connect, heal, teach, and inspire. His insights into family, forgiveness, courage, and conscience help readers and viewers understand themselves and others. For families of faith, his stories can start gentle, honest talks about choices, truth, mercy, and how to live with hope when life is hard. The beauty of his words opened the door for the King James Bible, making scripture more powerful to hear and understand. Shakespeare’s work reminds us that Heavenly Father can use human creativity to teach eternal truths in every age.

sources.name: The British Library: Who was William Shakespeare?
Shakespeare Birthplace Trust: The Life of William Shakespeare
Encyclopaedia Britannica: William Shakespeare

fp19.evidence: Historians have found strong evidence for Shakespeare’s life and work. His baptism was recorded in 1564 in Stratford, and his will proves he died in 1616. Some original printed editions of his plays and poems still survive, signed by friends in his theater company, showing which works he created. The Globe Theatre was rebuilt in modern London, using records of the old one Shakespeare helped design. Scholars analyze old documents, such as letters, court records, and references in other books to piece together his biography. While a few people once questioned if he wrote all the plays, most experts trust the evidence that William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon was the true author.
fp19.happened: William Shakespeare was born in 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon, England. He grew up to become the most celebrated writer in the English language. Shakespeare wrote 37 plays, from tragedies like 'Hamlet' and 'Macbeth' to comedies such as 'A Midsummer Night’s Dream' and histories like 'Henry V.' These plays were performed in London, often at the Globe Theatre, and have been continuously performed for over 400 years. Shakespeare also wrote 154 sonnets, special poems about love, time, beauty, and faith. His works captured every feeling and part of the human experience—joy, sorrow, betrayal, forgiveness, and hope—in ways no one had before. Shakespeare's language was so creative that he invented more than 1,700 new words and phrases. His writing changed how people speak and think, and his influence is still seen in books, movies, and conversations today. Families and audiences of all kinds can find lessons in his characters as they struggle, fail, love, and change.
fp19.scripture: Many scriptures celebrate the power of words and stories to teach hearts. Proverbs 25:11 says, 'A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.' The Book of Mormon reminds us that 'the pleasing word of God … healeth the wounded soul' (Jacob 2:8). Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 counsels us to seek 'words of wisdom' from good books. These passages support the idea that creative, thoughtful language—like Shakespeare’s—can prepare us to receive and share truth.
fp19.background: England in Shakespeare’s time was alive with excitement and change. This was the era of the Renaissance, when people were hungry for learning, new discoveries, and artistic beauty. Queen Elizabeth I was the monarch for much of Shakespeare’s life, and she encouraged the arts. Most people lived in small towns or the countryside, working farms or learning crafts, but cities like London were growing fast. The printing press had been invented just over a century earlier, making books much more available, including the newly translated King James Bible. Most families read scripture together and enjoyed stories and songs in their homes. Watching plays at the theater became a favorite pastime for people of every class, bringing together rich and poor, old and young.

fp20.talk: What would you do if you discovered something true, even if people around you didn’t believe you?
fp20.child: Galileo looked at the sky through a little telescope and saw amazing things, like moons around Jupiter. He found out the Earth really goes around the sun. Some people didn’t like this, but today we know he was right.
fp20.learn: From Galileo’s life, we learn the courage to ask questions and keep looking for answers, even when others are afraid or disagree.
