w01.happened: Around 3500 BC, in a place called Sumer, people began to build the very first cities the world had ever seen. These cities, like Ur, Uruk, and Eridu, were special because they were not just big villages; they had walls, markets, temples, and places for people to gather and trade. The Sumerians also started something brand new—writing. Their system, called cuneiform, was first used to keep track of goods and trades, but it soon told stories and shared laws. For the first time, rules were written down for everyone to see, making it easier for people to understand what was right and fair. Sumerians worked together to build large temples (ziggurats), created irrigation systems to water their fields, and traded with people far away. This helped their cities grow even bigger and stronger. The way Sumerians organized their lives—with leaders, workers, priests, and families—set the pattern for how many people have lived in cities ever since. Their ideas about cities, laws, and writing shaped the world for thousands of years.
w01.background: Before Sumer, most people lived in small villages or as wandering herders and farmers. Life was simpler but also harder, with families mostly taking care of themselves. The land known as Mesopotamia, which means 'between the rivers' (Tigris and Euphrates), was very fertile, which made it a good place to grow crops and settle down. The Sumerians were among the first to use irrigation to bring water right to their fields, which meant they could produce enough food for many people. Daily life in a Sumerian city might include farmers working outside the city, craftsmen making pottery or tools, traders exchanging goods, and children helping their families. Cities were busy places, but deeply connected by faith and community. People worshiped in large temples, believed their king spoke for the gods, and kept careful records of what happened in their lives.
w01.matters: Sumer matters to us because it shows how people, working together, can invent new ways of living. The first cities and writing systems helped people remember important things and keep peace with fair laws. These same patterns of working together, writing down what's important, and living by good rules help families and communities today. For families of faith, it’s meaningful that Abraham, the father of the covenant people, was born right in this place. His story reminds us that Heavenly Father can guide His children wherever they live, even in the world’s first great cities. Learning about Sumer helps us see how God’s plan works in all times and places.
w01.scripture: The Bible shares that Abraham was born in 'Ur of the Chaldees'—a city in ancient Sumer (Genesis 11:28, 31; Abraham 1:1 in the Pearl of Great Price). This is one of the oldest connections between a prophet’s family and a real city from ancient history. While the Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants do not mention Sumer, they teach that God works through families and communities (for example, Moses 1:39; 1 Nephi 1:1). These scriptures show that God's plan has always centered on families, no matter where or when they live.
w01.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found ruins of the first cities in southern Iraq, along with clay tablets covered in cuneiform writing. There are thousands of these tablets, and they are clearly from a time before any other known writing. Ancient city walls, ziggurats, pottery, tools, and even school tablets used by Sumerian children have been uncovered. These discoveries help us know exactly where these cities were and how Sumerians lived. Scholars have even found legal codes, like the famous Code of Ur-Nammu, which is one of the world’s oldest sets of written laws. These findings are agreed upon by experts, and new discoveries are still being made.
w01.learn: Studying Sumer teaches us that families, when they work together with others, can create wonderful things—like safe cities, ways to remember important lessons, and just rules. It reminds us that even the oldest civilizations started with people making choices every day. We see that new tools, like writing, can bring blessings or challenges, depending on how we use them. This can help us think about how we use our own tools wisely, to help and not to harm.
w01.child: A long time ago, people in Sumer made the first cities where lots of families lived together. They were the first to make writing, and their rules helped everyone know what was fair. Abraham, a prophet, was born in one of these cities.
w01.talk: Why do you think writing things down can help families and cities stay safe and happy?

w02.happened: Around 2560 BC, workers in ancient Egypt finished building the Great Pyramid at Giza. This huge stone monument was erected as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu, the ruler of Egypt at that time. The pyramid originally stood about 146 meters high and for thousands of years it remained the tallest man-made structure in the world. Building it was a massive project: thousands of workers, including skilled builders, laborers, and craftsmen, worked for about 20 years to move and set more than two million stone blocks, some weighing more than two tons each. The pyramid was built with such precision that its sides are almost perfectly straight and aligned to the four cardinal points of the compass. It was the centerpiece of a complex of buildings, including temples and smaller pyramids, and was designed to honor the Pharaoh and help him travel to the afterlife, according to Egyptian beliefs. Today, the Great Pyramid still stands, reminding us of the incredible abilities of ancient people.
w02.background: Egypt at this time was ruled by powerful pharaohs, who were considered both gods and kings. The land around the Nile River was rich and fertile, so people could grow plenty of food. Most people lived in small villages and worked as farmers, but some served the pharaoh as builders, craftsmen, or officials. Life was centered around the river, the seasons, and the many gods the Egyptians worshipped. Before the Great Pyramid, Egyptians had already been making tombs for their great leaders, first as simple mounds, then as step pyramids. Building such huge monuments showed the pharaoh's power, and people believed these grand tombs were needed for their kings to enjoy life after death.
w02.matters: The Great Pyramid matters for many reasons. For the world, it shows us the wonders human hands and minds can create, even without modern technology. People still study how ancient workers planned and built such a lasting structure. For a family of faith, this event invites us to think about what we build in our own homes and hearts. While the Egyptians built a giant pyramid from stone, God was quietly working to form families who would keep covenants and bless the world, a work which is still going on today.
w02.scripture: There is no record in the Bible or other scriptures about the Great Pyramid or ancient Egypt in this era, but scriptures often use the idea of building—like wise builders in Matthew 7:24-25 and Helaman 5:12—to teach about making strong, lasting foundations in our lives. While Egypt was building monuments to man’s greatness, God was working through faithful families like Noah’s and, later, Abraham’s, to keep His covenants alive (Genesis 9:9, Genesis 12:1-3).
w02.evidence: Archaeologists have learned much about the Great Pyramid. They have studied the nearby workers’ villages, tools, and quarries, which show that teams of skilled workers—not slaves—built the pyramid, probably out of duty to their king and religion. The stones came from nearby, moved on sledges and possibly lubricated with water. Today, the pyramid stands nearly as it was, though the smooth outer casing stones are mostly gone. While some details are still studied, the date and purpose of the pyramid are very well supported by written records from later Egyptians, tomb discoveries, and scientific studies of construction marks and techniques.
w02.learn: We can learn that people, even long ago, could plan and achieve mighty things when they worked together. But we also remember that the most important things we build are not always seen, like loving families and personal faith. It takes daily effort and patience, but what we build in our hearts can last longer than stone.
w02.child: A long time ago in Egypt, people built a giant pyramid for their king, using big stones they carried and placed by hand. It is still standing today! God wants us to build strong families, just like those workers built strong buildings.
w02.talk: What is something we could build in our family that would last a long time, even if you can't see it?

w03.happened: During the 5th century BC, Athens experienced a remarkable period known as its Golden Age. This era was marked by significant advancements in art, philosophy, and governance. Under the leadership of Pericles, Athens embraced democracy, allowing citizens to participate directly in decision-making. This political system fostered a sense of community and responsibility among Athenians. Culturally, the city flourished with the construction of iconic structures like the Parthenon, a temple dedicated to the goddess Athena, showcasing the architectural prowess of the time. The arts thrived as playwrights such as Sophocles and Euripides introduced enduring works of tragedy and comedy. Philosophers like Socrates began exploring profound questions about ethics and knowledge, laying the groundwork for Western philosophy. This period also saw the recording of historical events by figures like Herodotus, often referred to as the 'Father of History.' The Golden Age of Athens set enduring standards in various fields, influencing civilizations for centuries to come.
w03.background: Before the Golden Age, Greece was emerging from the Dark Ages, a period following the fall of the Mycenaean civilization. During this time, Greek society was fragmented into city-states, or 'poleis,' each with its own governance and customs. Daily life was primarily agrarian, with communities relying on farming and local trade. The 8th century BC saw the composition of Homer's epic poems, the 'Iliad' and the 'Odyssey,' which played a crucial role in shaping Greek identity and values. The establishment of the Olympic Games in 776 BC marked a unifying cultural event, fostering a sense of shared heritage among the Greek city-states. These developments set the stage for the cultural and political advancements that would define the Golden Age.
w03.matters: The Golden Age of Athens is significant because it laid the foundations for many aspects of Western civilization. The democratic principles established during this time have influenced countless governments worldwide, promoting the idea of citizen participation and equality before the law. The philosophical inquiries initiated by thinkers like Socrates encouraged a tradition of critical thinking and ethical reflection. For families of faith, this period underscores the importance of seeking knowledge and understanding, recognizing that such pursuits can lead to greater wisdom and moral clarity. The achievements of the Golden Age remind us that periods of peace and prosperity can foster remarkable cultural and intellectual growth, benefiting not only contemporary society but also future generations.
w03.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly reference the Golden Age of Greece, they emphasize the value of wisdom and understanding. Proverbs 4:7 states, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' This aligns with the Greek pursuit of knowledge and philosophy during their Golden Age. Additionally, the New Testament was written in Greek, a language that had become widespread due to the cultural influence of Greece, facilitating the dissemination of the gospel message.
w03.evidence: Historical and archaeological evidence supports the existence and significance of Athens' Golden Age. Structures like the Parthenon stand as testaments to the architectural advancements of the period. Writings from historians such as Herodotus and Thucydides provide detailed accounts of events and daily life in ancient Greece. Artifacts, including pottery and sculptures, reflect the artistic achievements and cultural values of the time. These sources collectively offer a comprehensive understanding of the era's impact and legacy.
w03.learn: From Athens' Golden Age, we learn that periods of peace and stability can lead to significant cultural and intellectual advancements. It highlights the importance of fostering environments where arts, philosophy, and governance can flourish. For families, it serves as a reminder to value education, critical thinking, and active participation in community life, recognizing that such engagement can lead to lasting positive contributions to society.
w03.child: A long time ago, the city of Athens was very special because people there built beautiful buildings and thought about big questions. They made plays and talked about right and wrong, helping us learn how to think and live better today.
w03.talk: Why do you think learning and asking questions are important for us?

w04.happened: In the year 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther made history in the small town of Wittenberg. Luther was deeply concerned about certain practices in the Catholic Church, especially the selling of 'indulgences,' which many people believed could buy forgiveness from sins. Frustrated, Luther wrote a list of 95 statements, called the '95 Theses,' which challenged these practices and called for changes in the Church. He nailed this document to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg, a common way to invite public discussion at the time. Luther’s challenge quickly spread, thanks to the newly invented printing press, and sparked a major religious movement called the Protestant Reformation. Many people began to question church leaders, and new Christian groups formed. One essential change was that the Bible started to be translated from Latin, which most people couldn’t read, into everyday languages like German and English. This gave ordinary families a chance to read the scriptures for themselves, learn about Jesus, and pray in their own words. Luther and others risked much to make these changes, believing everyone should have access to God’s word without needing special permission or church officials to interpret it for them.
w04.background: Before the Reformation, Europe was mostly Catholic, and the Church played a big role in governments and daily life. Almost all church services and scriptures were in Latin, a language only educated priests or scholars understood. Most families depended on priests to tell them what the Bible said and how to live their faith. The printing press had just been invented, making it easier and cheaper to share ideas quickly. The rise of cities, growing literacy, and new ways of thinking (sometimes called the Renaissance) were changing the world. People were starting to ask more questions about faith, science, and how society worked. Martin Luther was just one of many who wanted faith to be genuine and based on scripture, not just tradition or money.
w04.matters: The Protestant Reformation matters because it changed how millions of people experienced faith. For families who value personal scripture study, prayer, and direct guidance from God, this event opened the way. When the Bible was put into everyday languages, people didn't have to depend only on church leaders—they could study God's word as a family. For Latter-day Saints, these changes helped prepare the world for later events like the Restoration and the First Vision. The Reformation's spirit of seeking truth and standing up for what is right continues to inspire faithful families everywhere.
w04.scripture: Several scriptures speak to the importance of seeking truth and having access to God’s word. In 2 Timothy 3:16-17, the Bible says all scripture is given by inspiration of God and is profitable for teaching. Doctrine and Covenants 123:12 reminds us that many are kept from the truth simply because they do not know where to find it. The Book of Mormon also highlights the power of reading and pondering scripture, as found in 2 Nephi 31:20, which encourages believers to feast upon the word of Christ. The work of the Reformation matches the principle that God's word should be available to all.
w04.evidence: Historians have many contemporary records that show Martin Luther did write and distribute his 95 Theses in 1517. There is some debate about whether he literally nailed them to the church door, but the event itself is well documented through letters, published copies, and church archives. The rapid spread of Luther’s ideas was made possible by the printing press, and early German Bibles and translations by Luther still exist in libraries today. The Reformation's effects on religious practice, education, and even politics are traceable in records from the 16th century onwards. Archaeologists and historians also track changes in church buildings and family Bibles, evidence of this time when ordinary people began to access the scriptures themselves.
w04.learn: Families can learn that the courage to ask questions, seek truth, and stand up for what is right can bring blessings to many people, even generations later. We also see that having the scriptures in a language we understand is a very special gift—one that others long ago gave much to make possible. It can remind us to treasure our ability to read and share God’s word together, and to be grateful for those who helped provide it.
w04.child: Martin Luther wanted everyone to have the Bible in words they could read. He made a big list of things to change and shared it with many people. After that, more families could read about Jesus together.
w04.talk: Why do you think it’s important for us to have the scriptures in a language we can understand?

w05.happened: In the summer of 1776, leaders from thirteen British colonies met in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to talk about their future. These colonies were tired of being ruled by a king in England who made laws and taxes without letting them have a say. On July 4, 1776, a group of men called the Continental Congress agreed to the Declaration of Independence. This document said the colonies were now a free country, no longer under England's control, and would be called the United States of America. Over the next years, the people fought a hard war, called the Revolutionary War, to protect their new country. After the war, leaders wrote the Constitution, creating strong rules for how the country would be governed. It made sure everyone would have certain rights—including the right to pray and worship as they chose, called religious freedom. The Constitution was finished in 1787, and the Bill of Rights, including the First Amendment about religious freedom, was added in 1791. This made the United States different from most places in the world at that time, as it protected the right for people to follow their own faith.
w05.background: Before the United States was founded, most of the people living in the thirteen colonies were from Europe, especially England, but also Germany, the Netherlands, and other countries. Many had come because they wanted to practice their religion without being forced to follow the king’s church. Daily life was simple and hard—most people farmed or worked as tradesmen. There were only a few big towns. Governments were mostly local and based on English traditions, but the king and British laws still had the final say. Sometimes, local rules would punish people for being different in religion or for speaking against the government. Most people read the Bible and believed in God. Leading up to 1776, there were many arguments about fairness, and people started talking about new ideas, like liberty and the right to choose their leaders.
w05.matters: The founding of the United States matters because it changed history—not just for Americans, but for the whole world. This new country was built on ideas of freedom, including letting people worship God as they believed was right. For families of faith, this is especially important because those freedoms led to a country where people could read the scriptures, pray openly, and even start new churches, like The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The protection for religious freedom continues to be a blessing to families today, making it possible to practice faith in peace.
w05.scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 teaches that the Constitution was set up by wise men whom Heavenly Father raised up for that very purpose. This ties the founding of the United States to God’s plan and the coming Restoration. In the Book of Mormon, Ether 2:12 says the land is a land of promise, protected as long as its people serve God. The Bible talks about liberty too—2 Corinthians 3:17 says ‘where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.’ Members of the Church believe the First Amendment was part of allowing Joseph Smith to pray, see God, and start Christ's restored church.
w05.evidence: Historians agree that the Declaration of Independence was signed in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776. The original Declaration is kept at the National Archives, and copies from that time can be seen in museums. Letters, diaries, and official records from those years show us exactly what was discussed and why the founders wanted independence. The U.S. Constitution, which set up religious freedom, is also preserved. Scholars study these documents carefully and agree that the First Amendment was meant to stop the government from controlling religion. Archaeological evidence from 1700s America, like buildings and everyday objects, also matches written records, helping us understand life back then. The facts about these events are documented and widely agreed upon.
w05.learn: We learn from this event that God can prepare places and people for good things to happen. When a nation is built on freedom, especially freedom to worship, wonderful things can follow. Families can talk about what it means to use that freedom in wise and loving ways, and how to be grateful for those who came before and stood up for what was right. It reminds us that Heavenly Father cares about our freedom to choose and worship.
w05.child: A long time ago, people in America decided they wanted to be free from the king of England. They wrote special rules so everyone could pray and choose how to follow God. Because of this, Joseph Smith could pray and start the Church too.
w05.talk: Why do you think it’s important that people are free to choose how they worship God?

ct01.happened: About five thousand years ago, Uruk became a place unlike any the world had seen before. In the land we now call Iraq, Uruk grew from a cluster of small farming villages into a bustling city. By around 2800 BC, it may have held as many as 80,000 people, making it the largest settlement anywhere on earth at that time. People built huge structures called ziggurats, which were stepped temples made of mud bricks. These were places to worship their gods and gather for important events. Uruk was also the place where humans first invented writing. Using a reed and wet clay, scribes pressed symbols, called cuneiform, onto tablets. These marks helped them keep track of trades and stories. Markets filled with people selling grain, cloth, and pottery, while craftsmen and builders shaped the city's future. With strong walls and organized streets, Uruk stood as a center for trade, religion, art, and government, showing how people could share their ideas and work together in ways that would shape all cities to come.
ct01.background: Before Uruk, most people lived in small farming villages or moved from place to place with their animals. The land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers was rich and good for growing crops, so families started settling there. Water from the rivers helped them grow fields of wheat and barley. People in these villages worked together to dig canals and store food. Over hundreds of years, some villages grew bigger as people shared work and built temples. Eventually, in places like Uruk, the population grew much larger, and people started doing specialized jobs—some farmed, others made pottery, and a few kept records with the new system of writing. Life was busy, with markets, festivals, and worship at the big temple at the heart of the city.
ct01.matters: Uruk matters because it was the first city where so many parts of civilization came together: government, trade, writing, and worship. From its inventions and way of life, we gained tools that still bless families—like writing down stories, laws, and prayers. For people of faith, it is incredible to know that the first scriptures were made possible by the same gift of writing. The growth of cities like Uruk also set the stage for later prophets, including Abraham, to share God’s word and live among people who could record and remember His covenants. It reminds us that even ancient inventions can help us build faith today.
ct01.scripture: Although the city of Uruk is not named in the Bible, Genesis 10:10 speaks of Nimrod’s kingdom and lists Babel, which is identified with Babylon, another great Mesopotamian city. The story shows that cities and kingdoms were part of early human life, where God’s work among His children could unfold. Abraham, who lived in the same land a few centuries later (Genesis 11:31), was called by God in this region. In Latter-day Saint scripture, Abraham 1:1 also speaks of “the land of the Chaldeans.” Principles from these verses show that cities can serve as centers for learning and faith when filled with good purposes.
ct01.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered vast ruins in what is now Warka, Iraq, the ancient city of Uruk. They have found the remains of giant ziggurats, long city walls, and thousands of clay tablets with writing from that time. These discoveries match ancient stories and support the idea that Uruk was indeed the world’s first great city. The oldest layers reveal the earliest cuneiform writing, showing records of trades and temple offerings. Over many years of study, scientists pieced together the story of a place where farming, religion, trade, and culture all met in new ways. While some details, like the exact number of people, are estimates, the evidence for Uruk as the first major city is strong.
ct01.learn: From Uruk, we learn how bringing people together can lead to great new ideas. Living close to others meant people could share what they knew and build things they could not do alone. We also see that inventions, like writing, can be used for both practical needs and for sharing the important things of the heart, including stories of faith. This helps us remember that every good thing we create can be used to bless others as Heavenly Father intends.
ct01.child: Uruk was the very first big city in the world, long before cars or even horses. People there made the first writing by pressing marks into clay, and they built huge temples where they worshipped. Many good things like writing and working together started in cities like Uruk.
ct01.talk: What is something our family could create or share with others if we all worked together, like the people of Uruk did?

ct02.happened: Around 3100 BC, Memphis rose as the first capital of united ancient Egypt. This great city grew near the place where the Nile River divided into its many branches. For more than a thousand years, Memphis was the heart of Egypt’s power—its kings, called pharaohs, ruled from here, shaping laws, religion, and art for the whole land. As Egypt’s center, Memphis was so important that even the famous pyramids at Giza, where pharaohs were buried, were built just outside the city’s reach to honor its rulers. Many travelers and traders came through Memphis, filling its streets with languages and crafts from far places. During the time of the Old Testament, the city was already centuries old. Abraham came to Egypt, likely passing near Memphis. Joseph, who was sold into slavery, ended up serving one of the city’s royal households and became one of its most trusted leaders. Later, Moses was born to a Hebrew family tied to the region, growing up in Pharaoh’s household with the city’s grand temples and palaces all around. Memphis was a place where faith, power, and family histories crossed in ways that would shape the larger story of God’s people.
ct02.background: Memphis was built in a world of villages along the Nile. Before Egypt became one country, separate kings ruled the northern and southern parts of the land. Memphis became the first capital after these kingdoms joined, giving Egypt strong leadership and the ability to create great works like the pyramids. The people of Memphis were skilled farmers, builders, and artists. Daily life for most workers involved growing grain, weaving cloth, making bricks, or building. Religion was very important; they believed their pharaoh was chosen by the gods and helped keep order in the world. Music, festivals, and family life also filled their days. The city stood at the center of travel and trade for hundreds of miles in every direction, and its people saw new things and ideas from all over the ancient world.
ct02.matters: Memphis mattered because it showed how a city could bring people and ideas together to achieve great things, both good and hard. For families of faith, the fact that Abraham, Joseph, and Moses all spent part of their lives in this city is a powerful reminder that God often places His people exactly where they need to be, even in unfamiliar or challenging places. Memphis helped preserve not only food and learning, but the stories and families that shape faith today. Remembering its role helps us see history as Heavenly Father’s work unfolding over time.
ct02.scripture: The story of Joseph’s rise to power in Egypt is found in Genesis chapters 37 to 50. Abraham’s visit to Egypt is told in Genesis 12 and also in Abraham 2. Moses’ early years are described in Exodus chapters 1 and 2. Each passage shows how God guided His servants in Egypt. Joseph’s service in Pharaoh’s court, in particular, is shown as an example of faithfulness and God’s ability to turn hardships into blessings for many.
ct02.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of Memphis, confirming its size and importance. The ruins include temple foundations, statues, and the famous alabaster Sphinx. Ancient records from stone inscriptions and papyrus scrolls back up its role as Egypt’s capital for more than a thousand years. The tombs and pyramids built nearby, especially at Saqqara, show the wealth and skill of its people. While the Bible’s stories of Abraham, Joseph, and Moses are not detailed in Egyptian records, the existence, power, and culture of Memphis during their time are well established. Many historians agree on the city’s influence, though the timeline of the biblical narratives does not perfectly match every archaeological layer, which is common for events so far back in time.
ct02.learn: We learn that cities can be places where God’s work moves forward, even if they sometimes seem overwhelming or foreign. Memphis reminds us that great things often happen when faithful people trust God, even far from home. In family life, Memphis teaches that every place and season—no matter how strange—can be part of God’s plan to help us learn, help others, and carry on His promises.
ct02.child: A long time ago, Memphis was the biggest and most important city in Egypt. People built huge pyramids nearby, and Bible stories tell us that Joseph and Moses lived close to this city. God helped His children, even in this busy place.
ct02.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father put Joseph and Moses in such a big, busy city like Memphis?

ct03.happened: Around the year 1000 BC, Jerusalem was taken by King David, who made it the capital for all the tribes of Israel. Before this, Jerusalem was a small city held by the Jebusites, a local Canaanite tribe. David’s army managed to enter the city using a clever strategy, likely through underground water tunnels. Once gained, Jerusalem became more than just a city—it was a new start for God’s people, a place to unite the twelve tribes under one king. Later, David’s son Solomon built a grand temple there, following God’s command. The temple became a place where Israelites would come from far and wide to worship Heavenly Father, offer sacrifices, and learn His law. Over hundreds of years, Jerusalem rang with the prayers and music of the Psalms and the bold voices of prophets calling the people to remember God. It witnessed triumphs, betrayals, and moments when the people turned back to Heavenly Father. In centuries to follow, it became the setting for the last days of Jesus’s life, His sacrifice, and resurrection. Jerusalem’s name and its sacredness have echoed through history, drawing the attention and devotion of millions and—sometimes—battles over who would call it home.
ct03.background: Before David conquered Jerusalem, it was a city-state belonging to the Jebusites, one of many groups living in the land of Canaan. Israel was a new nation made up of former slaves from Egypt who had wandered in the desert and slowly settled in the land they believed God gave them. Their early life was marked by tent living, simple farming, and herding animals. They built their homes with stone or mud-brick, grew wheat and barley, and kept goats and sheep. Their days started early, working in the fields or tending livestock. Religion was woven into their lives—festivals, prayers, and the commandments given to Moses. Before Jerusalem became Israel’s capital, the people worshipped at the Tabernacle, a movable tent sanctuary, wherever it was set up. With David conquering Jerusalem, Israel gained a city that was both strong and easy to defend, sitting on hills with good water sources.
ct03.matters: Jerusalem still matters deeply because it became a symbol of God’s promises and presence with His people. For families of faith, it reminds us that God keeps His promises and invites His children into covenant with Him. The temple Solomon built there shaped worship for centuries, and its pattern influences Latter-day Saint temples today. The greatest events of Jesus’s earthly mission happened in this city. For the world, Jerusalem remains a spiritual and historical treasure, valued by Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike. Its long story helps us remember that God works His plan in real places, with real people, across many generations.
ct03.scripture: Scriptures like 2 Samuel 5 describe how David took Jerusalem and made it his capital. 1 Kings 6–8 tells of Solomon building the First Temple. The Psalms—many composed in Jerusalem by David and others—invite us to worship in the house of the Lord. In the New Testament, Matthew 21–28 and Acts 2 describe Jesus’s death and resurrection, then Peter’s preaching at Pentecost, all in Jerusalem. Doctrine and Covenants 124:39 connects temple ordinances today to ancient temple worship. The vision of a future holy city is echoed in Revelation 21, where the New Jerusalem descends from heaven.
ct03.evidence: Archaeology has uncovered layers of ancient Jerusalem, showing it was a fortified hill city in David’s time. Excavations have found remains of massive walls and tunnels, including the famous Warren’s Shaft, which might have helped David’s army sneak into the city. Artifacts, including pottery and fortifications from the 10th century BC, match the era of David and Solomon, though the scale and details of the kingdom are still discussed among historians. Ancient texts outside the Bible rarely mention David directly, but records like the Tel Dan Stele refer to the 'House of David,' offering historic support for his dynasty. Scholars agree Jerusalem was a major city by Solomon’s time, serving as a center for religion and government.
ct03.learn: From Jerusalem’s story, we learn that Heavenly Father often works His greatest miracles in ordinary places and through imperfect people. The city saw times of faith and failure, peace and conflict, but God’s promises moved forward. Like the people there, we can choose to make our homes places where God’s spirit can dwell. We also see that what we do in faith can have lasting effects far beyond our own lifetimes.
ct03.child: A long time ago, King David made Jerusalem the special city for his people, and King Solomon built a beautiful temple there. Jesus visited and taught in Jerusalem, and some important things in His life happened there. Many people still care about Jerusalem today, and it helps us remember God’s promises.
ct03.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father chose special places for His work, like Jerusalem or the temples today?

ct04.happened: Around 600 BC, the city of Babylon reached the height of its greatness under King Nebuchadnezzar II. Babylon became not only the largest city in the world, possibly home to as many as 200,000 people, but also the richest, most splendid, and most influential. Its walls were tall and thick, decorated with bright blue tiles and roaring lions on the famous Ishtar Gate. Inside the city, myths say, the Hanging Gardens stood—lush with plants and water even in the desert, though today historians debate if they truly existed. Babylon was famous for its temples and ziggurats, grand stair-stepped towers reaching for the sky, and for canals that made the city green. Nebuchadnezzar conquered far and wide, capturing Jerusalem, destroying its temple, and bringing many Israelites—including Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—into captivity. Daniel and his friends ended up serving right in the king’s court, where their faith would be tested again and again. Later, the prophet Isaiah would declare, remarkably, that Cyrus of Persia would someday conquer Babylon—over a century before it took place. Babylon’s power and beauty made it legendary, but also turned it into a symbol of worldliness and pride.
ct04.background: Babylon sat in what is today Iraq, along the Euphrates River. The people were very skilled builders, artists, and scholars. Before reaching its peak, Babylon had a long history, often being ruled by powerful kings and sometimes falling to other empires, like the Assyrians. Daily life in Babylon included crowded markets, busy streets, grand religious festivals, and bustling workshops. The people worshipped many gods in large temples and followed complex laws. Families lived in mud-brick houses and wore clothes of linen or wool. Many could read and write, using clay tablets. Babylon attracted people from many lands, so its streets were filled with many languages, trades, and customs. It was a busy, brilliant place at the heart of its world.
ct04.matters: Babylon matters as an example of how worldly power and culture can rise to amazing heights, and yet still fall. For families of faith, the story of Babylon reminds us that no matter where we live—even if it’s the most powerful or impressive city—following God is always possible, as Daniel and his friends showed. Babylon also stands in scripture as a symbol of worldly pride and opposition to God, reminding us to seek after heavenly things first. Its history helps us think about how we use our own gifts and influence in a world full of choices.
ct04.scripture: The Book of Daniel (Daniel 1–6) tells the story of Daniel and his friends in Babylon, showing their faithfulness to God in a foreign land. 2 Kings 24–25 and 2 Chronicles 36 describe Babylon’s conquest of Jerusalem and the temple’s destruction. Isaiah 44:28–45:1 names Cyrus as the future conqueror of Babylon long before it happens. Jeremiah 29 records a letter to those taken to Babylon, teaching them to seek the peace of their new city while holding to their faith. Revelation 18 later uses 'Babylon' to stand for worldly pride and wickedness. The Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants also warn against 'Babylon' as a symbol of worldliness (1 Nephi 13:9, D&C 133:14).
ct04.evidence: Archaeological digs in Iraq have uncovered much of ancient Babylon, including remains of grand gates, walls, temples, and the foundations of the ziggurat called Etemenanki, often connected to the Tower of Babel. The Ishtar Gate, with its beautiful blue tiles and images of lions and dragons, has been reconstructed in museums. Cuneiform tablets tell us about Babylonian laws, markets, and daily life. There is strong evidence that Nebuchadnezzar II ruled a vast empire from Babylon, and that Jerusalem was destroyed around 587 BC as recorded. However, the existence of the Hanging Gardens is debated—no clear archaeological remains have been found, and some historians suggest they might have been in another city. Still, the overall picture of Babylon’s power and culture is well supported by many findings.
ct04.learn: From Babylon, we learn that even in the world’s busiest, brightest places, we can live and stand for what is right, just as Daniel and his friends did. Great cities and cultures can inspire beauty but also tempt us to forget God. Moments of change and challenge can become chances for faith and courage. Heavenly Father often puts His servants in the very heart of the world’s troubles, so that their light can shine.
ct04.child: Babylon was once the biggest, richest city in the world, with tall towers, lions on the gates, and huge gardens. Daniel was taken there and chose to follow God, even when it was hard. He showed that we can be brave and true, no matter where we live.
ct04.talk: What do you think helped Daniel stay true to Heavenly Father while living in such a big, different city?

ct05.happened: During the years from about 480 to 400 BC, Athens became a shining center for thinking, learning, and creating. In this time, known as the Classical Age, the city welcomed some of the world’s most famous minds. Socrates walked the streets, talking with young men and asking questions that made everyone think deeply about truth, goodness, and justice. Plato, his student, wrote these conversations down and started a school called the Academy. Aristotle, Plato’s student, became one of the greatest teachers and scientists, who studied everything from plants to stars. At this same time, Athens was alive with the voices of playwrights like Sophocles—who wrote plays still read today—and historians like Herodotus and Thucydides, who carefully collected stories and facts about the past. People built grand temples like the Parthenon, shared ideas in open meetings, and shaped the meaning of democracy. This city became a place where the search for truth and beauty was central to life, and its influence has lasted for centuries.
ct05.background: Before Athens rose to greatness, Greece was made up of many small cities called city-states. These cities often argued or even fought each other, but they shared a language, customs, and stories of ancient gods. Most people in Athens lived in simple homes and worked as farmers, craftsmen, or traders. In the years just before its golden age, Athens had survived great danger during wars with Persia. After these battles, Athenians built their city even more beautifully and confidently. At home, freedom of speech and open discussion were important—citizens would gather in assemblies to vote and debate on what was best for the city. Most families lived simply, and while some could vote, many—including women, slaves, and foreigners—could not. Yet curiosity about the world and the power of ideas filled Athens with energy.
ct05.matters: Athens left a treasure of ideas that still matter today. Its thinkers gave the world many of the questions and words we use to talk about right and wrong, about how to build strong communities, and about the nature of God and the soul. For families of faith, Athens shows how Heavenly Father can prepare people with questions and wisdom before full answers come. When Paul later spoke in Athens, he used the language and ideas the Athenians loved, showing us how God can work through any culture to teach His truths. Even though not every answer from Athens was right, the honest searching for truth is something God values and can use to bless His children.
ct05.scripture: Acts 17 tells how Paul came to Athens and taught on Mars Hill, speaking to philosophers about the 'Unknown God' and explaining God's true nature as the Creator who can be found by those who seek Him. This story shows an apostle using the questions and words the Athenians understood to point them toward Jesus. In Proverbs 4:7, the Bible teaches, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' This principle honors honest searching for truth, showing that Heavenly Father values wise questions and thoughtful learning.
ct05.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered much of ancient Athens, including the remains of the Parthenon and the Agora, where people gathered to talk and decide what happened in the city. Writings from Athenians themselves, like those of Plato, Aristotle, Herodotus, and Thucydides, have been copied and passed down to us, giving a clear window into their thoughts and debates. Inscriptions, statues, and buildings from Athens back up many stories told in history books. While it's hard to know every detail about Athenian daily life, there is strong evidence that Athens in the 5th century BC was a lively, thoughtful place at the heart of the ancient Greek world.
ct05.learn: We can learn from Athens that Heavenly Father values learning and seeking wisdom. Asking questions, studying carefully, and discussing ideas can help us grow—especially when those habits lead us closer to truth and to God. The story of Athens shows how God can plant good seeds of knowledge in many places, preparing the world for even greater light through His prophets and through Jesus Christ.
ct05.child: A long time ago in Athens, people loved to ask big questions and learn new things. They talked about right and wrong, built beautiful temples, and wrote plays. Even though they didn’t know everything about God, their search for answers helped many people later on, including when Paul taught about Jesus there.
ct05.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to ask questions and learn new things?

ct06.happened: Rome rose from a group of villages by the Tiber River to become the largest and most influential city in Western history for hundreds of years. Around 44 BC, Rome was already the heart of a vast empire stretching from Britain to Egypt. Over one million people may have lived there at its peak, making Rome the biggest, busiest city of the ancient world. Its grand roads connected far-away lands, allowing messages, goods, and people to travel faster and safer than ever before. Rome’s government developed laws and systems that shaped what we now call Western civilization. But Rome was not just about power and armies. It became a place where different cultures, ideas, and faiths met. It was also in Rome where two of Jesus Christ’s Apostles, Peter and Paul, came to preach the gospel. Both gave their lives there for their testimony of Christ, sparking the growth of Christianity even under threat. Over time, the very city where the gospel was once fiercely persecuted became the center of the Christian world, as Roman leaders later accepted Christianity and made it the empire’s official religion. To this day, the Vatican—the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church—sits in the heart of Rome, showing how deep and lasting the city’s religious influence is.
ct06.background: Before Rome, Italy was home to groups like the Etruscans and Greeks, who built cities and traded across the sea. Most Romans were farmers, soldiers, merchants, or builders. Daily life in Rome was busy: markets thrived, schools taught Greek and Latin, and homes ranged from little apartments to grand villas. The empire ran on the work of free citizens, women, and many enslaved people from conquered lands. People worshipped Roman gods like Jupiter and Mars, but the city’s many cultures brought new beliefs, such as Judaism and later Christianity. Emperors ruled after Julius Caesar, commanding both respect and fear. Despite wars and famines, Rome’s public baths, aqueducts, and forums made city life lively. The peace known as ‘Pax Romana’ helped people travel and share ideas across the empire, which allowed the spread of new faiths like the gospel of Christ.
ct06.matters: Rome matters because it set the stage for much of our world today, especially in government, law, and religion. For families of faith, the story of Rome reminds us how Heavenly Father can use even powerful empires to prepare the way for His gospel. The roads, peace, and shared language of Rome helped Apostles like Peter and Paul teach about Jesus to people from many lands. The seeds of Christianity that were planted in trial and hardship in Rome eventually grew to bless millions, showing that truth and faith can flourish even in hard places.
ct06.scripture: The New Testament tells of Paul’s journey to Rome, his preaching, and his time as a prisoner there (Acts 28). Peter also spent his final years in Rome, as hinted in his epistles (1 Peter 5:13). In Doctrine and Covenants 64:33, we learn that “out of small things proceedeth that which is great,” which fits how the gospel quietly spread through the great city of Rome. These scriptures remind us that great changes in history often begin with faithful acts by ordinary people, even in times of trial.
ct06.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found much evidence of Rome’s size, organization, and religious history. Ancient texts by writers like Tacitus, Suetonius, and Luke (in Acts) describe daily life and events. Archaeological digs have uncovered streets, shops, temples, Christian catacombs, and the remains of the Colosseum, showing how many people lived and worshipped in Rome. The existence of the Vatican and centuries-old churches confirms that Christianity took root in the city soon after the time of Peter and Paul. Coins and inscriptions also prove how laws, language, and faith spread across the Roman world. Scholars agree that Rome’s influence continued long after its political fall in 476 AD, mainly through the Christian church and preserved Roman culture.
ct06.learn: We can learn that God can use all people and places, even those that seem hard or unlikely, for good. Rome reminds us that faith is not stopped by trials—and that the tools of the world (like roads, language, and even governments) can serve God’s plans if we use them well. Just as early Saints in Rome kept the faith despite danger, we can look for ways to share and live the gospel in our own communities, using every resource for good.
ct06.child: Rome was the biggest city in the world back then, with so many people and grand buildings. Peter and Paul went there to teach about Jesus, even though it was dangerous. Because of brave people like them, the gospel spread all across the world.
ct06.talk: How do you think Peter and Paul felt teaching about Jesus in such a big and powerful city?

ct07.happened: In the year 330 AD, the Roman Emperor Constantine made a bold decision to build a brand new capital city for his empire. He chose the ancient Greek city of Byzantium and rebuilt it, naming it Constantinople after himself. This city was placed on land that sits right between Europe and Asia, which made it perfect for trade, travel, and protecting the empire’s borders. Over time, Constantinople became one of the richest and most powerful cities in the world. It was known for its strong walls, wonderful markets, and beautiful churches. The most famous building was the Hagia Sophia, a church with an enormous dome, completed in 537 AD. For over a thousand years, Constantinople was the heart of the Byzantine Empire and the main center of Eastern Orthodox Christianity. In 1453, after months of siege, the city finally fell to the Ottoman Turks. The fall of Constantinople marked the end of the medieval era for Europe and changed history forever.
ct07.background: When Constantine chose Byzantium for his new city, the Roman Empire was already very old and too big to manage easily. Many people spoke Greek in the east, and Latin in the west. Constantine wanted a fresh start for the empire, away from Rome’s old problems. Life in Constantinople was busy and full of new ideas. People from many nations lived and traded there. The city roads were filled with traders selling spices, silks, and foods from far-off lands. Families lived in houses close together, and most people would visit markets, churches, and public baths. They also spent time in grand places like the Hippodrome, where chariot races took place. Daily life mixed Roman traditions with Christian faith, and the city’s leaders worked to keep the peace and care for the people.
ct07.matters: Constantinople matters because it became a bridge between worlds—between East and West, old and new. It preserved ancient knowledge and Christian faith during times when much of western Europe was struggling. When the city fell in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Europe, bringing precious old books with them. These books helped spark the Renaissance, a time of great learning. The Renaissance led to the invention of the printing press, which made it easier for people to read the Bible for themselves. This helped create space for important changes in Christianity and made it possible for the world to hear the message of the Restoration. For families of faith, it is a powerful example of how even hard things like the fall of a city can bring unexpected blessings.
ct07.scripture: Though the scriptures do not mention Constantinople directly, the principle of God using events for good is woven throughout. In Romans 8:28, Paul teaches that "all things work together for good to them that love God." In the Book of Mormon, Ether 12:4 shares how faith can lead to hope and good things, even in times of destruction or trial. Doctrine and Covenants 1:17-23 also speaks of God preparing the way for the Restoration, showing how He works through history to bring about His purposes.
ct07.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found much evidence for the story of Constantinople. Written histories from both Christian and Muslim sources describe the city’s rise and its dramatic fall in detail. Travelers and merchants wrote about its crowded markets and sturdy walls. The walls and buildings, like the Hagia Sophia, still stand in Istanbul today, showing the skill of ancient builders. Archaeologists have dug up coins, art, and tools that belonged to the people who lived there. The movement of Greek scholars and their books after the fall of the city is well documented, and historians agree that this greatly influenced the Renaissance in Western Europe.
ct07.learn: We can learn that even when big changes happen—like the fall of a great city—Heavenly Father can use them to help His work move forward in unexpected ways. He can turn something that seems like a loss into a new start, blessing many people. Just as Constantinople’s fall helped bring new knowledge to the world, hard times in our lives can lead to unexpected blessings when we trust in God’s plan.
ct07.child: A wise emperor built a city called Constantinople to be strong and full of beautiful buildings. For over a thousand years, it stood where Europe and Asia meet. When the city was taken by others, it helped spread important books and ideas that changed the world.
ct07.talk: Why do you think God sometimes uses hard things to help good things happen later?

ct08.happened: Around the year 800, Baghdad was at its brightest moment under the Abbasid Caliphate. The city became the largest in the world, growing quickly because it was the heart of a vast empire stretching across lands that today include Iraq, Iran, Syria, and Egypt. Scholars from across Asia, Africa, and Europe gathered here, drawn by the promise of learning and discovery. The famous House of Wisdom was not just a library—it was a research center where people worked together to translate and preserve important books from Greek, Roman, Indian, and Persian writers. New ideas came alive in medicine, astronomy, algebra, and more. People in Baghdad worked carefully to keep old knowledge safe and to make new discoveries, advancing science in a way that wouldn’t be matched for many centuries. The city’s streets bustled with traders, families, poets, scientists, and craftsmen, all part of a living tapestry of faiths and cultures. The work done here was so important that when Europe entered difficult times—often called the Dark Ages—much of what was known about math, science, and philosophy was saved by the scholars of Baghdad, ready to be rediscovered later by others searching for truth.
ct08.background: Before Baghdad rose to greatness, much of the learning of Greece and Rome had already faded from daily life in Europe, partly due to invasions and unstable times. The people of the Abbasid Caliphate, whose leaders followed Islam, spoke Arabic and came from many lands, bringing their traditions, foods, and beliefs with them. The caliphs loved learning, so they invited scholars of all backgrounds: Muslims, Christians, Jews, and others, to join them. Daily life in Baghdad was lively and colorful. Markets sold silks and spices. Children learned to read and write. The city’s location on the Tigris River helped it grow wealthy, and its grand buildings and peaceful gardens were famous. Parents and children, just like today, hoped for a safe, good life and enjoyed stories and celebrations. The city’s people believed that seeking knowledge was pleasing to God.
ct08.matters: Baghdad’s work matters because it kept much of the world’s knowledge alive so that it could later be shared in new ways. Heavenly Father loves all His children and uses people in many places to help further His work. The advances of Baghdad—algebra, scientific method, medicine—are still helping us today, from the classroom to the doctor’s office. For families of faith, it is humbling to see how God guided many hands and hearts, sometimes far away from our own beliefs, to prepare the world for future times of learning and faith.
ct08.scripture: The scriptures teach about the value of knowledge and wisdom, even if these verses do not directly mention Baghdad. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, the Lord commands us to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." Proverbs 4:7 tells us: "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." These verses show that Heavenly Father values knowledge wherever it is found and encourages us to seek it diligently. The story of Baghdad fits with this principle—it is a place where people worked together to seek understanding and preserve precious truths.
ct08.evidence: Many historical records support Baghdad’s leading role in learning during the Abbasid period. The names of scholars, their books, and their discoveries are found in manuscripts and catalogs preserved in libraries from East to West. The House of Wisdom and stories of its translation movement are described by both Muslim and non-Muslim writers. Archaeologists have uncovered remnants of Baghdad’s old walls, buildings, and objects showing the city’s wealth and culture. Although not every story about the House of Wisdom can be proven in detail, historians agree that Baghdad was the center for science, translation, and math at this time, and its influence stretched well beyond its walls.
ct08.learn: From Baghdad’s example, we learn that God cares about knowledge and works through many peoples and cultures—sometimes in ways not easy to see at the time. The gifts of math, science, and understanding are blessings meant to help all people, not just one nation or faith. Seeking knowledge honors Heavenly Father and prepares us to help others. We also learn to be grateful for the work of those who came before, preserving truth even in difficult times.
ct08.child: Baghdad was once the biggest, busiest city in the world, where people gathered to learn and share ideas. Smart helpers saved many important books there, which has helped us learn about math and science today. God wants us to keep learning and sharing good things.
ct08.talk: How do you think learning and sharing ideas can help people, even if they come from different countries or religions?

ct09.happened: Between 1550 and 1900, London transformed from a medieval city into the world's largest metropolis. In the mid-16th century, it was a bustling center of trade and culture, with a population of about 70,000. By 1600, this number had nearly tripled to 200,000, and by 1800, it had soared to over a million. This rapid growth was fueled by its expanding role in global commerce and the establishment of trading companies like the East India Company in 1600. London became the heart of the British Empire, overseeing colonies across continents. The city was also a hub of religious and cultural change. The King James Bible, commissioned in 1604 and completed in 1611, was produced in London, providing an English translation of the scriptures that would influence Christian worship for centuries. Additionally, the Puritans, seeking religious freedom, departed from London's ports in the early 17th century, leading to the establishment of settlements in the New World. The Industrial Revolution, which began in the late 18th century, saw London's factories and industries flourish, further cementing its status as a global powerhouse.
ct09.background: In the mid-16th century, London was a city on the brink of transformation. The English Reformation was reshaping religious practices, leading to the dissolution of monasteries and the redistribution of church lands. This period also saw the rise of Protestantism, with London at its epicenter due to its commercial ties with Protestant regions in Europe and its vibrant print industry. Daily life was marked by a growing population, with migrants from rural areas and abroad seeking opportunities in the city. The streets were bustling with merchants, artisans, and traders, and the River Thames was a vital artery for commerce. The city's expansion beyond its medieval walls began, setting the stage for its future growth.
ct09.matters: London's evolution during this period had profound implications for the world and for families of faith. The production of the King James Bible in London provided a unified English translation of the scriptures, making the word of God more accessible to English-speaking believers. The Puritans' journey from London to the New World laid the foundation for religious communities seeking freedom and self-governance. The spread of the English language, facilitated by London's global influence, prepared the way for the Restoration's messages to reach a vast audience. This period underscores how Heavenly Father can use the developments of nations and cities to further His work and bring His children closer to Him.
ct09.scripture: The scriptures remind us of the importance of spreading the word of God to all nations. In Matthew 28:19-20, Jesus commands His disciples to "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations..." The production of the King James Bible in London and the subsequent spread of the English language align with this divine directive, enabling the gospel to reach a broader audience. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 90:11 speaks of every person hearing the gospel in their own tongue, emphasizing the significance of language in sharing the Lord's message.
ct09.evidence: Historical records and scholarly research provide ample evidence of London's growth and influence during this period. Studies indicate that London's population grew from about 70,000 in 1550 to 200,000 by 1600, and continued to expand rapidly thereafter. The establishment of trading companies like the East India Company in 1600 highlights London's central role in global commerce. The commissioning and completion of the King James Bible between 1604 and 1611 in London is well-documented, showcasing the city's pivotal role in religious history. These developments are corroborated by various historical sources and academic studies.
ct09.learn: From London's transformation, we learn that cities and nations can be instruments in Heavenly Father's plan. The spread of the English language and the production of the King James Bible in London facilitated the dissemination of the gospel to a wider audience. This teaches us that even amidst political and social changes, the Lord's work progresses, and He prepares ways for His children to receive His word.
ct09.child: Long ago, London grew from a small city into a big one, becoming very important. People there made a special English Bible called the King James Bible, so more people could read God's word. This helped many people learn about Jesus.
ct09.talk: How do you think having the Bible in English helped people learn about Jesus?

ct10.happened: In the sweltering summer of 1776, Philadelphia became the heart of a brave new idea. Men from the thirteen American colonies gathered at the Pennsylvania State House, known today as Independence Hall, to decide how they wanted to govern themselves. These men, called delegates, came from many places, brought different beliefs, and faced great risk, but they shared a deep desire for liberty. On July 4, after much debate, they approved and signed the Declaration of Independence. This document announced to the world that the colonies were no longer part of the British Empire, but free and independent states. Eleven years later, in the same city, many of these leaders gathered again to write a new set of laws for the country, called the Constitution. These documents spelled out freedoms and rights that had never existed before at such a scale—most importantly, the right for people to choose their leaders, speak freely, and worship according to their conscience. That summer in Philadelphia set the foundation for a nation built on liberty.
ct10.background: Before 1776, the American colonies were governed by Great Britain, a powerful empire across the Atlantic Ocean. Life in the colonies was often hard; people farmed, built small towns, and lived under strict British laws. Over time, colonists grew frustrated with rules that limited their freedoms, like taxes they had to pay without having a say in how the money was used. The people involved in writing the Declaration and Constitution were generally educated men—farmers, lawyers, merchants—who felt a duty to secure liberty for themselves and their children. Philadelphia was then the largest city in North America, a busy place filled with people from many backgrounds, and a hub for new ideas. It was the natural place for leaders to meet and dream big.
ct10.matters: This event is so important because it gave birth to religious freedom in America. The ideas agreed upon in Philadelphia meant people could worship as they wished, without fear of the government stopping them. For families who believe God has a plan for nations, this freedom was essential for the Restoration of the gospel and the growth of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The Declaration and Constitution built a society where faith can thrive, and where missionaries could one day travel freely, sharing what they know is true.
ct10.scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 says that God raised up wise men to write the laws protecting rights and freedom. Many members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints see this as Heavenly Father preparing the way for the Restoration, allowing Joseph Smith to teach and organize the Church in safety. The Bible also teaches about liberty, such as in Galatians 5:1, where Paul reminds us to "stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free." These scriptures show that freedom to choose and worship is a gift from God.
ct10.evidence: There is strong historical evidence for these events. The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution are preserved and displayed in museums. Letters, journals, and notes from the men who attended the meetings give us a clear picture of what happened day by day. Independence Hall still stands in Philadelphia, and historians have carefully studied its records. Over the centuries, these documents have been read, debated, and upheld in courts and government. The facts surrounding the signing, the people involved, and the intent of their meetings are all supported by solid historical records and artifacts.
ct10.learn: From Philadelphia’s story, we learn that freedom doesn’t happen by accident. It comes when people work together, guided by their beliefs and a vision for something better. Heavenly Father prepares places and people for His work, sometimes in ways no one expects. When we use our freedom to do good, we honor the sacrifices of those who made it possible and help continue God’s work on earth.
ct10.child: Philadelphia is where brave people met to write America’s most important rules, giving everyone freedom to choose and believe. They worked hard so we could worship, speak, and learn safely. Because of their work, we can live our faith and help others too.
ct10.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wanted us to have freedom to choose and worship?

ct11.happened: In the year 1820, near the frontier town of Palmyra, New York, a young boy named Joseph Smith Jr. went into a quiet grove of trees near his family’s farm to pray. He was worried and confused about which church to join. As he knelt to ask God for help, something miraculous happened: Joseph said he saw Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ, who told him not to join any of the churches, for the true Church would be restored. This event is called the First Vision. Later, Joseph was led to a hill nearby, the Hill Cumorah, where he said he found ancient golden plates buried in the earth. These plates, translated by Joseph through the gift and power of God, became the Book of Mormon. The first copies of this new scripture were printed in Palmyra, in the shop of E.B. Grandin, making the town a beginning place for the Restoration of Jesus Christ’s gospel in the latter days.
ct11.background: Palmyra in the 1820s was a small but growing town, home to about 4,000 people. It was part of the American frontier, filled with farms, thick forests, and new settlers seeking land and opportunity. Life was humble: families grew much of their own food, children helped with chores, and people gathered to read the Bible and pray together. New religious ideas and revivals were common—many people wanted to know which church to follow and how to find God. The Erie Canal, then being built, would soon make Palmyra a busy place for trade and travel. The Smiths, like many others, worked hard and turned to faith for answers to life's hardest questions.
ct11.matters: For millions of Latter-day Saints, the events in Palmyra mark the return of living prophets and the restoration of lost gospel truths. The humble setting shows that Heavenly Father can work through ordinary people in everyday places—He does not require great wealth, power, or fame. For families today, Palmyra reminds us that God knows and loves each of His children, and that prayer and faith can bring miracles and answers, even in quiet or unlikely places.
ct11.scripture: The story of the First Vision is told in Joseph Smith—History 1:14–20 in the Pearl of Great Price. This scripture teaches about asking God for wisdom, just as found in James 1:5, which inspired Joseph to pray. The Book of Mormon, which began its journey in Palmyra, is another testament of Jesus Christ and is spoken of in 2 Nephi 3 and Doctrine and Covenants 20, which discuss the bringing forth of new scripture and the Restoration.
ct11.evidence: Historical records strongly support the existence of early nineteenth-century Palmyra, the Smith family, and the publication of the Book of Mormon by E.B. Grandin in 1830. The grove of trees (now called the Sacred Grove) and the Smith farm can still be visited. While there is no physical evidence for the heavenly vision Joseph described, many documents, letters, and accounts from family, friends, and neighbors support that Joseph shared this story from a young age. The printing press used and the first edition of the Book of Mormon are preserved and can be seen today. The details of Joseph's vision are matters of religious experience, but the setting, people, and printing of the book are well documented.
ct11.learn: We can learn that God can answer sincere prayers in unexpected but simple ways. Great things often start with small acts of faith. The story also teaches us to seek out truth directly from God and to trust that answers can come, even when we feel ordinary. Just as the Smith family turned to the scriptures and prayer, we can find guidance and hope, wherever we live.
ct11.child: Joseph Smith was a boy who prayed in the woods and saw Heavenly Father and Jesus. He later found a special book hidden in a hill nearby. God can talk to anyone who asks with a sincere heart.
ct11.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father answered Joseph Smith’s prayer in a quiet, simple place instead of a big city?

ct12.happened: In the summer of 1847, after enduring years of persecution and displacement, Brigham Young led a group of 148 pioneers—comprising 143 men, three women, and two children—on a journey westward in search of a sanctuary where they could practice their faith freely. Departing from Winter Quarters, Nebraska, in April, they traversed over 1,000 miles across the Great Plains and the Rocky Mountains. On July 24, 1847, Brigham Young, who had been delayed by illness, entered the Salt Lake Valley and, upon surveying the landscape, is reported to have declared, "This is the right place, drive on." The pioneers immediately began preparations for the arrival of thousands more Saints, laying out the city and initiating irrigation projects to make the arid land cultivable. This marked the founding of Salt Lake City, which would become the headquarters of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
ct12.background: Prior to the arrival of the Latter-day Saint pioneers, the Salt Lake Valley was inhabited by Indigenous groups, including the Northwestern Shoshone and the Western Goshute. These communities utilized the valley for hunting and gathering but did not establish permanent settlements there. The mid-19th century was a period of westward expansion in the United States, with many seeking new opportunities and religious freedom. The Latter-day Saints, facing severe persecution in the eastern states, sought a remote location where they could establish a community based on their religious principles without external interference.
ct12.matters: The establishment of Salt Lake City was a pivotal moment for the Latter-day Saints, providing a secure base from which the Church could grow and flourish. It demonstrated the resilience and faith of the pioneers, who transformed a barren desert into a thriving community. For families of faith, this event underscores the importance of perseverance, unity, and trust in divine guidance when facing challenges. The city's founding also highlights the significance of creating spaces where religious freedom can be exercised and communities can thrive.
ct12.scripture: The journey and settlement of the Latter-day Saint pioneers resonate with scriptural themes of faith and divine guidance. In the Book of Mormon, Lehi's family embarks on a journey to a promised land, relying on the Lord's direction (1 Nephi 2:2-4). Similarly, the Doctrine and Covenants speaks of gathering to designated places for safety and spiritual growth (Doctrine and Covenants 101:20-21). These passages reflect the pioneers' belief that they were led by God to the Salt Lake Valley to establish a place of peace and worship.
ct12.evidence: Historical records, including journals and official Church documents, provide detailed accounts of the pioneers' journey and the founding of Salt Lake City. The National Park Service documents the 1847 trek, noting the organized nature of the migration and the immediate efforts to cultivate the land upon arrival. Additionally, the Church's own historical resources offer insights into the experiences and challenges faced by the pioneers during this period. These sources collectively affirm the events surrounding the establishment of Salt Lake City.
ct12.learn: The story of the pioneers teaches us the value of faith, determination, and community. It reminds us that, even in the face of adversity, trusting in divine guidance and working together can lead to the creation of something enduring and meaningful. This history encourages us to support one another and to remain steadfast in our beliefs, knowing that challenges can be overcome through unity and perseverance.
ct12.child: A long time ago, a group of people called pioneers traveled a very long way to find a new home where they could live peacefully and follow their faith. They worked hard together to build a city in a place that was dry and empty, turning it into a beautiful place to live.
ct12.talk: Why do you think the pioneers were willing to travel so far and work so hard to build a new home?
