w001.happened: The Greco-Persian Wars were a series of conflicts between the Persian Empire and Greek city-states, occurring from 499 to 449 BC. The initial spark was the Ionian Revolt (499–493 BC), where Greek cities in Asia Minor rebelled against Persian rule. Athens and Eretria supported this revolt, leading to Persian King Darius I's desire for retribution. In 490 BC, Darius launched the first Persian invasion of Greece, culminating in the Battle of Marathon, where the Athenians achieved a surprising victory. A decade later, Darius's son, Xerxes I, led a massive invasion. The Greeks, under Spartan King Leonidas, made a legendary stand at Thermopylae but were ultimately overcome. However, the Greek navy, commanded by Themistocles, secured a decisive victory at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC. The following year, Greek forces triumphed at the Battle of Plataea, effectively ending Persian ambitions in Greece. These victories ensured the survival and flourishing of Greek civilization.
w001.background: In the late 6th century BC, the Persian Empire, under Cyrus the Great and later Darius I, expanded its vast territories, encompassing diverse cultures and regions, including the Greek-inhabited areas of Ionia. The Greeks, organized into independent city-states like Athens and Sparta, valued their autonomy and democratic practices. Daily life in these city-states revolved around agriculture, trade, and civic participation. The Persian approach of appointing local tyrants to govern the Greek cities in Ionia led to unrest, as the Greeks resisted external control and sought to preserve their way of life.
w001.matters: The Greek victories in the Greco-Persian Wars were pivotal in preserving their unique culture, political structures, and philosophies. This cultural preservation had profound implications for the development of Western civilization. For families of faith, these events underscore the importance of resilience and unity in the face of overwhelming challenges. The survival of Greek language and thought provided a foundation for the dissemination of the gospel centuries later, as the New Testament was written in Koine Greek, making it accessible to a broad audience across the Mediterranean world.
w001.scripture: While the Bible does not directly reference the Greco-Persian Wars, the principle of God's providence in guiding nations and events is evident throughout scripture. In Acts 17:26, Paul speaks of God determining the times and boundaries of nations, suggesting a divine hand in historical events. This aligns with the belief that the preservation of Greek culture and language was instrumental in the spread of the gospel, as the New Testament was written in Koine Greek, facilitating its reach across diverse populations.
w001.evidence: Historical records from both Greek and Persian sources, including Herodotus's 'Histories,' provide detailed accounts of the Greco-Persian Wars. Archaeological findings, such as weaponry and fortifications, corroborate these narratives. The widespread use of Koine Greek in the Eastern Mediterranean during the first century AD is well-documented, with numerous manuscripts of the New Testament written in this dialect, indicating its role as the lingua franca of the time.
w001.learn: The Greco-Persian Wars teach us the value of courage, unity, and the defense of one's principles against formidable challenges. They remind us that the preservation of culture and language can have far-reaching impacts, influencing future generations and the spread of transformative ideas, such as the teachings of Christ.
w001.child: A long time ago, the Greeks fought to keep their homes safe from a big empire called Persia. They worked together and won, which helped keep their way of life and language alive. Later, this language was used to write about Jesus, so many people could learn about Him.
w001.talk: Why do you think it's important to stand up for what you believe in, even when it's hard?

w002.happened: The Punic Wars were a series of three major wars fought between Rome and Carthage over a period of more than 100 years, from 264 to 146 BC. Carthage was a powerful city in North Africa that controlled much of the western Mediterranean. Rome was growing fast and wanted to have more influence. The first Punic War started because both cities wanted control of the island of Sicily. After more than 20 years of fighting, Rome won and took control of Sicily. The second war is famous for the Carthaginian general Hannibal, who led his soldiers and elephants over the Alps to surprise the Romans. Even though Hannibal won many battles, Rome did not give up. The Romans, led by Scipio Africanus, eventually defeated Carthage near their own city. The third Punic War happened because Rome still saw Carthage as a threat, so they attacked and destroyed the city completely. More than a million people are thought to have died in these wars, and Carthage was wiped out as a power. After Rome won, they controlled much of the Mediterranean and built strong roads so their army could move quickly and their empire would be safe.
w002.background: Long before the Punic Wars, the Mediterranean world was a busy place full of traders, farmers, and soldiers. The people of Carthage were great sailors and traders, coming from Phoenician settlers. They grew rich from trade and had colonies all over North Africa, Spain, and some islands. The Romans started as a small city on the Tiber River in Italy. As Rome grew stronger, it slowly took over its neighbors. By the time of the Punic Wars, Rome and Carthage were the two most powerful cities in the western Mediterranean. People lived in stone houses or mud-brick homes. Many worked on farms or traded goods like grain, oil, and wine. Most people walked everywhere, but armies traveled on dirt paths that later became important Roman roads.
w002.matters: The Punic Wars matter because their outcome shaped the world that Jesus and His apostles entered. They helped Rome become the greatest power in the region, making the Pax Romana, a long period of peace and stability. The Romans built safe roads across their empire for soldiers, but later these roads helped missionaries like the Apostle Paul travel and share the gospel. For families of faith, it reminds us that even big, difficult events in history can play a part in God’s work and in preparing the world for His message.
w002.scripture: The Bible does not mention the Punic Wars directly, but the Apostle Paul’s journeys across the Roman world are recorded in Acts 13–21. Paul, called by God, used Roman roads and ships built for empire safety. In Doctrine and Covenants 1:23, we are reminded that the Lord works through all nations and prepares the way for His purposes. The wars show us how God can use even the actions of many people over hundreds of years to prepare the earth for His gospel to move forward.
w002.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered the ruins of Carthage in modern-day Tunisia, showing a city with strong walls and busy marketplaces. Roman records and writings tell us about the wars, the leaders, and the battles, especially about Hannibal’s daring march with elephants into Italy. Ancient coins and weapons have been found, confirming much of the story. Some details—like the numbers involved—are still debated, but the main facts are well-supported by both Roman and Carthaginian sources from the time and confirmed with physical evidence dug from the ground.
w002.learn: From the Punic Wars, we learn that the choices of nations and leaders can shape history for centuries. We also see that Heavenly Father can use even the tools and plans of powerful empires to prepare for His messengers and His teachings. As families, we can trust that the Lord sees the bigger picture and can use even hard times for His good purposes.
w002.child: A long time ago, Rome and Carthage fought three big wars. Rome won, built strong roads, and later those roads helped Paul and other early Christians tell people about Jesus. God used things from those wars to help His work later.
w002.talk: How do you think something that looks like a problem, like a war, could ever help something good happen later?

w003.happened: In the year 70 AD, the Roman armies, under the leadership of General Titus, captured the city of Jerusalem after a long and terrible siege. The people inside the city were already suffering from hunger and disease because they had been surrounded for months. When the Romans finally broke through the walls, a huge battle broke out in the streets. The Romans set fire to the city, and the great Temple – the center of worship for the Jewish people – was completely destroyed. This Temple, built hundreds of years before, was the heart of Jewish faith and life. Many people lost their lives, and those who survived were taken away as prisoners or scattered into other lands. Historians from that time, including a Jewish man named Josephus who witnessed it himself, wrote that over one million people died during the fighting and the hardships. The destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple marked a turning point for the Jewish people, as they were sent away from their homeland and would not return in large numbers for many centuries.
w003.background: Judea, the land of the Jewish people, was under Roman rule during the first century. The Romans allowed some religious freedom but tightly controlled the country and taxed its people heavily. Many Jews longed for freedom and believed God would send a deliverer called the Messiah. Some groups rebelled against Rome, leading to growing tensions. Daily life for most families was centered around farming, crafts, and observing Jewish laws and festivals. The Temple in Jerusalem was the center of worship and sacrifice for all Jews. It was a beautiful and sacred place, visited by people from many lands. However, the constant presence of Roman soldiers, heavy taxes, and a sense of injustice brewed anger and unrest, which finally erupted into open revolt in 66 AD.
w003.matters: The destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple changed Jewish faith and history forever. With the Temple gone, Jews around the world began to worship in synagogues and focused more on scripture and prayer rather than sacrifices. For followers of Jesus, it confirmed His prophecy that not one stone would be left upon another. Families of faith can see in this event proof that God’s words are sure, even when their fulfillment takes time or brings sorrow. It also teaches us to prepare spiritually and temporally for hard times and to keep faith in God’s bigger plan, even when what we love most seems lost.
w003.scripture: In the New Testament, Jesus foretells the destruction of Jerusalem in Matthew 24:1-2, saying that not one stone of the Temple will be left standing. He gives further details about signs of the times and what His followers should do. The Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants do not mention this event directly, but Doctrine and Covenants 45:20-21 refers to the Lord’s warning to flee Jerusalem. Scriptures teach the principle of listening to prophets and being spiritually prepared for trials (Matthew 24; D&C 45:20-21).
w003.evidence: Archaeologists have found remains of the city’s destruction, including stones from the Temple thrown down by Roman soldiers, as well as piles of ash and burned materials in the old city of Jerusalem. Ancient historians like Josephus wrote detailed accounts of the siege, describing the famine, battles, and final destruction. Roman records and artifacts, such as the Arch of Titus in Rome, show images of Roman soldiers carrying treasures from the Temple, including the sacred menorah. Modern studies of these sources agree that the destruction happened much like the records say, with very little debate about the main facts. The evidence strongly supports the biblical account.
w003.learn: We can learn the importance of listening to God’s guidance and preparing when warnings are given. Even when life is hard or traditions change, faith and scripture can help hold a family together. The scattering of the Jewish people helped preserve the scriptures in new places, showing how God can turn even loss into blessing over time. These lessons can encourage us to trust Heavenly Father’s care, even in difficult times.
w003.child: Jerusalem was a city where Jesus and many people worshiped God. Long ago, soldiers destroyed the city and its big Temple, just like Jesus said would happen. Even when things seem sad or scary, God can help us and keep His promises.
w003.talk: Why do you think Jesus wanted His friends to be ready before hard times came?

w004.happened: The Crusades were a series of nine military campaigns that took place from 1095 to 1291 AD. These campaigns began when the Pope in Rome called Christian knights and soldiers from Europe to travel to the Holy Land—mainly the area around Jerusalem—claiming they needed to rescue it from Muslim control. Many answered the call, believing they were serving God. Over two centuries, thousands journeyed from Europe to the Middle East. The first major Crusade, in 1099, captured Jerusalem, but it was taken back and forth between different groups over the years. The Crusaders built castles, fought battles, and sometimes made alliances, but also committed terrible acts—killing or harming not just Muslims, but Jews and Eastern Christians, too. The violence and destruction, carried out in the name of Jesus, caused deep hurt and division that is remembered even today. Even those trying to do good sometimes acted out of fear, misunderstanding, or a belief that faith could excuse harming others.
w004.background: Before the Crusades, the Middle East was home to Muslims, Christians, and Jews, who often lived side by side, though not always peacefully. The city of Jerusalem was special to all three religions. In Europe, most people were Christian, and life was mostly rural and tough, with kings, lords, peasants, and the church playing big roles in society. News traveled slowly and people rarely left their villages. When Muslim rulers began to restrict Christian pilgrimages to Jerusalem, European leaders claimed this as a reason to launch wars, though many other political and economic motives were involved. The Crusades drew people from many backgrounds, often young men looking for adventure, wealth, or a new life.
w004.matters: The Crusades matter because they are a powerful example of how religion can be misused, leading to suffering and injustice when people lose sight of God's love and the true teachings of Jesus. For our families, remembering the Crusades invites us to teach compassion and the importance of respecting others’ beliefs. Understanding this history can help families see how Heavenly Father wants us to build peace, not war, and to use the gifts of faith and knowledge to lift instead of harm. The contact between cultures during these wars did bring some good, such as the sharing of science, philosophy, and stories that helped spark the European Renaissance.
w004.scripture: No scripture justifies violence in the name of Christ, but the Savior’s teachings in the New Testament remind us to love our enemies (Matthew 5:43-44) and to do good to those who persecute us. In the Book of Mormon, the example of the people of Ammon (Alma 24:17-18) shows a willingness to lay down weapons for peace. Doctrine and Covenants 98:16 invites believers to seek peace and not revenge. These principles encourage members of Christ's Church to oppose hatred and to seek understanding and kindness for all people, even during conflict.
w004.evidence: Historians have studied the Crusades through written records from both European and Middle Eastern sources—including letters, chronicles, and official reports. Archaeological finds, like the ruins of Crusader castles, coins, and weapons, confirm that large armies traveled through the region, built fortifications, and fought many battles. Jewish, Muslim, and Christian documents record abuses and atrocities. While many details are still debated—such as the motivations of individual leaders or soldiers—the main facts about where, when, and what happened are widely agreed on by experts. The evidence also shows the significant cultural exchange that took place, as ideas and inventions moved between East and West.
w004.learn: The Crusades show that using faith as an excuse for violence leads to pain and lasting harm. We can learn to carefully examine why we do things, making sure our faith leads us to Christlike actions—kindness, service, and peace. When we use technology, knowledge, and power for good, we honor Heavenly Father's trust. By studying the Crusades, we can help prevent misunderstanding and conflict in our own day, choosing to respect and learn from others, even if we have differences.
w004.child: A long time ago, people went to war over a city that was special to many religions. Some did terrible things, even though they thought they were doing good. We can remember to love others, even when we don’t agree, just like Jesus taught.
w004.talk: Why do you think Jesus wants us to love people who are different from us?

w005.happened: The Thirty Years War was one of the longest and deadliest wars in European history, taking place from 1618 to 1648, with its most intense moments around the year 1632. This war started in the Holy Roman Empire, in what is now Germany and nearby countries. At first, it was a fight about religion, mainly between Catholics and Protestants who disagreed on how to worship God. But as years passed, kings and rulers joined the conflict for political power, money, and land. Armies marched from one city to another, destroying homes, farms, and even whole villages. The fighting brought famine, disease, and suffering to millions of people—up to a third of the people in Germany died, either from violence or starvation. The war finally ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, a set of agreements that didn't just stop the fighting but also introduced a new idea: that people should be allowed to choose their religion without rulers forcing them one way or the other. This was a big change for Europe and for the world.
w005.background: Before the Thirty Years War, Europe was a patchwork of small kingdoms and territories, often ruled by powerful princes or kings under the Holy Roman Emperor. Most everyday people were farmers or craftsfolk, living simply and closely with their land and families. Religion shaped almost every part of life—your community, your celebrations, and even what rulers you might obey. When Martin Luther began the Protestant Reformation more than a hundred years earlier, it sparked growing divisions between Catholics and Protestants. By the early 1600s, these tensions were like dry wood ready for a spark, and when conflict broke out in Prague in 1618, the whole region was drawn in. Armies were made up of soldiers from many countries, and life for villagers and townsfolk quickly became dangerous and uncertain as battles swept through their homelands.
w005.matters: The Thirty Years War matters deeply even centuries later because it changed how governments in Europe and eventually around the world thought about religious freedom. Instead of rulers deciding everyone’s faith, the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 made religious tolerance a key part of political agreements. For families of faith, this was a stepping stone protecting the right to worship freely. This idea later became important in the United States, including the First Amendment that protected Joseph Smith and all who would seek to worship according to their beliefs. It reminds us that even from terrible suffering, God can bring about changes that open doors for freedom and faith.
w005.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention the Thirty Years War, the principle of agency—the power to choose for ourselves—is taught throughout. In Joshua 24:15, Joshua tells the people, 'choose you this day whom ye will serve.' In modern scripture, Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 says government should not punish people for their beliefs, so long as their actions respect the law and others’ rights. These teach that Heavenly Father honors our ability to choose, including our faith, and wants governments to protect that gift.
w005.evidence: Historians have strong evidence about the events of the Thirty Years War. Documents like treaties, royal letters, church records, and even diaries from soldiers and villagers survive today. Archaeologists find battlefields, abandoned villages, and mass graves that confirm the war’s devastations. Population studies show that in some regions of Germany, up to one third of people died during these years, supporting the terrible accounts from the time. The Peace of Westphalia is also a well-documented agreement, with original papers still preserved in museums and archives. This history is well studied by experts and its events are clearly established.
w005.learn: From the Thirty Years War, we learn how important it is to protect the freedom to worship and believe as our hearts guide us. Even though the war brought immense suffering, it led to greater understanding that governments must allow people to follow their faith. It also teaches us compassion for those hurt by conflict, and the need to work for peace wherever we can. God can help good come even from very hard times, if we choose to follow Him and respect others’ agency.
w005.child: A long time ago, many people in Europe fought a big war that hurt a lot of families because they disagreed about religion. After the war, leaders made a rule that people could choose their own beliefs. This helped families like Joseph Smith’s long after, so everyone could pray and worship how they felt was right.
w005.talk: Why do you think it is important for everyone to be able to choose how to worship?

w006.happened: In 1781, the American Revolutionary War reached a decisive turning point. Early in the year, on January 17, American forces under General Daniel Morgan achieved a significant victory at the Battle of Cowpens in South Carolina, effectively crippling British operations in the South. This success set the stage for further American advances. In the fall, General George Washington, leading a combined force of American and French troops, initiated the Siege of Yorktown in Virginia. After weeks of bombardment and encirclement, British General Charles Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781, effectively ending major combat operations and paving the way for American independence.
w006.background: Before 1781, the American colonies had been engaged in a prolonged struggle against British rule. The war had seen various battles across the colonies, with both victories and setbacks. Daily life for many was marked by uncertainty, as communities were divided between those loyal to the British Crown and those seeking independence. The involvement of foreign allies, particularly France, provided crucial support to the American cause, influencing the course of the war.
w006.matters: The events of 1781 were pivotal in securing American independence. The victory at Yorktown demonstrated the effectiveness of the alliance between American and French forces and underscored the resilience of the Continental Army. For families of faith, this period highlights the importance of perseverance and the belief that righteous endeavors, even against formidable odds, can lead to freedom and the establishment of principles that protect individual rights.
w006.scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 states, "And for this purpose have I established the Constitution of this land, by the hands of wise men whom I raised up unto this very purpose, and redeemed the land by the shedding of blood." This passage reflects the belief that the establishment of the United States was divinely guided, with the Constitution serving as a foundation for religious freedom and the Restoration of the Gospel.
w006.evidence: Historical records, including official documents, personal letters, and contemporary accounts, provide detailed insights into the events of 1781. The surrender at Yorktown is well-documented, with artifacts and preserved battlefields serving as tangible evidence of this pivotal moment.
w006.learn: The events of 1781 teach us the value of unity, strategic alliances, and unwavering commitment to righteous causes. They remind us that, with faith and perseverance, it is possible to overcome challenges and achieve lasting freedom.
w006.child: In 1781, American soldiers worked together with their friends from France to win an important battle. This victory helped America become a free country where people could choose how to worship God.
w006.talk: Why do you think working together with others can help us achieve important goals?

w007.happened: In 1863, the United States was in the middle of its Civil War, a brutal and painful struggle between the Northern states (the Union) and the Southern states (the Confederacy). The main cause of the war was slavery—whether it should continue or be abolished. That year, President Abraham Lincoln gave the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring freedom for enslaved people in the rebellious Southern states. Battles raged across the country, with families divided, towns ruined, and great suffering felt by soldiers and civilians alike. Major battles like Gettysburg took place in 1863, and many people died or were wounded. The war seemed endless, and hope was sometimes hard to find. Yet, despite the darkness, many felt God still cared about the nation, and some leaders—including President Lincoln—spoke openly about the nation's need to repent for the sin of slavery and to seek forgiveness and healing. Slowly, the Union began to gain the upper hand, but at a great cost.
w007.background: Before the Civil War, life in America was different depending on where you lived. In the North, many people lived in cities and worked in factories, while in the South, most people lived on farms and relied on the labor of enslaved people. Disagreements about slavery grew worse as new states joined the country. Some wanted slavery to spread, while others thought it was wrong. The issue was about more than just work—it touched deep beliefs about freedom, family, and the meaning of the nation. People in the 1800s didn't have electricity, cars, or even telephones. Most children helped on the farm or learned trades from family members. There were parades, church gatherings, and simple pleasures, but life could turn hard and scary during the war.
w007.matters: The Civil War was a turning point in American and world history, ending slavery in the United States and forcing the country to face, at great cost, its own founding contradictions. For families of faith, this war preserved the Constitution and the freedoms that would allow the Restoration of the gospel to flourish in safety. It is a lesson in the danger of allowing societies to ignore sacred truths about equality and the worth of souls. The hard rebuilding after the war showed the strength that comes from repentance, forgiveness, and working to right terrible wrongs.
w007.scripture: The scriptures do not mention the American Civil War directly, but Doctrine and Covenants 87 contains a prophecy from Joseph Smith about war beginning in South Carolina and spreading through all nations. Verses 1–3 predict the Civil War and warn of great suffering. The Book of Mormon teaches that contention and pride can destroy nations (3 Nephi 11:29). The Bible calls us to love our neighbor and seek peace (Matthew 22:39; Matthew 5:9). These principles remind us that division and hatred bring sorrow, but God's way is forgiveness and unity.
w007.evidence: The events of the Civil War have been carefully recorded through letters, diaries, official documents, photographs, and newspapers. Archaeological remains from battlefields, soldiers' camps, and preserved sites still teach us about the era. The Emancipation Proclamation and Lincoln's speeches are preserved and widely studied. Modern historians continue to confirm the scale of suffering, the number of deaths (about 750,000, as updated by recent studies), and the war's central conflict over slavery. Museums, parks, and civil rights memorials keep the memory of these years alive for all to learn from.
w007.learn: From the Civil War, we learn that wrongs as deep as slavery cannot stand forever and that whole societies need courage to change. We also see the blessings of freedom and the importance of standing up for what is right, even when it is costly and hard. The Lord can help nations and people heal, but it often requires humility, repentance, and a willingness to forgive and build something better.
w007.child: A long time ago, people in America fought a terrible war because some people wanted to keep others as slaves. Many people suffered, but in the end, the law changed, and everyone became free. God wants us to treat everyone with kindness and love.
w007.talk: Why do you think it is important to stand up for people who are being treated unfairly?

w008.happened: World War I, often called the Great War, lasted from 1914 to 1918 and caused devastating loss and change. Over four years, more than 20 million people died—soldiers and civilians—from fighting, hunger, and disease. The war began as nations in Europe made alliances and competed for power, but it quickly spread to involve many parts of the world, including the Middle East and Africa. New weapons like machine guns, tanks, and airplanes brought danger and destruction never before seen. By the end, four great empires—the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman—collapsed under the strain. In December 1917, British General Allenby entered the city of Jerusalem on foot, ending over 400 years of Ottoman rule. This act was careful and respectful, as many saw Jerusalem as a holy place. The end of the war in 1918 left the world exhausted and grieving, but it also set in motion big changes that would shape the rest of the 20th century, including new nations and borders, and efforts to bring peace through groups like the League of Nations.
w008.background: Before World War I, Europe was full of powerful empires, royal families, and busy cities. Many people lived on farms or in small towns, working hard to support their families. Life could be peaceful, but there was tension as countries competed for land and power. The Industrial Revolution had brought factories and trains, making life faster, but also making weapons more deadly. The Ottoman Empire had controlled Jerusalem and much of the Middle East for centuries, and people there lived under strict rule. Different languages, religions, and traditions mingled in cities like Jerusalem, and many Jewish families still hoped for a time when they would return to their ancient homeland, as their scriptures promised. Most people, however, had little warning that such a large and sudden war was coming.
w008.matters: World War I mattered deeply for everyone alive at the time, and for generations after. The end of Ottoman rule in Jerusalem opened the way for both new discoveries in the Holy Land and the building of a modern state of Israel—a key part of ancient prophecy for many believers, including Latter-day Saints. The war taught the world bitter lessons about the cost of conflict and the need for peace. For families of faith, it is a reminder that terrible things can happen when people forget to see each other as brothers and sisters, and that sometimes Heavenly Father can use painful events to prepare the way for greater blessings later on.
w008.scripture: Although the Bible and Book of Mormon do not mention modern wars like World War I, scriptures speak of Jerusalem's importance and the gathering of Israel in the last days. The Lord promises in Isaiah 11:11-12 and Doctrine and Covenants 133:13-35 that He will gather His people from all nations and that Jerusalem will be restored. Zechariah 12:2-3 also speaks of Jerusalem's future challenges and blessings. These passages help believers see events like the return of Jerusalem to non-Ottoman hands as part of a long story that God is guiding, even through sorrow or struggle.
w008.evidence: History is clear about the facts of World War I; we have thousands of photographs, newspapers, letters, and official records showing what happened. The British capture of Jerusalem in 1917 was widely reported, and General Allenby's respectful entry on foot is described in many accounts. Since the Ottoman Empire collapsed, archaeologists have been able to explore the Holy Land more freely. They have found ancient scrolls, artifacts, and ruins which match details from the Bible, adding evidence that many of those stories are based on real places and events. These finds don't prove every detail of scripture, but they have strengthened faith for many and given scholars a clearer picture of ancient life.
w008.learn: Families can learn from World War I about the dangers of pride, anger, and forgetting the worth of every soul. It shows how small arguments can grow into great trouble if not solved with kindness and patience. We see that even in dark times, Heavenly Father is aware of His children and can prepare the way for good things later. When we work for peace and remember our shared humanity, we honor Him and help His work go forward.
w008.child: World War I was a huge war that affected millions of people all over the world and changed history. It ended a long time of rule in Jerusalem and helped make it possible for people to learn more about the land where Jesus lived. Even sad times can prepare for blessings later.
w008.talk: Why do you think it's important to remember what happens in times of war and peace?

w009.happened: In 1944, World War II had reached a critical point. The war was being fought across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific, with nations from all over the world involved. That year, the Allies—countries like the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union—planned and launched major attacks against Nazi Germany, which was led by Adolf Hitler. One of the most famous moments was D-Day, on June 6, 1944, when over 150,000 Allied troops landed on the beaches of Normandy, France. This was the biggest seaborne invasion in history and helped turn the tide against the Nazis. At the same time, terrible things were happening. Millions of Jewish people and others were being murdered in concentration camps as part of the Holocaust. Families were separated, cities were bombed, and entire communities were destroyed. But as the Allies fought back, they began to liberate these camps and free the people held there. By the end of 1944, it was becoming clear that the Allies were winning the war, though the fighting would continue for another year.
w009.background: The world at this time was deeply divided by powerful governments and armies. Many people lived in fear because of harsh dictatorships and constant fighting. In many places, even basic things like food, safety, and freedom were hard to find. Jewish families especially lived with daily fear under Nazi rule, and many tried to hide or escape. In the United States and other countries, men and women joined the military or worked in factories to support the war effort. Children often helped at home, collected supplies, and faced shortages of everyday items. The war changed nearly every part of life, reminding people all over the world how precious peace can be.
w009.matters: This event matters because World War II shaped the world we live in today. It ended some of the most evil acts in history, like the Holocaust. For families of faith, the war’s end meant the survival of the Jewish people, through whom Jesus Christ came. It paved the way for the modern nation of Israel—a fulfillment of ancient promises God made to gather His people again. Families can find hope in knowing that even after great darkness, God’s purposes can still move forward, and people can help by choosing to do good.
w009.scripture: The Bible speaks of the scattering and gathering of Israel, such as in Isaiah 11:11-12 and Ezekiel 37:21-22, where God promises to gather His people from the nations. Doctrine and Covenants 133:13 also speaks of the gathering of Israel in the last days. While the war itself is not specifically mentioned in scripture, these passages teach that God is mindful of His covenant people and keeps His promises. The Book of Mormon also testifies that the Lord will remember Israel and bring them together (see 3 Nephi 21:26-29).
w009.evidence: There is a great deal of evidence for these events. Photographs, official government documents, diaries, and countless eyewitness accounts tell the story of World War II and the Holocaust. Historians have records of the battles, the concentration camps, and the liberation of Europe. Museums, such as the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, hold many artifacts and testimonies from survivors. The Normandy beaches and concentration camp sites still exist today as reminders of what happened. These facts are supported by decades of careful study, making this one of the best-documented parts of human history.
w009.learn: From these events, we can learn the importance of standing up for what is right, even when times are dark. We see the blessings that can come from working together to protect others, and the way choices—good or bad—can affect history. As families, we are reminded that God can bring good from hardship, and we can be part of that by being kind, brave, and faithful in our own lives.
w009.child: During World War II, many countries fought because some leaders wanted power and hurt many people, especially the Jewish people. Good people joined to help stop the hurting and bring freedom. Even when things were very hard, Heavenly Father never forgot His promises to gather His people.
w009.talk: Why do you think it's important to help others, even if it's difficult?

w010.happened: In the early hours of June 25, 1950, North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel, launching a full-scale invasion of South Korea. This aggressive move aimed to unify the Korean Peninsula under communist rule. The North Korean army, equipped with Soviet tanks and artillery, rapidly advanced southward, capturing the capital city of Seoul within days. In response, the United Nations, led predominantly by the United States, intervened to assist South Korea. General Douglas MacArthur orchestrated a daring amphibious landing at Inchon in September 1950, which turned the tide of the war, allowing UN forces to recapture Seoul and push the North Korean army back across the 38th parallel. However, as UN forces advanced toward the Yalu River, the border with China, Chinese troops entered the conflict in October 1950, launching a massive counteroffensive that forced UN forces into retreat. The war then settled into a grueling stalemate, with both sides engaging in fierce battles along the front lines. After three years of intense fighting and heavy casualties, an armistice was signed on July 27, 1953, effectively ending the hostilities. The agreement established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border that still divides North and South Korea today. Despite the cessation of active combat, a formal peace treaty was never signed, leaving the two nations technically still at war.
w010.background: After World War II ended in 1945, Korea, which had been under Japanese rule, was divided along the 38th parallel into two occupation zones: the Soviet Union controlled the north, and the United States controlled the south. This division was intended to be temporary, but differing political ideologies led to the establishment of two separate governments. In the north, a communist regime was established under Kim Il-sung, while the south formed a democratic government led by Syngman Rhee. Tensions between the two Koreas escalated as both leaders sought to reunify the peninsula under their respective governments. Daily life in both regions was marked by the challenges of post-war reconstruction, political unrest, and the looming threat of conflict. The global context was also significant, as the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union influenced international relations and regional conflicts, including the situation in Korea.
w010.matters: The Korean War had profound implications for the Korean Peninsula and the world. It solidified the division between North and South Korea, leading to the establishment of two distinct nations with vastly different political, economic, and social systems. For families of faith, particularly those who believe in the importance of religious freedom, the war's outcome in South Korea allowed for the growth and flourishing of Christianity. South Korea has since become one of the world's most vibrant Christian nations, sending missionaries worldwide and contributing significantly to global Christian outreach. The preservation of a free South Korea provided a fertile ground for religious expression and the spread of the gospel.
w010.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the importance of agency and the blessings that come from choosing righteousness. In the Book of Mormon, we read about the people of Alma who, despite facing severe persecution, remained faithful and were eventually delivered by the Lord (Mosiah 24:13-16). Similarly, the preservation of South Korea's freedom allowed its people to exercise their agency in matters of faith, leading to a flourishing Christian community. This aligns with the principle that the Lord supports those who seek Him and strive to live according to His teachings.
w010.evidence: Historical records and scholarly research provide extensive evidence about the Korean War. Documents from the U.S. Army Center of Military History detail the sequence of events, military strategies, and outcomes of the conflict. Additionally, studies on the war's impact on Christianity in Korea highlight how the conflict influenced religious dynamics in both the North and the South. For instance, research indicates that the war intensified the division between the communist North, which suppressed religious practices, and the democratic South, where Christianity experienced significant growth. These sources offer a comprehensive understanding of the war's causes, progression, and lasting effects.
w010.learn: The Korean War teaches us about the resilience of the human spirit and the importance of standing firm in our beliefs, even in the face of adversity. It also underscores the value of freedom and the opportunities it provides for individuals and communities to grow and thrive. For families of faith, the war's outcome in South Korea serves as a reminder of how preserving agency and religious freedom can lead to the flourishing of spiritual communities and the spread of the gospel.
w010.child: A long time ago, there was a big fight between the northern and southern parts of Korea. Many countries helped, and after the fighting stopped, South Korea became a place where people could freely choose their beliefs. Today, many people in South Korea believe in Jesus and share His teachings with others around the world.
w010.talk: Why do you think it's important for people to have the freedom to choose their beliefs?

w011.happened: Between 1989 and 1991, a great change swept across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. For many years, these countries had strict communist governments that did not allow people to choose their own leaders, practice their faith freely, or even travel and speak as they wanted. The Cold War was a time when the world felt divided, with the United States and its allies on one side and the Soviet Union on the other—often even afraid of each other. In 1989, one of the biggest symbols of this divide, the Berlin Wall, was torn down by crowds of ordinary people in Germany. The wall had separated families and friends for almost thirty years. Soon after, countries like Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and others held peaceful protests, voted for new leaders, and changed their governments. By the end of 1991, the Soviet Union itself came to an end, breaking apart into many new countries, including Russia. Most of this happened without violence, as people hoped for a better future. For the first time in over seventy years, missionaries were allowed to enter these lands to share their message, and churches could meet again without fear. It was a time when millions were free to choose new paths and learn new ideas, especially about faith and hope for something better.
w011.background: Before these changes, Eastern Europe and the lands of the Soviet Union were under communist rule after World War II. The governments controlled almost every part of life: jobs, schools, newspapers, and even what people could believe. Many families stood in long lines for food, and secret police made sure no one spoke against the leaders. Churches were often closed or watched very closely. Despite this, parents and grandparents quietly taught children about faith, kindness, and doing good, even if they had to do it in secret. Most people wanted peace and a better life for their children, just like parents everywhere. By the late 1980s, many people were hoping things would change—asking for more freedom, fairness, and the chance to worship without fear.
w011.matters: The end of the Cold War changed millions of lives almost overnight. Suddenly, people could speak their minds, read the scriptures, and invite missionaries into their homes. Families could pray together and choose their faith openly, something that had been very hard or impossible for generations. For members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, this was a moment when long-held prayers were answered. It reminds us that the freedom to believe and to share what we know is precious and not to be taken for granted. As a family of faith, we see in these events a sign that our loving Heavenly Father is aware of all His children and can prepare a way for the gospel to reach them, even after long years of waiting.
w011.scripture: The scriptures teach that the Lord prepares the hearts of people to receive the gospel, sometimes in ways we do not expect. Doctrine and Covenants 1:2 prophesies that the gospel will go to all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people, and Revelation 14:6 speaks of the "everlasting gospel" being shared with every nation. These passages remind us that the work of spreading the gospel is in the Lord's hands, and He can open doors that once seemed locked. While the Bible and Book of Mormon do not mention these recent events directly, their teachings about freedom, agency, and the worth of each soul are deeply connected to moments like these.
w011.evidence: Historians and journalists recorded the events of 1989–1991 in great detail. There are photographs and videos of people gathering at the Berlin Wall, pulling it down, and celebrating together. Documents from government meetings and interviews with leaders show that most of the changes were planned and carried out peacefully, often with encouragement from the people themselves. The collapse of the Soviet Union is also well recorded in the news of the time and in the official government records that became public after it ended. There is strong, clear evidence that after these changes, religious freedoms grew, and faith communities—including Latter-day Saint missionaries—were able to enter these countries, as shown by Church records and local news reports.
w011.learn: From this event, we can learn that things can change for the better, even after many years of difficulty. Courage, hope, and faith make a real difference in people's lives, and gentle, peaceful action can sometimes do what force cannot. This history helps us remember to never give up hope, to pray for those who are not yet free, and to value the blessings we have. It invites us to look for ways to help and serve others quietly, trusting that Heavenly Father sees and remembers His children, no matter where they live.
w011.child: A long time ago, some countries didn't let people go to church or talk about what they believed. Then, the countries changed, and people could learn about Jesus again. Missionaries were happy to help them, and many families found new hope.
w011.talk: How do you think it would feel to wait for years to talk about Jesus, and then finally be able to share your faith?

ex01.happened: Between 334 and 323 BC, Alexander the Great embarked on an ambitious campaign that extended from Greece to the edges of India. After uniting the Greek city-states, he crossed into Asia Minor, defeating the Persian Empire and continuing eastward. In 327 BC, Alexander entered the Indian subcontinent through the Khyber Pass, aiming to expand his empire further. He faced formidable resistance from local rulers, notably King Porus of the Paurava kingdom. In 326 BC, at the Battle of the Hydaspes River, Alexander employed strategic tactics to overcome Porus's forces, which included war elephants. Impressed by Porus's valor, Alexander reinstated him as a satrap, or governor, of his own territory, fostering loyalty among the local populace. Alexander's army, weary from years of campaigning and facing the prospect of confronting the powerful Nanda Empire further east, eventually refused to march beyond the Hyphasis River (modern Beas River). Respecting his soldiers' wishes, Alexander turned back, marking the easternmost extent of his conquests. On his return journey, he founded several cities, many named Alexandria, to serve as administrative centers and to spread Greek culture. His campaign facilitated significant cultural exchanges between the Greek and Indian civilizations, leaving a lasting impact on art, architecture, and language in the regions he traversed.
ex01.background: Before Alexander's conquests, the Greek world was composed of city-states, each with its own government and culture, yet sharing a common language and religious beliefs. The Persian Empire, a vast and powerful entity, controlled much of the known world, including parts of Asia Minor and the Middle East. Daily life in these regions varied, with agrarian societies in the countryside and bustling trade centers in cities. The Indian subcontinent was home to diverse kingdoms and cultures, with advanced urban centers, rich traditions in art and science, and complex social structures. The interaction between these civilizations was limited, with trade being the primary form of contact. Alexander's campaign changed this dynamic, creating new routes for cultural and commercial exchange.
ex01.matters: Alexander's journey to India was more than a military expedition; it was a bridge between East and West. By establishing cities and encouraging the mingling of cultures, he set the stage for the Hellenistic period, where Greek language and ideas blended with those of the East. This fusion influenced art, philosophy, and governance, enriching both civilizations. For families of faith, this historical event underscores how diverse cultures can come together, sharing knowledge and traditions. It also highlights how the spread of a common language, like Koine Greek, can facilitate the sharing of important messages, much like the New Testament was later written in this accessible dialect, allowing the teachings of Jesus Christ to reach a broader audience.
ex01.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention Alexander the Great, the principle of God preparing the way for His purposes is evident. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-79, the Lord instructs us to seek learning in various fields, including history and languages, to be better prepared to serve Him. Alexander's conquests, which spread the Greek language and culture, can be seen as part of this preparation, creating a common linguistic foundation that later facilitated the spread of the gospel through the New Testament.
ex01.evidence: Historical records from ancient historians like Arrian and Plutarch provide detailed accounts of Alexander's campaigns, including his battles and interactions with local rulers. Archaeological findings, such as the remains of cities founded by Alexander, support these narratives. The spread of Hellenistic art and architecture in regions as far as India indicates a significant Greek influence. Additionally, the adoption of Koine Greek as a common language across these territories is evidenced by inscriptions and documents from the period. These pieces of evidence collectively confirm the historical reality of Alexander's journey to India and its lasting impact.
ex01.learn: From Alexander's journey, we learn the power of cultural exchange and the importance of communication. By sharing languages and ideas, societies can grow and enrich each other. This history teaches us to value and respect different cultures, recognizing that such interactions can lead to greater understanding and unity.
ex01.child: Long ago, a leader named Alexander traveled from Greece to India, meeting new people and sharing ideas. His journey helped different cultures learn from each other, making the world more connected.
ex01.talk: How can learning about other cultures help us understand and love our neighbors better?

ex02.happened: Xuanzang was a Buddhist monk from China who, in 629 AD, left his home in the city of Chang’an and began an incredibly long journey all the way to India. He made this trip mostly on foot, leaving behind almost everything he knew, and facing deserts, tall mountains, hunger, and even dangers from robbers along the way. Xuanzang’s goal was to find original Buddhist scriptures and bring them back to China, so people at home could learn from them, too. Over 16 years, Xuanzang traveled roughly 10,000 miles, visiting many cities and famous Buddhist sites such as Nalanda, the great university of ancient India. He listened to teachers, copied many sacred texts, and learned new ideas about his faith. When Xuanzang finally returned home to China in 645 AD, he was welcomed warmly, and he spent many years carefully translating the scriptures he had gathered, sharing precious knowledge with many others. His adventure became one of the world’s most amazing stories, inspiring the beloved Chinese novel Journey to the West.
ex02.background: Xuanzang lived during the Tang Dynasty, a time when China was strong, open to new ideas, and bustling with people from many lands. Chang’an, his home city, was a huge, lively place—often called the world’s largest city at the time. Chinese people in this era valued learning, and religions like Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism shaped daily life. Most people farmed, made crafts, or traded goods in busy markets; some became scholars or monks. Buddhism had taken root in China about 400 years earlier, but many Chinese Buddhists worried their teachings, copied and re-copied from ancient Indian sources, might not be complete or correct. The journey overland from China to India was dangerous—across the Silk Road and over the Himalayas—yet stories of India as Buddhism’s birthplace drew serious seekers like Xuanzang to undertake the risk.
ex02.matters: Xuanzang’s journey matters because it shows us the power of seeking truth, even when it is hard or risky. His story reminds us that finding and sharing truth can bless whole nations—not just one community. For families of faith, Xuanzang’s devotion to gathering sacred writings is much like the faith of early Latter-day Saints who crossed great distances to have the scriptures and worship as they believed. Such journeys are powerful reminders that Heavenly Father honors great efforts to seek truth and share goodness with others.
ex02.scripture: There is no direct mention of Xuanzang or Buddhist journeys in Latter-day Saint scripture, but the principle of seeking truth through diligent effort is seen throughout. In the Book of Mormon, Lehi’s family traveled far to retrieve the brass plates (1 Nephi 3-5), risking much to preserve God’s word. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches to 'seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom,' encouraging faithful study from all good sources. These scriptures show how Heavenly Father values our effort to gather and learn sacred truth.
ex02.evidence: Historical accounts and archaeological evidence both confirm Xuanzang’s journey. Xuanzang himself wrote a detailed record of his travels, called the 'Great Tang Records on the Western Regions.' Many places he described—like the ruins of Nalanda University—have been found by archaeologists, and match his descriptions closely. Chinese historical records from the Tang Dynasty also mention and honor Xuanzang upon his return. The impact of his translations and the lasting popularity of Journey to the West in China provide further proof of his importance. While some small details of his adventure are hard to verify, the main events of his journey are confirmed by multiple sources.
ex02.learn: Xuanzang teaches us that the search for truth and wisdom takes courage, patience, and trust in Heavenly Father. Even when the road is long and uncertain, good things can come from persistence and faith. Families can be inspired to treasure their own scriptures and seek to understand the beliefs of others with kindness and curiosity.
ex02.child: A brave monk named Xuanzang walked all the way from China to India to find special books about his religion. He brought these books back so everyone in China could learn from them. His story shows how important it is to look for truth, even when it is hard.
ex02.talk: What is something you would walk a long way to learn or find?

ex03.happened: Marco Polo was a young man from Venice, Italy, when he began his famous journey in 1271 with his father and uncle. Their goal was to reach the court of Kublai Khan, the powerful ruler of China, whom Polo’s family had met years earlier. Their route took them along the fabled Silk Road, winding through deserts, mountains, and strange cities full of new sights and customs. After many hardships and years of travel, Marco Polo arrived in Khanbaliq, now Beijing, in 1275. There, he became a trusted envoy for Kublai Khan and spent about 17 years serving in the Khan's court, learning about the Chinese way of life, technology, and government. When he finally returned to Venice, Polo shared his stories of great cities, marvelous inventions, and nations that seemed almost magical to Europeans. His stories were gathered in a book called “The Travels of Marco Polo.” This book fascinated thousands of readers with tales of paper money, rapid communication across the empire, and everyday wonders like fireworks, printing, and spices unknown in Europe. These stories caught the attention of many, including explorers like Christopher Columbus.
ex03.background: Marco Polo lived during the Middle Ages, a time when most Europeans had little direct contact with the cultures of Asia. Venice, Marco’s home, was a bustling city of merchants and traders who exchanged goods with far-off lands. Travel was dangerous and slow, with many people spending their lives in the same towns or villages where they were born. China, on the other hand, was ruled by the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous empire the world has ever seen. Under Kublai Khan, China was highly organized, with thriving cities, grand roads, and incredible new technologies like papermaking, printing, and gunpowder. Life for most Europeans in this era was simple and hard; they depended on farming, lived in small stone or wooden homes, and learned most things from local priests, merchants, or travelers with news from afar. The journey Marco Polo made was rare and risky, but it opened a window between two very different worlds.
ex03.matters: Marco Polo’s journey brought news of China and the East to a Europe hungry for discovery. His stories gave Europeans their first big look into Asian civilization and its advanced technology, like papermaking and printing. These inventions would later help bring about the Renaissance and the invention of the printing press. From a faith perspective, it’s remarkable that one man’s curiosity helped set off a chain of learning and exploration that would eventually help the Bible, and later the Book of Mormon, be printed, carried, and read by millions. Marco’s story reminds families that God can use even the simplest beginnings—like a merchant's journey—to bring greater light to the world.
ex03.scripture: No scripture mentions Marco Polo by name, but there are principles that connect with his story. In the Bible, the Lord often invites His disciples to go to new lands and learn from many peoples. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-80, God tells us to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith,” and to “be instructed more perfectly in theory, in principle, in doctrine, in the law of the gospel, in all things…of countries and of kingdoms.” Marco Polo’s journey is a good example of seeking learning from the world, and sharing it for the good of others.
ex03.evidence: Scholars have examined Marco Polo’s book for hundreds of years. Most historians agree that he really did travel to China and witness many of the things he described. His detailed accounts of the size and richness of Beijing (then Khanbaliq), local customs, and technologies mostly match what Chinese records from the Yuan Dynasty say. Archaeologists and historians have found very few European artifacts or written evidence in China from that exact time, but the details and insights found in his book go well beyond what could have been known by hearsay in Europe. However, some minor errors and fanciful tales in his account have led some historians to wonder if Polo sometimes included second-hand stories he heard on his travels. On the whole, the journey and time at Kublai Khan’s court are considered well-attested by modern scholars.
ex03.learn: From Marco Polo we can learn that exploring new lands and learning from others can lead to unexpected blessings for many. One person’s courage, questions, and careful record-keeping can help people see the world in a new way and bring knowledge that opens doors. Families can remember that curiosity, guided by faith and a desire to do good, can be one of Heavenly Father’s tools in preparing the world for greater light and truth.
ex03.child: Marco Polo went on a long, dangerous trip from Italy to China. He saw many new things, like how the Chinese made paper and fireworks. Later, his stories helped people in Europe get excited about learning and exploring new places.
ex03.talk: Why do you think it mattered that Marco Polo wrote down what he saw and learned in China?

ex04.happened: Between 1405 and 1433, a Chinese admiral named Zheng He led seven enormous sea voyages, some of the most ambitious in human history. Zheng He was appointed by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming Dynasty to take fleets as large as 300 ships—many times bigger than anything in Europe at the time—from the busy city of Nanjing out into the vast Indian Ocean. These fleets sailed to lands far from China, including what we now know as Vietnam, Indonesia, India, Arabia, and all the way to East Africa. Zheng He’s ships carried silk, porcelain, and gifts to show China’s wealth and peace, while bringing back rare animals and goods, and returning with visitors and ambassadors from those distant shores. People in foreign lands were amazed by the size and order of the fleets. By 1415, the world seemed closer together than ever, with China at the center of a buzzing network of trade and diplomacy. But after these voyages ended, the Chinese government made a surprising decision: they stopped building large ships, closed their harbors to most foreign trade, and future emperors focused only on the land within their borders. In this way, a door to the wider world was closed for China for centuries.
ex04.background: The world of early 1400s China was vibrant and powerful. The Ming Dynasty stood as one of the richest civilizations, famous for its beautiful art, advanced technology, and busy cities. Most people lived in small farming villages, growing rice and vegetables, but the great cities buzzed with markets, workshops, and government officials. The emperor was considered the ‘Son of Heaven’ and ruled over a vast land with millions of subjects. Other civilizations, such as the Indian kingdoms and the powerful trading cities of Arabia and East Africa, were also prospering. Travel by land and sea was slow and sometimes dangerous, but rare goods, stories, and ideas traveled far. At the time, no European ships had sailed around Africa, and few outside of Asia knew much about China or its mighty fleets. Daily life for Zheng He's sailors included strict routines, careful navigation by the stars, and the immense teamwork needed to sail across oceans.
ex04.matters: Zheng He’s voyages changed the way the world connected, even if only for a short time. They showed how far humans can reach when they cooperate, plan, and trust in new ways of doing things. For families of faith, this story teaches that great opportunities come, but also that timing matters greatly in God’s work. The Chinese choice to turn inward after these voyages left room for others—like the Portuguese and Spanish—to explore and change the world. That opened the door for the Americas to be discovered by Europeans at a particular moment in God’s timing, when later, religious reformers would seek a new land for freedom. It reminds us to look for God’s hand in the way history flows, even if we can’t see the reasons right away.
ex04.scripture: There is no scripture that directly tells the story of Zheng He or ancient Chinese explorers. However, principles from scripture do relate. Doctrine and Covenants 1:23 teaches that God acts in His own due time and in a way that the world might be prepared for His work. Likewise, in Acts 17:26, the Apostle Paul explains that Heavenly Father “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation.” These verses remind us that the Lord is mindful of all nations and peoples, guiding the movements of history according to divine wisdom and purpose.
ex04.evidence: We have strong historical evidence for Zheng He’s voyages. Ancient Chinese records, including detailed logs of the fleets, names of the crew, and official orders, have survived. Archaeologists have found relics of Ming-era ceramics in places like East Africa and India—far from China’s shores—confirming the reach of the expeditions. The size of Zheng He’s largest ships, described as up to 120 meters long, is debated, but the grand scale is confirmed by shipyards found in Nanjing. Records from the countries Zheng He visited, such as inscriptions in Sri Lanka, also describe the arrival of the Chinese fleets. After the voyages, written imperial edicts show a clear shift to focus only on China’s lands and to curtail overseas journeys. Historians agree China could have easily continued exploring, but internal changes—such as the death of supporters at court and concern over costs—caused the sudden end.
ex04.learn: We learn that the world changes in unexpected ways. Sometimes plans are set aside or great work is paused, and we don’t always know why. But looking back, we can often see God’s wisdom or preparation in the timing, even if it felt disappointing at first. We are also reminded to use the gifts and opportunities Heavenly Father gives us, knowing that He always cares for all His children around the world.
ex04.child: A Chinese leader named Zheng He once sailed big ships to faraway lands, meeting many new people. After his journeys, China stopped exploring and stayed at home. That gave other countries a chance to find new lands later on.
ex04.talk: What do you think would happen if people shared what they learned with others from faraway places?

ex05.happened: In 1488, Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias led an expedition that became the first European venture to round the southern tip of Africa. Departing from Lisbon in August 1487, Dias commanded two caravels and a supply ship. The journey down the West African coast was arduous, with the crew facing strong storms that pushed them out to sea. After 13 days without sight of land, they turned northeast and, on February 3, 1488, anchored in what is now Mossel Bay, South Africa. This confirmed they had navigated around the continent's southernmost point. Dias continued eastward along the coast but, due to dwindling supplies and a restless crew, decided to return to Portugal. On the return voyage, they sighted the southern tip of Africa, which Dias named the "Cape of Storms" due to its treacherous weather. King John II of Portugal later renamed it the "Cape of Good Hope," reflecting the optimism of establishing a sea route to India. Dias returned to Lisbon in December 1488, having opened the way for future maritime trade between Europe and Asia.
ex05.background: In the late 15th century, European nations were eager to find new trade routes to Asia, especially after the overland routes became more perilous due to the rise of the Ottoman Empire. Portugal, under King John II, was at the forefront of maritime exploration, seeking a sea passage to the lucrative markets of India and the East. Bartolomeu Dias, a nobleman and experienced sailor, was chosen to lead this critical expedition. Daily life for sailors like Dias was grueling, with long months at sea, limited provisions, and the constant threat of unknown territories and hostile encounters. The success of such voyages depended on courage, navigational skill, and the ability to endure hardships.
ex05.matters: Dias's successful navigation around the Cape of Good Hope was a monumental achievement that paved the way for a direct sea route from Europe to Asia. This breakthrough diminished the Islamic monopoly on overland trade routes, reshaping global economic and political dynamics. For families of faith, this event underscores the belief that Heavenly Father prepares the way for His purposes. The opening of new trade routes facilitated the spread of ideas, cultures, and, eventually, the gospel to distant lands, aligning with the divine plan to bring His children closer together.
ex05.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention maritime exploration, they emphasize the importance of seeking knowledge and understanding. Proverbs 25:2 states, "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter." This suggests that exploration and discovery are noble pursuits that can lead to greater understanding of God's creations. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:79 encourages learning about "things which are at home, things which are abroad," highlighting the value of expanding our knowledge of the world.
ex05.evidence: Historical records, including logs from Dias's expedition and accounts from the Portuguese court, provide detailed information about the voyage. Archaeological findings, such as the padrões (stone crosses) erected by Dias along the African coast, serve as tangible evidence of his journey. These markers, placed at key points, signified Portuguese claims and navigational achievements. The Cape of Good Hope itself remains a geographical testament to Dias's exploration, with its treacherous waters and strategic location continuing to be significant in maritime history.
ex05.learn: From Dias's journey, we learn the value of perseverance and courage in the face of the unknown. His expedition teaches us that seeking new paths can lead to significant advancements and blessings. It also reminds us that, with faith and determination, we can overcome obstacles and contribute to the greater good.
ex05.child: Long ago, a brave sailor named Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the bottom of Africa, finding a new way to reach faraway lands. This helped people trade and share ideas across the world.
ex05.talk: Why do you think it's important to explore new places and learn about different people?

ex06.happened: In 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail from Spain with three ships: the Niña, the Pinta, and the Santa María. His goal was to find a shortcut to Asia by sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean. After weeks at sea, he and his crew finally spotted land, which turned out to be one of the islands now called the Bahamas. Over the next twelve years, Columbus made four voyages to the lands he discovered, visiting parts of what are now the Caribbean islands, Central America, and South America. Columbus met many people who already lived there, whom he called 'Indians,' thinking he had reached Asia. Though others would later understand this was actually a ‘New World’ unknown to Europeans, Columbus himself died believing he had found a new route to Asia. His voyages changed the world by opening up the Americas to European explorers, settlers, and traders, leading to big changes for the people and places on both sides of the Atlantic.
ex06.background: Before Columbus sailed, Europe, Africa, and Asia were connected by long trade routes, but the Americas were not known to these continents. Most Europeans had never heard of the large lands or the millions of people living there. Daily life in late 1400s Spain was shaped by farming, small towns, and the Catholic faith. People traveled by horse or by foot, and kings and queens ruled over the land. Ships were powered by wind and sailed based on the stars. The world felt smaller then, separated by huge oceans. The people Columbus met in the Americas had rich cultures, languages, and ways of living that had grown for thousands of years. Their daily lives included farming, fishing, building homes, and worshiping in their own traditions.
ex06.matters: Columbus’s voyages are important because they connected two parts of the world that had not known each other. This set in motion changes—some wondrous, some very hard. For families of faith, these events led to the founding of countries like the United States, where religious freedom later made the Restoration of the gospel possible. A family can see how Heavenly Father can use even ordinary people, with their strengths and weakness, to accomplish purposes that echo through history. We can talk about the blessings and also the great responsibilities that come with discovery and change.
ex06.scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 says God raised up wise people to establish freedom in America. In 1 Nephi 13:12, the Book of Mormon prophet Nephi has a vision of a man guided by the Spirit across 'the many waters' to the promised land—many Latter-day Saints see this as describing Columbus’s voyage. Columbus’s own writings say he felt guided by God in his journey. The Bible also teaches that great journeys can be led by the Lord, such as with Abraham or Moses (see Genesis 12:1-3 and Exodus 3-4).
ex06.evidence: Historians know a lot about Columbus’s voyages. His own journals and letters have survived, along with reports from his crew. Archaeological finds support stories about the places he landed. We have old maps showing where he sailed, and even today, experts study what the world was like before and after Columbus. Evidence shows there were already millions of people living in the Americas with their own societies. While Columbus opened the door for huge exchanges between continents, these contacts also brought diseases and conflict that had profound effects on native peoples. The date of his first landing (October 12, 1492) and his route are very well established by historical documents.
ex06.learn: From Columbus’s story, we learn that exploring new ideas and places can lead to great blessings, but also challenges. We can see that even big, world-changing events are filled with choices—some wise, some mistaken. Families can learn to recognize the ways Heavenly Father prepares people and places for His work, and also to act with care as we meet new people and places.
ex06.child: Columbus sailed far across the sea because he wanted to find new lands. When he landed, he met people he’d never seen before, and the world was never the same. His trips helped lead to where we live and what we enjoy today.
ex06.talk: Why do you think Columbus felt God was helping him sail to new lands?
