ex07.happened: In 1497, a brave Portuguese explorer named Vasco da Gama set sail from Lisbon, Portugal, on a mission to find a sea route to India. He and his crew sailed south along the coast of Africa, then around the stormy tip known as the Cape of Good Hope. After many months at sea, facing hunger, sickness, and storms, they finally reached the shores of Calicut, India, in 1498. This was the first time Europeans had sailed all the way from Europe to India by sea, instead of traveling over hard and dangerous land routes. Da Gama was welcomed by local rulers, though there were many challenges in making the new trade arrangements work. When he returned home, he brought back spices and valuable goods worth much more than the cost of his voyage. His successful journey opened the door for Europeans, especially the Portuguese, to trade directly with Asia, which changed world trade forever and started a new era of exploration.
ex07.background: At the end of the 15th century, Europe was changing quickly. New inventions like the compass, better ships, and improved maps made it possible for sailors to travel farther than ever before. Most goods from Asia, like spices and silk, reached Europe over land through many middlemen on the Silk Road. This made them very expensive and rare. Ordinary families often never saw such goods. Portugal, a small but determined country, had already sent explorers like Bartolomeu Dias to the coast of Africa, hoping to find a path around it. Vasco da Gama’s voyage was like the next step in a long race. Most people in Europe lived in small towns or the countryside, working as farmers, fishers, or craftsmen, and news of da Gama’s journey would have been both exciting and strange to them.
ex07.matters: Vasco da Gama’s journey changed the way the world traded. By finding a sea route to India, he helped end the monopoly that overland traders had on Asian goods, especially spices. The wealth from this trade helped fund many changes in Europe, including the printing of Bibles and books that supported the spreading of knowledge and faith. For families of faith, these events are reminders that Heavenly Father can use even simple things like ships, trade, and curiosity for His greater purposes—to help the gospel eventually reach more people.
ex07.scripture: The scriptures don’t mention Vasco da Gama or the sea route to India, but they do speak about the Lord preparing ways for His work to be done. In 1 Nephi 17:8-14, the Lord commands Nephi to build a ship to cross the ocean, promising guidance and protection. Acts 8:27-40 also tells us about Philip sharing the gospel with an Ethiopian traveler, showing that the Lord can use travel and trade to carry the gospel further. These passages teach us that new paths, discoveries, and technologies can serve God's purposes in preparing the world for more truth and light.
ex07.evidence: Historians have many records from Portugal about Vasco da Gama’s voyage, including ship logs, letters, and royal documents. Archaeologists have found remains of ships from similar journeys and traded goods in ports across Africa and India that match what was described from da Gama’s time. Portuguese writings and Indian accounts both describe the meeting between Vasco da Gama and the Zamorin of Calicut, showing that this contact really happened. There are also maps from the period that show the expanding knowledge Europeans gained about Africa and Asia after these voyages. The overwhelming agreement among historians is that Vasco da Gama’s journey to India by sea was a real and documentable event.
ex07.learn: From Vasco da Gama’s story, we learn that courage and curiosity can open up new worlds. We also see how inventions and hard work can change many lives, not just the ones on the ships, but families and communities all over the globe. For a family of faith, it’s a reminder that Heavenly Father can use all kinds of events—even business and adventure—to bless His children and prepare the world for greater light and knowledge.
ex07.child: Vasco da Gama got in his boat and sailed all the way from Portugal to India. He found a new way to get spices and treasures by going around Africa, and that changed how people traded. His adventure helped more people in Europe learn and get new things, like books and Bibles.
ex07.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father sometimes lets people find new places or ways to do things?

ex08.happened: In 1519, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan set sail from Spain with a fleet of five ships and approximately 270 men, aiming to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. The journey was fraught with challenges, including treacherous waters, mutinies, and dwindling supplies. After navigating the strait at the southern tip of South America—later named the Strait of Magellan—the expedition entered the vast Pacific Ocean. They endured a grueling three-month crossing before reaching the Philippines in 1521. There, Magellan was killed during a conflict on the island of Mactan. Despite this loss, the expedition pressed on. Under the command of Juan Sebastián Elcano, the remaining crew continued westward, eventually returning to Spain in 1522 aboard the ship Victoria. Out of the original 270 men, only 18 completed the journey, marking the first recorded circumnavigation of the Earth.
ex08.background: In the early 16th century, European nations were fervently seeking new trade routes to access the lucrative spices of the East Indies. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 had divided the newly discovered lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal, prompting Spain to explore westward routes. Daily life for sailors was arduous, with long voyages exposing them to the risks of scurvy, starvation, and shipwreck. Navigation relied on rudimentary tools, and uncharted waters posed constant dangers. The world was still largely unknown to Europeans, and voyages like Magellan's were ventures into the vast, mysterious expanses of the globe.
ex08.matters: Magellan's expedition was a monumental achievement that provided tangible proof of the Earth's roundness and the vastness of its oceans. For families of faith, this journey underscores the unity of Heavenly Father's creation, demonstrating that all lands and peoples are interconnected. The successful circumnavigation paved the way for future exploration and missionary work, making it geographically possible to fulfill the divine mandate to spread the gospel to every nation.
ex08.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the unity and interconnectedness of all God's children. In Acts 17:26, it is stated, "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." This passage highlights the shared heritage and unity of humanity, aligning with the realization brought about by global exploration that all people are part of a single, divine creation.
ex08.evidence: Historical records, including the detailed accounts of Antonio Pigafetta, a member of the expedition, provide firsthand insights into the journey. Archaeological findings, such as artifacts from the voyage and the remains of the ship Victoria, corroborate these accounts. Additionally, navigational charts and maps from the era document the route taken, further validating the expedition's accomplishments.
ex08.learn: Magellan's journey teaches us about the resilience and determination required to explore the unknown. It reminds us of the importance of faith and perseverance in the face of adversity. For families, it serves as an example of how courage and a desire to learn can lead to groundbreaking discoveries that benefit all of humanity.
ex08.child: A long time ago, a man named Magellan sailed around the world, showing that the Earth is round. His journey helped people understand that we are all connected.
ex08.talk: How do you think Magellan's journey helped people learn more about the world?

ex09.happened: Between 1768 and 1779, Captain James Cook, a British naval officer and explorer, sailed across the vast Pacific Ocean on three separate voyages. Starting in Plymouth, England, Cook led the HMS Endeavour and later two other ships to places European maps hardly touched. On his first voyage, he sailed to Tahiti to observe the passing of Venus across the sun, which would help astronomers calculate the distance from Earth to the sun. Afterward, he mapped the coastlines of New Zealand, proving there were two main islands, and then charted much of the eastern coast of Australia, being the first European to do so in detail. Along these journeys, Cook and his crew made first European contact with many Pacific islanders, including the Māori of New Zealand and the Aboriginal Australians. On his later voyages, Cook traveled further north to the Hawaiian Islands, where he also became the first known European visitor. Sadly, during his third voyage, Cook died in Hawaii during a conflict. His voyages changed maps and brought the cultures, plants, and animals of the Pacific Islands into European awareness.
ex09.background: Before Captain Cook’s voyages, European knowledge of the world’s oceans and distant lands was limited. Sailors and mapmakers from Portugal, Spain, and the Netherlands had charted parts of the Pacific, but vast regions were blank or filled with guesses. The people of Polynesia, Australia, and New Zealand had rich cultures, centuries-old traditions, and expert navigation skills, moving between islands by reading stars and ocean currents long before Europeans arrived. In places like Tahiti, life was guided by chiefs and priests, with fishing, farming, and gathering at the heart of daily tasks. In England, the Enlightenment was taking hold—an age of seeking knowledge, science, and discovery. Cook himself had risen from humble beginnings, learning navigation and math as a sailor before being chosen to lead these great voyages.
ex09.matters: Captain Cook’s explorations opened new connections between peoples and lands that had long been apart. For families of faith, these voyages mattered because they made the way safer and clearer for those who would follow, including missionaries. Within about a lifetime after Cook’s arrival, missionaries—including those from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints—came to share the gospel in New Zealand and Hawaii. Today, these islands are home to strong and vibrant Latter-day Saint communities. Cook’s careful mapping also set an example of preparing the way for others, much like how families prepare the way for each other in faith and love.
ex09.scripture: The scriptures do not mention Captain Cook, but the idea of exploring new lands and sharing knowledge is woven throughout. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:79, saints are told to seek learning "by study and also by faith"—including about the earth, its kingdoms, and peoples. In the Bible, the Lord often sends travelers to prepare His work, like Paul’s missionary journeys in Acts. The Book of Mormon also teaches that the Lord guides people across the waters to new lands (1 Nephi 18). These passages remind us that journeys, maps, and learning can serve Heavenly Father’s purposes.
ex09.evidence: Historians have many detailed records of Cook’s voyages, including his own journals, crew logs, and maps made during the trips. These documents match with the places he visited, and many locations in New Zealand, Australia, and Hawaii still remember his arrival. Archaeological digs have found evidence of his visits, and museums preserve objects collected on the voyages. Polynesian oral histories recall encounters with Europeans, often describing Cook’s ships and crew from the Islanders’ point of view. While there are debates about the effects of these meetings on island peoples, the events themselves are well documented. Cook’s charts of the Pacific were so precise that navigators used them for decades afterward.
ex09.learn: From Cook’s story, we can learn the value of exploring, learning, and preparing the way for others. Sometimes, going into the unknown is part of how we keep growing, both in faith and as a family. Mapping new places took courage and careful attention, just like learning new things or serving others does today. We also learn how important it is to respect and learn from other cultures, as many of those Cook met had lessons and skills of their own, given by God.
ex09.child: Captain Cook sailed really far from England to islands in the big Pacific Ocean. He made maps so other people could find their way, too. Some of the places he visited later became homes for lots of church members, like Hawaii and New Zealand.
ex09.talk: Why do you think it was brave for Captain Cook to sail to places no one from his country had seen before?

ex10.happened: In 1804, two men named Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out from a place called Camp Dubois in Illinois with a group called the Corps of Discovery. Their mission was to explore the huge stretch of land the United States had just bought from France—known as the Louisiana Territory—and try to find a route all the way to the Pacific Ocean. For over two years, Lewis, Clark, and their team traveled up the wide Missouri River, over the steep Rocky Mountains, and down the fast rivers to the Pacific coast. Along the way, they met many Native American nations, some of whom helped them with food and directions. The group carefully mapped the land, wrote down their discoveries, and collected plants and animals new to science—over 300 species in all. When they finally reached the Pacific Ocean, they built a home for winter called Fort Clatsop. When spring came, they made the long journey back to St. Louis. Their 8,000-mile trip helped the United States learn what the land was like, where rivers and mountains stood, and who lived there.
ex10.background: In 1803, the United States doubled in size almost overnight by purchasing the land from France in the Louisiana Purchase. Most Americans lived east of the Mississippi River, in cities and towns, with few knowing what lay beyond. This was a time before cars, trains, or even good roads—most travel was by riverboat, horseback, or walking. Lewis and Clark were both former soldiers chosen for their experience and care. Their team included French interpreters, men skilled at hunting and carpentry, a young Native American mother named Sacagawea who helped them communicate and survive, and Clark’s enslaved man York. For many Native peoples, these new visitors marked the beginning of huge changes. Daily life for most Americans meant working farms, making clothes by hand, and living close to the land.
ex10.matters: Lewis and Clark’s journey matters because it opened up the West for new families, settlers, and future explorers. Their maps and reports let others know the land could be crossed, and that it had rich resources and beauty. For families of faith, we can see this as an example of preparation—Heavenly Father let good people gather knowledge so others could follow safely later. Without their careful notes across Wyoming, Idaho, and the Rockies, it might have been much harder for pioneers—including those led by the Prophet Brigham Young—to make their way to the Salt Lake Valley.
ex10.scripture: No scripture tells the story of Lewis and Clark directly, but their journey shows the value of seeking knowledge, exploring new lands, and preparing the way for others. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:78–80, the Lord commands us to seek learning by study and by faith and to prepare ourselves in all things. Their efforts can also remind us of Nephi’s journey into the wilderness, trusting the Lord would prepare a way (1 Nephi 3:7). Both stories teach how faith and diligent work can help people do hard things for good reasons.
ex10.evidence: The story of Lewis and Clark is very well supported by evidence. Their journals, letters, and maps are preserved and studied by historians and scientists today. Many places along their route have been identified by the things they described—rivers, mountains, plants, and animals. Their discoveries, such as prairie dogs and grizzly bears, matched what scientists later found in those places. Archaeologists have found remains of forts, campsites, and trading sites where the Corps of Discovery passed, and museums display items and drawings from the expedition. Descendants of Native American tribes remember the visitors and keep their own records. Because of all this evidence, historians are certain the journey happened much as the journals describe.
ex10.learn: We can learn from Lewis and Clark that preparing, working together with people who have different strengths, and trusting in a good purpose can help us do things that seem impossible. Their teamwork with each other and with Native peoples made their survival possible. Just as they paved a path for others, we too might be preparing ways for others without realizing it, and Heavenly Father can guide us as we do hard things for His work.
ex10.child: Lewis and Clark went on a long trip across wild country that no one from their country had seen before. They made maps and found out what animals and plants lived there, so other people could travel safely later. People could travel west because Lewis and Clark found the way.
ex10.talk: How can learning new things help your family or someone who will come after you?

ex11.happened: In December 1831, Charles Darwin, a young naturalist, embarked on a five-year journey aboard the HMS Beagle, a British naval ship set to survey the coastlines of South America and other regions. During this voyage, Darwin meticulously observed and collected a vast array of specimens, including plants, animals, and fossils. In 1835, the Beagle reached the Galápagos Islands, a remote archipelago in the Pacific Ocean. There, Darwin noted subtle differences among species from one island to another, particularly among finches. These observations led him to consider how species might change over time. Upon returning to England in 1836, Darwin collaborated with experts to analyze his collections. His studies culminated in the publication of "On the Origin of Species" in 1859, where he introduced the theory of natural selection, proposing that species evolve over generations through the survival and reproduction of individuals best suited to their environments.
ex11.background: In the early 19th century, the prevailing belief in Europe was that species were unchanging creations. The idea that species could evolve was not widely accepted. Charles Darwin, born in 1809, initially studied medicine and theology before developing a keen interest in natural history. The HMS Beagle's voyage provided him with an unparalleled opportunity to explore diverse ecosystems and gather extensive data, challenging existing notions about the natural world.
ex11.matters: Darwin's work revolutionized our understanding of biology, introducing the concept that all species, including humans, share common ancestors and have evolved over time. For families of faith, this perspective can deepen appreciation for the complexity and diversity of life, reflecting the grandeur of Heavenly Father's creations. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has stated that it has no official position on the theory of evolution, emphasizing that the details of the physical creation are matters for scientific study, while affirming that humans are children of God.
ex11.scripture: While the scriptures do not provide specific details about the mechanisms of creation, they affirm that God is the Creator of all things. In the Book of Moses, it is written, "And I, God, created all things... spiritually, before they were naturally upon the face of the earth" (Moses 3:5). This passage emphasizes that all creation is divinely orchestrated, though the exact processes are not detailed.
ex11.evidence: Historical records, including Darwin's own journals and correspondence, provide detailed accounts of his observations and the development of his theories. The specimens he collected, particularly the finches from the Galápagos Islands, are preserved in museums and have been studied extensively, offering tangible evidence of the variations that inspired his ideas. Modern genetic research has further supported the concept of common ancestry among species, aligning with Darwin's conclusions.
ex11.learn: Darwin's journey teaches us the value of curiosity and careful observation in understanding the world around us. It reminds us that seeking knowledge, both spiritual and scientific, can lead to profound insights about our existence and the wonders of creation.
ex11.child: Long ago, a man named Charles Darwin sailed on a big ship to faraway places. He saw many different animals and plants and wondered how they became so different. His questions helped people learn more about how all living things are connected.
ex11.talk: What do you think we can learn from studying the different animals and plants that Heavenly Father created?

ex12.happened: On July 20, 1969, two American astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, became the first humans to walk on the moon. Their spaceship, Apollo 11, launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida and traveled about 240,000 miles to reach the moon. After four days in space, their lunar module called the Eagle landed in a flat area named the Sea of Tranquility. Millions of people watched on television as Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface and spoke the famous words: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Buzz Aldrin joined him moments later, and together they spent about two and a half hours walking, collecting moon rocks, and taking photos. Their safe return to Earth was a huge moment for people everywhere, showing what can be achieved when many minds and hands work together. The moon landing became a symbol of hope, courage, and the power of technology to reach new heights.
ex12.background: The 1960s were a time of immense change and challenge in the world. The United States and the Soviet Union were locked in a race to space, each determined to prove their strength and innovation. Yuri Gagarin from the Soviet Union became the first person in space in 1961, which inspired America's President John F. Kennedy to set a goal: land a man on the moon before the decade ended. Ordinary families watched news of these events on black and white TVs. Many people lived with the memory of recent wars and hoped science could bring peace and progress. The men who flew to the moon were test pilots, engineers, and scientists—brave, but also regular people with families waiting for them back home. They depended on thousands of ground crew, technicians, and planners, mostly in their twenties and thirties, showing that great things can happen when people work closely together.
ex12.matters: For everyone on Earth, seeing humans land on another world made the impossible seem possible. Families realized how small and precious our planet is when photos showed the Earth floating like a blue marble in the vast dark of space. For families of faith, the moon landing echoes beliefs about human potential and our divine heritage. Exploring God's creations, even beyond our own world, can help us feel awe and gratitude for His handiwork. This moment also reminds us that curiosity and courage, when guided by righteous desires, can bless everyone.
ex12.scripture: The scriptures speak about the greatness of God's creations and the eternal potential of His children. In Doctrine and Covenants 130:10–11, it is taught that all the worlds and their inhabitants are part of Heavenly Father's plan, and that knowledge of these worlds will become known to the faithful. Genesis 1 in the Bible tells of God creating the moon and stars to give light and be signs for seasons. The experience of seeing the Earth from the moon also aligns with scriptures teaching that we are all one family under God, sharing a common home, as seen in Acts 17:26.
ex12.evidence: There is strong evidence confirming the Apollo 11 moon landing. Physical samples such as moon rocks, which are different from any material found on Earth, have been studied by scientists across the world. Thousands of photos and hours of video were broadcast during the mission, and the exact moment Armstrong stepped onto the moon was shown live to millions. Equipment left on the lunar surface by the astronauts, such as scientific instruments and the American flag, can still be observed using modern space cameras. Testimonies from astronauts, engineers, and international observers, plus detailed mission records, make it one of the best-documented events in history.
ex12.learn: The story of the moon landing teaches us to never stop reaching for worthy dreams, no matter how impossible they seem. With faith, teamwork, and hard work, barriers can be overcome. Exploring new frontiers—even the moon—can help us appreciate the beauty of our earth, the power of human unity, and the wonders of creation that Heavenly Father invites us to discover.
ex12.child: People from Earth flew to the moon in a rocket and walked on it. They were brave and worked with lots of helpers. God wants us to learn about all His amazing creations.
ex12.talk: How do you think the astronauts felt seeing Earth from the moon for the first time?

mg01.happened: Around 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, a small group of modern humans, people just like us called Homo sapiens, began a long journey out of East Africa. Leaving the grasslands and forests that had been their home for thousands of years, these families traveled into new lands—first to the Middle East, then much further into Asia, and eventually across the globe. Their journey took generations. Step by step, their children and grandchildren followed rivers, crossed dry lands, and learned to live with new plants and animals. Over thousands of years, their descendants spread into Europe, Australia, and later the Americas. This journey was one of the most important in all of human history. DNA studies have shown that every person alive today can trace at least a part of their ancestry to this first migration out of Africa. It means that all of us, no matter where we live or what we look like, are part of one big human family who started out together.
mg01.background: Before this great migration, the world was much quieter than today. Modern humans lived in small, close-knit groups in Africa. They used stone tools, cooked over fires, and worked together to hunt animals, gather plants, and care for their families. Life was simple but challenging. There was no writing, metal, or cities—everything people knew was passed from parent to child by showing and storytelling. Other kinds of humans, like Neanderthals and Denisovans, also lived in different parts of the world, but it was the Homo sapiens of Africa who would eventually fill every continent. Nights were dark except for the stars and firelight, and every day was shaped by the search for food, water, and safety.
mg01.matters: This event matters because it shows how all people are connected by family lines that go back to the same beginnings. For families who want to follow Heavenly Father, it teaches us not to fear or judge those who look or live differently from us. We are truly brothers and sisters, called to love and learn from each other. Understanding our shared history helps us appreciate the richness of every nation and culture, knowing Heavenly Father invites all His children to come unto Him and work together to build His family across the earth.
mg01.scripture: While the scriptures do not tell about this migration directly, they teach the principle that God created men and women, and that all are alike unto Him (Genesis 1:27; 2 Nephi 26:33). The Apostle Paul declared in Acts 17:26 that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men." This matches what science has uncovered—that all humans share common ancestors. The Gospel also teaches that we are all literally children of God (Romans 8:16), linked by ancestry and spirit.
mg01.evidence: Scientists have found strong evidence for this migration using DNA from living people all over the world. Studies show that genetic differences between people today are very small, and all humans living outside Africa have traces of common early ancestors who once lived in Africa about 60,000 years ago. Archaeologists have also found ancient tools and fossils along routes from Africa into the Middle East and further into Asia, supporting the idea of gradual movement over thousands of years. While some details are still studied and debated, the overall pattern of humans spreading out from Africa is widely accepted among scientists today.
mg01.learn: From this journey, we learn that our differences in culture and appearance are part of the beauty and gift of being human, designed by our Heavenly Father. The great migration teaches us to seek understanding and unity, remembering that everyone we meet is truly part of our extended family. Trusting that Heavenly Father guides His children throughout history allows us to look for His hand in the stories of all people.
mg01.child: Long ago, our great-great-great grandparents left Africa and spread across the world. That means all people are part of one big family. We are all more alike than we are different!
mg01.talk: What do you think it would be like to leave your home and travel to a new land, not knowing what you would find?

mg02.happened: During the last Ice Age, between approximately 25,000 and 10,000 BC, sea levels were significantly lower due to vast amounts of water being locked in glaciers. This drop in sea levels exposed a landmass known as the Bering Land Bridge, or Beringia, connecting what are now Siberia and Alaska. This land bridge provided a route for humans and animals to migrate from Asia into North America. Early hunter-gatherer groups, following herds of large mammals like mammoths and bison, traversed this bridge, gradually spreading throughout the Americas. Over thousands of years, these groups adapted to diverse environments, from the Arctic tundra to tropical forests, becoming the ancestors of the indigenous peoples of North and South America.
mg02.background: The world during this period was characterized by extensive ice sheets covering large parts of the Northern Hemisphere. In regions not covered by ice, such as parts of Siberia and Alaska, tundra and steppe environments prevailed, supporting herds of large mammals. Human groups in these areas were nomadic hunter-gatherers, relying on these animals for food, clothing, and tools. The Bering Land Bridge itself was not a barren expanse but featured a variety of ecosystems, including grasslands and wetlands, providing resources for both humans and animals. Recent research suggests that the landscape of the Bering Land Bridge was more boggy and featured meandering rivers, which may have influenced migration patterns.
mg02.matters: The migration across the Bering Land Bridge is a foundational event in human history, marking the beginning of human presence in the Americas. For families of faith, this migration underscores the belief that Heavenly Father has guided His children across the earth, placing them in various lands to fulfill His purposes. Understanding this event helps us appreciate the diversity and resilience of human societies and the shared heritage of all God's children.
mg02.scripture: While the scriptures do not provide specific details about the migration across the Bering Land Bridge, they affirm that Heavenly Father has a plan for all His children and guides them according to His purposes. In the Book of Mormon, the Lord led Lehi's family to the Americas, indicating that the land was prepared for His people (1 Nephi 2:2-4). This principle suggests that the migration of ancient peoples to the Americas was also part of His divine plan.
mg02.evidence: Archaeological and genetic evidence supports the theory of human migration across the Bering Land Bridge. Artifacts such as stone tools and animal remains have been found in Alaska and other parts of North America, dating back to around 14,000 years ago. Genetic studies show a connection between indigenous peoples of the Americas and populations in Siberia, indicating a common ancestry. Recent research has also revealed that the Bering Land Bridge was submerged until about 35,700 years ago, suggesting that the window for migration was shorter than previously thought.
mg02.learn: This event teaches us about the adaptability and resilience of human beings, who have migrated and settled in diverse environments throughout history. It also reminds us of the interconnectedness of all people and the shared journey of humanity. For families of faith, it highlights the belief that Heavenly Father has a plan for all His children, guiding them to fulfill their divine potential.
mg02.child: A long time ago, when much of the world was covered in ice, people walked from Asia to America across a land bridge. They followed animals like mammoths and bison to find food and new places to live. These people became the ancestors of Native Americans.
mg02.talk: How do you think the first people felt when they arrived in a new land?

mg03.happened: Between about 3000 and 1000 BC, brave families set out in long, strong outrigger canoes, sailing away from Taiwan and Southeast Asia. These were the ancestors of the Polynesian people. They weren’t just following a breeze; they read the stars, watched how the ocean waves moved, and paid close attention to where birds flew. Some of these journeys stretched over thousands of miles of open water. These travelers found new homes on islands scattered far apart—places like Samoa, Tonga, Tahiti, Hawaii, New Zealand, and Easter Island. Bit by bit, they became the settlers of the greatest ocean migration in human history. They carried with them seeds, animals, stories, and traditions. What made this even more amazing is that they repeated these voyages, linking far-off islands together in a web of trade and kinship, growing into many different but related Polynesian cultures. Today, their descendants remember these voyages with pride, and their skills are still honored and even practiced by modern navigators, keeping their old knowledge alive.
mg03.background: The world of the early Polynesians was warm and full of mystery, with islands separated by large stretches of ocean. Before these voyages, families and small groups lived in southeastern Asia, Taiwan, and nearby lands. Most people farmed, fished, and made things by hand—tools, pottery, and canoes from what the land and sea provided. Daily life came with risks and joys: watching the weather, tending crops like taro, and cooking meals over fires. Strong families and oral traditions passed down stories and skills. As populations grew and people needed new resources, some families set out to sea, trusting in their knowledge and in each other. They brought with them not just their tools and foods, but songs, names, and deep respect for their ancestors, who they believed helped guide them to safe harbors.
mg03.matters: This matters because it shows how families, using wisdom and courage, could cross incredible distances and create new homes. For families of faith, it can remind us that Heavenly Father is in the details, preparing a way for His children. The skills of these voyagers—watching nature and trusting guidance—echo the gospel principle of seeking direction from heaven. The Polynesian legacy is seen today in their strong family ties and respect for genealogy, which connects deeply with Latter-day Saint beliefs. Their story helps inspire us to be brave, work together, and remember those who came before us.
mg03.scripture: While Polynesian migrations aren’t directly described in scripture, the Book of Mormon teaches that God can guide people to new lands when they listen for His voice and trust in His way (see 1 Nephi 18:22-23, Ether 6:4-12). The Bible contains similar journeys, like the children of Israel following Moses. The principle that God prepares lands and people for His purposes is found throughout scripture (see Alma 37:7, Isaiah 42:16). The faith, preparation, and unity of the Polynesian voyagers reflect these same divine patterns.
mg03.evidence: Archaeologists and scientists have found strong evidence that Polynesian ancestors began their great migrations from Taiwan and Southeast Asia. They studied ancient pottery, DNA from living people and ancient remains, and the languages spoken across the Pacific. All show that people spread out over huge distances and that many island groups share a common heritage. Modern sailors from Polynesian cultures have shown it is possible to sail long distances using traditional tools—no compass or maps—by carefully watching stars and waves. The story is mostly confirmed, though exact dates and routes are still studied. Trustworthy sources, including the Smithsonian and National Geographic, agree that this is one of humankind’s greatest achievements.
mg03.learn: We can learn that Heavenly Father gives people gifts and talents to accomplish things that may seem impossible. By working together, using the knowledge of the past, and trusting in Him, families can face new challenges bravely. The story of Polynesian voyagers is a reminder to honor our ancestors and use our gifts to bless others.
mg03.child: A long time ago, people sailed huge canoes across the biggest ocean in the world using just stars and nature to guide them. They found and settled new islands and became the first families in places like Hawaii and New Zealand. Today, their grandchildren still remember those hero journeys.
mg03.talk: What do you think it would feel like to travel across the ocean with only the stars to guide you?

mg04.happened: Around 1450 BC, the Israelites, who had lived in Egypt for generations, were finally set free from harsh slavery. This great movement, called the Exodus, began when Moses, chosen by God, courageously approached Pharaoh, the ruler of Egypt, many times with messages from God, asking him to let the Israelite people go. Pharaoh refused again and again, even as Egypt suffered through ten terrible plagues. Finally, after the last and most sorrowful plague, the death of the firstborn, Pharaoh agreed to let them leave. So, in the night, and in haste, hundreds of thousands of Israelite men, plus their families—women, children, and the elderly—gathered their belongings and left their homes in Goshen. They traveled together into the wilderness, led by Moses, with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night as signs of the Lord’s presence. Leaving behind a lifetime of bondage, they crossed the Red Sea, which God parted for them, and began a long and challenging journey through the desert wilderness. For forty years, the Israelites wandered, learning to rely on God for their daily needs like food, water, and guidance. During this time, they became a united people, receiving commandments and promises from God, shaping them into a nation ready for a new life in the land God had promised to their ancestors.
mg04.background: The Israelites were a group of families descended from Jacob (also called Israel), who came to Egypt during a famine and were welcomed at first. Over the centuries, the Israelites grew into a large people, but the Egyptians feared their numbers and made them slaves. The world at this time was ruled by powerful kingdoms, and Egypt, with its mighty pharaohs, great monuments, and strong armies, was among the richest. Daily life for Israelite slaves was harsh, full of hard work making bricks and building cities for the Egyptians. Egyptian religion was filled with many gods and festivals. For the Israelites, life was mostly about survival, family, and quiet remembrance of their God’s promises, whispered from one generation to the next.
mg04.matters: The Exodus is a central story for people of faith because it marks a moment when God reached out to free an entire nation, not just individuals. For families, this story shows how God can guide us through hard times to become something more than we were before. It matters in world history, too, as the birth of Israel as a people and a faith, whose story shaped many later faiths—including Christianity and Islam. The journey shows that God’s help sometimes comes in difficult, patient ways, preparing people and families for special purposes.
mg04.scripture: The Book of Exodus in the Old Testament, chapters 1-20, tells this story in detail, including the escape, the Red Sea crossing, and the giving of the Ten Commandments at Sinai. In the New Testament, Paul talks about the Exodus in 1 Corinthians 10, calling it a foreshadowing, or type, of Christ’s saving role. The Book of Mormon refers to the Exodus as an example of God’s power to deliver His people (1 Nephi 17:23-42), and Doctrine and Covenants 103:16 uses it as a promise of deliverance for later saints.
mg04.evidence: While there is strong tradition and scripture behind the Exodus story, historians and archaeologists still debate its exact details. No large-scale physical evidence for such a migration has been found in Egypt or Sinai to match the Bible’s numbers and timeline. However, some scholars think small groups of Semitic people did leave Egypt over time, and Egyptian records do mention foreign slaves and plagues, though not in a way that clearly matches the Bible’s account. Archaeology does show that the areas described, like Goshen and Sinai, were inhabited and traveled through. While the exact details remain uncertain, the story has deeply shaped Jewish, Christian, and Muslim faith traditions and identities.
mg04.learn: We can learn that God sometimes leads His people on hard journeys to prepare them for great blessings ahead. Even when help does not come quickly, or in the way we expect, faith and patience can turn hardship into a chance to grow and trust in God’s promises. Like the Israelites, families today can rely on God for guidance and daily help in their own wilderness moments.
mg04.child: God helped Moses lead His people out of Egypt, across the sea, and through the desert so they could be free. Even when things were hard, God was always with them, helping them learn and grow. Sometimes our journeys are hard, too, but God never leaves us alone.
mg04.talk: Why do you think God let the Israelites spend so many years in the wilderness before reaching their new home?

mg05.happened: Around 600 years before Jesus was born, Heavenly Father told a man named Lehi, who lived in Jerusalem, to take his family and leave their home. Jerusalem was about to be taken over and destroyed. Lehi listened to Heavenly Father's warning and led his family into the wilderness. At first, they traveled on foot, moving south along the hot, dry deserts of Arabia. Lehi’s sons returned to the city briefly to get their sacred scriptures, called the plates of brass, and brought back others who joined their journey, including Ishmael’s family. Together, they faced many hardships—hunger, heat, and disagreements—but they kept going because they believed God was guiding them. After years in the desert, they reached a beautiful, green place near the sea which they called Bountiful. There, the Lord told Nephi, one of Lehi’s sons, how to build a ship. With faith and help from Heaven, they built the ship and sailed across a great ocean, arriving at a promised land—described as somewhere in the Americas. This journey was hard and took great faith, but it set the stage for a new people and story.
mg05.background: Jerusalem at this time was a busy, walled city, home to many families and trades, ruled by kings who sometimes followed God and sometimes turned away. Lehi and his family were part of the House of Israel, descendants of Abraham. Families then often lived together in small, close homes, gathering food from markets, caring for livestock, and following ancient laws. The city streets would have been noisy and crowded, with merchants selling goods and priests teaching at the temple. But around Lehi, things were changing. The Assyrian and Babylonian empires were growing strong, and soon Jerusalem would be threatened and attacked. Lehi’s neighbors may not have understood why he left, but his family trusted Heavenly Father’s guidance.
mg05.matters: Lehi’s journey is important for many reasons. For families who believe, this story shows how trusting Heavenly Father—even when His directions are hard—can open the way for blessings. This migration brought the scriptures and the covenant promises to a new land, beginning the story that would become the Book of Mormon. The faith of Lehi’s family is a pattern for how we, too, can listen for God’s guidance and trust Him to lead us to safe places, even when we cannot see the whole path. The story reminds us that Heavenly Father cares for all His children, preparing ways for them to be safe and close to Him.
mg05.scripture: The Book of Mormon (1 Nephi chapters 1–18) tells the full story of Lehi’s journey, including his visions, their travels, and building the ship. The Old Testament, specifically 2 Kings and Jeremiah, describes the time of Jerusalem’s captivity and prophets warning the people, helping us understand the world Lehi left. The Doctrine and Covenants section 10 speaks about the coming forth of the Book of Mormon as another witness of Christ, tied to this family’s record. Together, these scriptures show how God’s plan works across the world.
mg05.evidence: Historians and archaeologists acknowledge the Babylonian threat to Jerusalem around 600 BC and the city’s eventual destruction. The route Lehi’s family took—from Jerusalem through Arabia—matches some real ancient trade paths and desert locations. Possible connections to the place Bountiful and the kind of ship Nephi built have been studied, but so far, no direct evidence has been found of Lehi’s specific family or their migration to the Americas. Many scholars view this migration as a matter of faith, as archaeological proof for Lehi’s crossing to the Americas has not been discovered. However, some details described in the Book of Mormon, such as the existence of ancient scriptural records on metal plates and certain desert locations, have some support in historical studies. The story’s core remains a matter of belief.
mg05.learn: Lehi's journey reminds us that Heavenly Father sometimes asks us to do hard things, not to punish us, but to bless and protect us. Their migration shows the importance of keeping God's word with us, listening to His guidance, and working together as a family even when the way is difficult. We learn to trust, to try again after hardships, and that new beginnings often come after we leave behind what we already know.
mg05.child: Lehi’s family left their home because Heavenly Father asked them to, even though it was scary and hard. They traveled a long way and built a ship to sail to a new land. Heavenly Father helped them because they trusted Him and stayed together.
mg05.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father sometimes asks us to do things that are hard or unknown?

mg06.happened: In the years after Jesus Christ lived, Jerusalem and the land called Judea were under Roman control. In 70 AD, after a long conflict with the Jewish people, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem, including its temple, which had been at the heart of Jewish worship for centuries. This event was not only a military defeat but shattered the center of Jewish religious life. Many people were killed or taken away as slaves, and the survivors were left without a country or a temple. In 135 AD, after another uprising called the Bar Kokhba Revolt, the Romans decided to force the remaining Jewish people to leave Judea entirely. They banned Jews from entering Jerusalem and sent them to live in other places throughout the empire. Jewish families spread out—some went to large cities like Rome and Alexandria, while others traveled as far as Spain, North Africa, Babylon (now Iraq), Persia, and even further. Over time, Jewish communities sprang up all across the known world. Even without a homeland, these communities held on to their faith, traditions, and most especially, the Hebrew scriptures. Over hundreds of years, they became the stewards of these writings, ensuring their careful copying and reading, even as they lived far from the land of their ancestors.
mg06.background: Before the Roman destruction, Jerusalem was not only the Jewish religious capital but also a vibrant city filled with markets, families, and daily prayers at the temple. For centuries, Jews had lived in Judea, with their own festivals, foods, and laws. The Romans, who ruled a huge empire stretching from Britain to Egypt, controlled the land and often clashed with the Jewish people, who wanted to worship God in their own way. Daily life in Judea included farming, trading, gathering for Sabbath, and raising families with strong community ties. But political unrest and harsh Roman taxes made life increasingly difficult. After multiple revolts against Rome, Jewish people faced severe punishments. Many lost their homes and were forced to move, becoming strangers in new and sometimes unfriendly places.
mg06.matters: The Jewish diaspora matters because it shaped both Jewish and world history. For families of faith, it’s a reminder that even in times of great hardship, God’s purposes can move forward. Because Jews were scattered across many lands, the Hebrew scriptures—the writings we know as the Old Testament—were carefully preserved in many different regions. Without this scattering, the scriptures might have been lost or changed. When the Dead Sea Scrolls were discovered in the 20th century, they matched the scriptures the diaspora had protected for so long, showing just how faithfully the scriptures were preserved. This event helps us see how God can use even difficult events to keep His word safe for future generations.
mg06.scripture: The Bible speaks of the scattering and gathering of Israel throughout its pages. In Deuteronomy 28:64, the Lord warns that Israel will be scattered among all peoples. Jesus also foretells the destruction of Jerusalem in Matthew 24:1-2. The Book of Mormon frequently teaches that the house of Israel would be scattered and later gathered again (see 1 Nephi 22:3-5). Doctrine and Covenants 110:11 refers to the return of Elijah to 'turn the hearts.' While these scriptures do not give all the historical details, they teach that God remembers His people even when they are scattered, and His promises will be fulfilled.
mg06.evidence: There is strong historical and archaeological evidence supporting the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD and the later Jewish expulsion in 135 AD. Roman historians like Josephus wrote about the siege and fall of Jerusalem, describing the devastation and its aftermath. Archaeologists have found Roman camp remains, burnt layers in Jerusalem, and Jewish artifacts in lands far from Judea, showing where Jews migrated. Synagogue ruins, ancient inscriptions, and Jewish graveyards across the Mediterranean and Middle East from this period confirm that Jewish communities took root in many places. The accuracy of the Hebrew scriptures over 2,000 years, as seen by comparing them with the Dead Sea Scrolls, is a powerful testament to their careful preservation during the diaspora.
mg06.learn: From this event, we learn that faith can survive even when people are separated from their homes and traditions. Sometimes, events that seem painful or difficult can actually help preserve important truths for future generations. The perseverance of the Jewish people shows the strength of community, tradition, and the importance of keeping sacred records safe. It reminds us to treasure the scriptures and our own faith heritage because they connect us to those who came before.
mg06.child: A long time ago, Romans made the Jewish people leave their homes. They traveled far and made new homes, carrying their special Bible stories with them. Because they were careful, we still have those stories today.
mg06.talk: How do you think the Jewish people felt when they had to leave their home, and what helped them stay strong?

mg07.happened: Between the years 800 and 1100 AD, Norse Vikings from Scandinavia set out on long sea journeys that changed world history. Leaving from what is now Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, these explorers, traders, and settlers sailed westward into the cold North Atlantic, reaching places few Europeans had ever seen. In 874, they settled Iceland—an island untouched by humans. Later, in 985, Erik the Red and his followers sailed even farther and started small farming colonies in the southern parts of Greenland. Most remarkably, around the year 1000, another group led by Leif Erikson reached the shores of North America, a place they called Vinland. This happened about five centuries before Christopher Columbus would cross the Atlantic. While the Vikings did build some houses and stayed for a few seasons, they did not create lasting settlements in North America. The Vikings also traveled east, founding new towns in what is now Russia and exploring rivers all the way to Constantinople and even trading in North Africa. Their ships, skills, and curiosity allowed them to reach places no one from Europe had before, but in time their settlements in Greenland faded, and their visits to North America became part of legend until rediscovered in modern times.
mg07.background: Before the time of Viking expansion, Northern Europe was home to farming and fishing communities that were tough and inventive. The climate was cold, and life could be harsh. The Norse people, whom we now call Vikings, lived in wooden houses, raised animals, and believed in many gods and legends. They became expert sailors, building longboats that could travel across open seas as well as shallow rivers. Families often moved together on these journeys, seeking new lands for farming and better living. The world was quite small in what people knew and traveled, but the Vikings’ skills made the world bigger. They were not just raiders or warriors—they were also traders, settlers, and storytellers.
mg07.matters: The Viking voyages across the Atlantic matter because they were the first known contacts between Europe and the Americas. Though these settlements faded, the Vikings proved it was possible to cross those great waters. For families of faith, it gives a glimpse into how Heavenly Father unfolds His plan over centuries. The Vikings arrived in North America but only stayed briefly. Later, the timing of the full opening of the Americas would be carefully prepared, leading to religious freedom and the Restoration. This teaches patience and respect for God’s timing in all things, big and small.
mg07.scripture: There is no scripture that tells directly of the Vikings, but scriptures do teach that God ‘doeth all things in wisdom and order’ (Alma 37:12). Acts 17:26 teaches that God ‘hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation,’ meaning God has a plan for each people and land. Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints believe the discovery and settlement of the Americas was guided to allow the Restoration to happen. We trust in Heavenly Father’s timing, even when brave explorers like the Vikings came before the world was prepared.
mg07.evidence: Historical and archaeological evidence clearly shows Vikings reached Greenland and Iceland, with farms, churches, and burial sites found there. At L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada, archaeologists unearthed remains of Norse-style buildings and iron tools dating from around the year 1000. These match exactly the kinds of structures Vikings built elsewhere. Today, historians are sure these are the real homes of Viking explorers in North America. Written Norse sagas tell of voyages to ‘Vinland,’ describing lands rich with resources. While the exact locations of all their landings remain uncertain, the evidence of temporary Viking presence in North America is settled by modern science.
mg07.learn: The story of the Vikings reminds us that courage, curiosity, and skill can lead to great discoveries, even if we cannot see all the results right away. Sometimes the good things we do prepare the way for blessings in the future, in God’s timing, not ours. We learn to be patient, to seek truth, and to honor the journeys of those who came before us, trusting Heavenly Father’s plan for every family and land.
mg07.child: A thousand years ago, Vikings from far across the sea found new lands like Iceland, Greenland, and even North America. They built homes and boats, and sailed in places where no one from Europe had been before. Even though they left, they showed others it was possible to reach these new lands.
mg07.talk: Why do you think the Vikings came to new lands and then left them behind?

mg08.happened: Between 1095 and 1300 AD, people called Crusaders journeyed from countries like France, England, Germany, and Italy toward the Holy Land: places such as Jerusalem, Antioch, and Acre. These Crusaders were mostly Christians who felt called to take back Jerusalem and Christian holy sites from Muslim rulers. The first large wave set out in 1096 after Pope Urban II asked knights and regular folk to go on a 'holy war.' Over eight major Crusades, hundreds of thousands traveled, but the journey was long and dangerous. Many died from illness, hunger, or in battles along the way. Some Crusaders stayed in the Holy Land and built states, making new towns and strong castles. Trade between Europe and the Middle East grew quickly, as spices, cloth, and new ideas moved along with people. Not everyone who went fought in wars; some wanted to see the places where Jesus had lived. Whether or not they reached Jerusalem, few ever made it home, and the Holy Land remained mostly under Muslim rule. Through all their efforts, the Crusaders left a mark on both Europe and the Middle East, changing language, art, food, and how people saw the world for centuries to come.
mg08.background: Europe in the 11th and 12th centuries was a land of small villages and powerful castles. Most people were farmers or craftsmen, living near churches that shaped their beliefs and habits. Cities in the Middle East, like Jerusalem, were centers of faith but also of learning, trade, and culture, home to Christians, Muslims, and Jews. In Europe, many people could not read, and life was hard, with wars and hunger never far away. The Church was very powerful, and religious leaders could call many to action, even far away. The Crusaders went on foot, horseback, or by ship, often fearing the unknown but trusting their leaders and faith. While their reasons were mixed—faith, riches, adventure, or forgiveness—those who set out were forever changed, meeting people, foods, animals, and inventions never seen before in their own lands.
mg08.matters: The Crusades mattered deeply because they brought together people and ideas from different parts of the world. Despite their failures and the violence, this period set in motion great changes. European Crusaders returned—if they survived—with new ways of thinking, learning, and trading. They carried back books about ancient science and math, stories from Arab and Jewish scholars, and even foods like lemons and rice. These pieces of knowledge and culture helped Europe grow smarter and richer, eventually leading to big changes in faith and thought, like the Reformation. For families who look to see God's hand in history, it's comforting to know that even in times of great tragedy and mistake, Heavenly Father can still bring about good from what people learned and shared.
mg08.scripture: While the scriptures do not describe the Crusades, principles found in them touch the heart of this history. For example, the Savior taught, 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9), reminding us that love and peace are better paths than war. From Doctrine and Covenants 121:36, 41-42, we learn that power and influence should be used through kindness and persuasion, not force. As Latter-day Saints, we are taught to learn from the past and seek knowledge, as found in Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, where we are told to 'seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom.' These passages invite us to choose peace and gain wisdom from all nations as we move through a challenging world.
mg08.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found much evidence of the Crusades. Castles built by Crusaders still stand in places like Acre and Krak des Chevaliers, showing the skill and determination of those who traveled far from home. Old records from Christian, Muslim, and Jewish writers tell of journeys, battles, and daily life. Coins, weapons, and art traded during this time show the mixing of cultures. Academics agree that the Crusades changed Europe and the Middle East in lasting ways, though the stories are often sad, filled with loss. Today’s historians keep learning by studying ruins, ancient texts, and what was left behind. These findings show a sweeping movement of people and ideas, with effects still felt in today's world.
mg08.learn: We can learn that even in mistakes or hard times, good things can grow. When people met others in different lands, they learned new things and shared ideas back home. Sometimes, Heavenly Father allows us to learn and grow even through struggles. By looking for ways to build peace and learn from everyone, we can help the Lord’s work move forward. Every family, in any day, can choose to seek understanding and kindness, learning from both the good and the bad parts of history.
mg08.child: A long time ago, many people from Europe traveled far to Jerusalem because they wanted to help their church. They met new people, found new foods and stories, and even though many never got home, they shared what they learned with everyone. Their big trip changed both their own country and the places they visited.
mg08.talk: What new thing do you think the Crusaders learned on their journey that helped others when they came home?

mg09.happened: Between 1620 and 1640, thousands of English men, women, and children embarked on a journey across the Atlantic Ocean to settle in New England. This movement began with the Pilgrims, a group of Separatists who, seeking freedom to practice their faith, sailed on the Mayflower and established the Plymouth Colony in 1620. A decade later, the Great Migration commenced, with approximately 20,000 Puritans leaving England to form the Massachusetts Bay Colony and other settlements. These Puritans aimed to create communities grounded in their religious beliefs, emphasizing personal Bible study, earnest prayer, and self-governance. They envisioned their new society as a "city upon a hill," serving as a beacon of righteousness and a model for others. This migration laid the foundation for a culture deeply rooted in religious devotion and communal responsibility.
mg09.background: In early 17th-century England, the Puritans sought to reform the Church of England, desiring a return to simpler, more scripturally based worship. Facing increasing persecution under King Charles I and Archbishop William Laud, many Puritans decided to leave England to practice their faith freely. Daily life in England was marked by strict social hierarchies and limited religious tolerance. The decision to migrate was not taken lightly, as it involved leaving behind familiar surroundings for the uncertainties of the New World. The journey was arduous, with families enduring long voyages and the challenges of establishing new communities in unfamiliar and often harsh environments.
mg09.matters: The Puritan migration significantly influenced the religious and cultural landscape of New England. Their emphasis on personal scripture study, community worship, and self-governance fostered a society that valued education and civic responsibility. This environment of religious devotion and inquiry set the stage for future spiritual awakenings and movements. For families of faith, the Puritans' commitment to living according to their beliefs, even in the face of adversity, serves as a powerful example of dedication and resilience. Their legacy reminds us of the importance of religious freedom and the impact of faith-driven communities on shaping society.
mg09.scripture: The Puritans' journey to establish a society based on their religious convictions echoes the experiences of the ancient Israelites. In Exodus 3:7-8, the Lord speaks to Moses, saying, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people... and I am come down to deliver them... unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey." Similarly, the Puritans viewed their migration as a divine calling to create a new "Promised Land" where they could worship freely. Their commitment to living according to God's commandments reflects the teachings found throughout the scriptures about obedience, faith, and the blessings of following divine guidance.
mg09.evidence: Historical records, such as the Cambridge Agreement of 1629, document the Puritans' plans to migrate and establish self-governing communities in New England. This agreement, signed by Puritan leaders including John Winthrop, outlined their intention to transfer the Massachusetts Bay Company's charter to the New World, allowing them to govern themselves without interference from England. The success of these settlements is evidenced by the rapid growth of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, which attracted thousands of settlers and became a thriving center of Puritan life. Archaeological findings, including remnants of early colonial structures and artifacts, further attest to the establishment and development of these communities.
mg09.learn: The Puritan migration teaches us the value of religious freedom and the importance of building communities based on shared beliefs and mutual support. It highlights the courage required to pursue one's convictions, even when it means facing significant challenges. Their story encourages us to reflect on our own commitments to faith and community, inspiring us to uphold principles of integrity, education, and service in our daily lives.
mg09.child: Long ago, many families sailed across the ocean to find a place where they could pray and read the Bible the way they wanted. They built new towns and helped each other, making a new home where they could live their faith.
mg09.talk: Why do you think the Puritans wanted to build a new home where they could worship freely?

mg10.happened: Between 1847 and 1869, about 70,000 Latter-day Saints—men, women, and children—journeyed from the eastern United States to the Salt Lake Valley in present-day Utah. Driven from their homes by persecution, they traveled over 1,300 miles, mostly on foot, pulling wagons or handcarts filled with their belongings. The first group, led by Brigham Young, reached the Salt Lake Valley in July 1847. Later, many came in large wagon trains, while others, unable to afford wagons or teams, pulled their belongings in simple handcarts. The journey was long and harsh, with dangers like river crossings, storms, disease, and a lack of food. The handcart companies of 1856 faced great suffering, with hundreds dying from cold and starvation before help arrived. Despite these hardships, the Saints saw their trek as a covenant journey—guided by faith, sacrifice, and a sense that God was leading them to a promised land where they could worship in peace and build their communities.
mg10.background: Before the pioneer migration, the Latter-day Saints began in the 1830s as a new religious movement in New York. They were often misunderstood and sometimes treated harshly because of their beliefs and different ways of living. As the church grew, they moved from New York to Ohio, then Missouri, then Illinois, facing violence and being forced out of their homes each time. Life for these early Saints was filled with trials—many were farmers, teachers, and craftsmen, trying to care for their families while building churches and towns. When threats and violence forced them to leave Nauvoo, Illinois, they gathered what little they could carry and set out into unknown territory, hoping to find a safe place to live their faith without fear.
mg10.matters: This migration matters deeply to Latter-day Saint families and to American history. It changed the westward movement of the United States, bringing thousands to settle the isolated valleys of the Mountain West. For families of faith, it stands as a remembrance of deep sacrifice and trust in God’s guidance. The pioneers’ story is a pattern of faith, teamwork, and holding to covenants—even when the way is hard. Their journey continues to inspire families to face challenges today with faith and hope in the future.
mg10.scripture: The idea of a covenant journey echoes many scriptural events. In the Bible, Moses led the Israelites from Egypt to their promised land (Exodus 3, 13–15). In the Book of Mormon, groups like Lehi’s and the Jaredites crossed oceans to new lands (1 Nephi 2–18; Ether 1–6). The Doctrine and Covenants often speaks of gathering in safety, notably in D&C 136, where Brigham Young was directed on organizing the trek west. These scriptures teach that God guides His covenant people when they follow Him in faith, even into the unknown.
mg10.evidence: There is strong historical evidence for the Latter-day Saint migration. Thousands of journals, letters, and official church records were kept by men, women, and children who made the journey. Many of their handcarts, personal belongings, and landmarks can still be seen along the Pioneer Trail today. Historians have used these primary sources to confirm the route, size, and outcomes of the migration. U.S. government records, as well as early newspaper accounts, also note the movement of so many people west. Archaeological work supports the locations of campsites and trails, matching the written histories. There are some parts—like specific miracles—that are a matter of personal faith, but the main events are well-documented and widely acknowledged by historians.
mg10.learn: We can learn much from the pioneer story. It teaches the value of courage when facing hard things, the importance of helping each other, and how faith can carry people through even the roughest journeys. We can remember that sometimes, blessings come after sacrifice, and that finding a place to live and worship in peace is worth working for. Most of all, their story asks us to trust Heavenly Father as we journey through our own ‘wildernesses.’
mg10.child: Long ago, families packed their things and walked across a huge land to find a safe home. They wanted to follow Jesus and worship in peace. Even when it was cold and hard, they kept going because they trusted Heavenly Father.
mg10.talk: What does it mean to trust Heavenly Father when things are hard, like the pioneers did?

mg11.happened: Between 1880 and 1924, the United States experienced a significant wave of immigration, with over 25 million people arriving from countries such as Italy, Poland, Russia, and China. Many of these immigrants entered through Ellis Island in New York Harbor, which became the nation's busiest immigration station. In 1907 alone, Ellis Island processed over one million immigrants, marking the peak of this migration period. These newcomers sought better economic opportunities and freedom from political and religious persecution. They brought diverse languages, cultures, and traditions, enriching American society. However, this rapid influx also led to challenges, including overcrowded urban areas and tensions with native-born citizens. In response, the U.S. government implemented restrictive immigration laws, such as the Immigration Act of 1924, which established quotas based on national origins, significantly reducing the number of immigrants from certain regions.
mg11.background: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, many parts of Europe and Asia faced economic hardships, political unrest, and social upheaval. Industrialization disrupted traditional economies, and religious and ethnic minorities often faced persecution. For example, Jews in Eastern Europe experienced pogroms, violent attacks sanctioned by authorities. These conditions prompted millions to seek refuge and opportunities in the United States, which was undergoing its own industrial revolution. American cities were rapidly expanding, offering jobs in factories, construction, and services. The promise of religious freedom and democratic ideals further attracted those fleeing oppression. Daily life for these immigrants was challenging; they often lived in crowded tenements and worked long hours in difficult conditions. Despite these hardships, they formed tight-knit communities, established cultural institutions, and contributed significantly to the nation's growth.
mg11.matters: This period of mass immigration profoundly shaped the United States, transforming it into a more diverse and multicultural society. The influx of new cultures, languages, and traditions enriched the American cultural landscape, influencing cuisine, music, and art. For families of faith, this era underscores the importance of compassion and understanding toward those seeking refuge and better lives. It serves as a reminder of the blessings that diversity brings and the opportunities to share and strengthen faith within a broader community. The experiences of these immigrants highlight the resilience of the human spirit and the enduring pursuit of freedom and opportunity.
mg11.scripture: The scriptures teach us to welcome and care for strangers. In Leviticus 19:34, it is written, "But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself." Similarly, in Matthew 25:35, Jesus says, "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in." These passages remind us of our duty to show kindness and hospitality to those who come seeking refuge and a better life.
mg11.evidence: Historical records from Ellis Island indicate that nearly 12 million immigrants were processed there between 1892 and 1954, with the peak year being 1907, when over one million individuals arrived. Census data from the early 20th century shows a significant increase in the foreign-born population, reflecting the impact of this immigration wave. Additionally, legislative records document the enactment of restrictive immigration laws in the 1920s, such as the Immigration Act of 1924, which established quotas based on national origins, aiming to limit the influx from certain regions. These records provide clear evidence of the scale and impact of immigration during this period.
mg11.learn: From this historical event, we learn the value of embracing diversity and the strength that comes from welcoming those seeking better lives. It teaches us the importance of compassion, understanding, and the positive contributions that immigrants bring to society. Recognizing the challenges they faced encourages us to support and uplift those in need, reflecting the principles of love and service taught in the scriptures.
mg11.child: Long ago, many people from different countries came to America to find a better life. They brought new foods, languages, and traditions, making our country more colorful and interesting. We can learn to be kind and welcoming to everyone, just like Jesus taught us.
mg11.talk: How can we show kindness to someone who is new to our community?
