mg12.happened: Between 1947 and 1950, a remarkable migration took place. After the end of World War II and the horrors of the Holocaust, Jewish people who had survived in Europe, as well as those living in the Middle East and North Africa, began returning in large numbers to the land of Israel. In 1948, Israel declared itself an independent nation, and this opened the doors for hundreds of thousands of Jewish people worldwide to come home to what they call the Promised Land. Some traveled by ship, others by foot or train, and some even by airplane, such as in Operation Magic Carpet, which airlifted about 50,000 Jews from Yemen in 1949 and 1950. These years saw the largest gathering of Jewish people into Israel since the time the Persian king Cyrus allowed the Jews to return from Babylon thousands of years before. The journey was not easy—many left everything behind, faced danger, and worked to build new lives in unfamiliar places, but their hope to return and rebuild was strong.
mg12.background: Before Israel was established in 1948, Jewish people lived scattered all over the world, a result of centuries of exile and displacement. Many lived in European countries, but daily life became tragic for millions during the Holocaust, when Nazi Germany killed six million Jews. Others lived in Arab and Muslim-majority lands, sometimes peacefully and sometimes facing persecution. By the 1940s, life for Jewish families was often uncertain or dangerous, and many longed for a safe place to belong. Zionist movements began growing in the late 1800s, encouraging Jews to return to their ancestral home. In cities and villages from Poland to Morocco, families met in secret, shared stories of Jerusalem, and prayed for Zion. When the United Nations voted to establish a Jewish state in 1947, hopes rose, even though wars with neighboring countries surrounded the new nation from the start.
mg12.matters: This migration, called Aliyah, changed the face of Israel and fulfilled dreams that had lasted for centuries. For Jewish families and Christians alike, it is seen as a modern miracle and a sign that God's promises are kept not only in ancient days but now, too. For families of faith, it is a visible reminder that Heavenly Father remembers His covenants, even over thousands of years. The gathering of Israel continues today, and for Latter-day Saints, it encourages us to notice where prophecy and real-world events meet, and to look for God's hand in history and in our own lives.
mg12.scripture: The Bible has many prophecies about the gathering of the Jewish people back to their ancient homeland. Isaiah 11:11-12 speaks of the Lord gathering His people a second time from all over the world. Ezekiel 37 tells of the dry bones coming to life as a symbol of Israel's return. Amos 9:14-15 promises the people will be planted in their land, never to be uprooted. The Doctrine and Covenants 45:25 speaks of the Jews being gathered back to their promised borders. Latter-day Saint leaders often reference these events as examples of prophecy fulfilled before our eyes.
mg12.evidence: Historians, museums, and news agencies document the return of Jewish families to Israel after the Second World War through records, photographs, and firsthand accounts. Government archives in Israel keep detailed records of new immigrants, and international organizations like the United Nations recorded many of the events. Operations like Magic Carpet are well-documented with newsreels and flight logs that confirm the transport of tens of thousands of Yemeni Jews by air. The numbers, the dates, and the experiences are noted in textbooks and recognized by Jewish and world history scholars alike. There is no real debate about the basic facts of these migrations—they are confirmed parts of history that people can see in photos and interviews.
mg12.learn: From this true story, we learn that even when people are scattered, lost, or frightened, Heavenly Father can gather and help them through very hard things. It reminds us that the promises He makes, He keeps, sometimes in ways we did not expect and after many, many years. We too might face challenges or feel far from home, but our faith tells us that God knows where we are and can open a way for us to return spiritually or physically as needed.
mg12.child: After World War II, many Jewish families went back to live in Israel, just like prophets in the Bible said they would. It was a very big move, and lots of people had to leave their old homes behind. God kept His promise to bring His people back to their land.
mg12.talk: Why do you think it was so important for Jewish families to go back to Israel after so many years away?

t01.happened: The Silk Road was a series of ancient trade routes that stretched more than four thousand miles from China in the East all the way to Rome in the West. It wasn’t a single road but many paths and caravan trails, crossing high mountains, wide deserts, and busy cities. Starting around 200 BC and lasting until about 1450 AD, the Silk Road helped traders carry silk, spices, paper, and even new discoveries like gunpowder from Asia to Europe. Caravans of camels or horses would carry goods in both directions, and trading posts and cities grew at stopping places along the way. It wasn’t just material things that traveled—people shared stories, art, music, and beliefs. Through these travels, religions such as Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam spread across Asia and Europe. The Silk Road made the world feel smaller as faraway places became connected, helping ideas and inventions reach people who might never have imagined such things before.
t01.background: Long before the Silk Road, people lived in small villages or cities, usually trading only with nearby neighbors. Ancient China, Persia, India, and Rome were already great civilizations with their own rich cultures, foods, and ways of thinking. Most travel was slow and dangerous, often by foot or with animals, and people depended on the land and their crafts to survive. Families grew their own food, spun their own cloth, and rarely saw outsiders except during local markets or festivals. As empires grew and rulers wanted exotic goods like silk or rare spices, people began to look farther beyond their borders. Caravan routes started as simple trails taken by herders and traders but grew as more people saw the value in exchanging goods and stories with distant lands.
t01.matters: The Silk Road is important because it brought the world together long before airplanes or the internet. For families of faith, it helps us see how God uses ordinary things—like roads and trade—to help His children learn from each other and spread His truth. The Silk Road made it possible for inventions like paper to travel to Europe, which later helped the Bible and other scriptures be printed and shared with many people. It’s a reminder that connecting with others can lead to wonderful changes and the spreading of good ideas.
t01.scripture: The Bible tells stories of travelers and journeys that changed the world, such as Paul’s missionary travels in Acts 13-21, where he brought the gospel across the Mediterranean, touching new lands and peoples. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:79, the Lord commands us to learn about “countries and kingdoms” so we can be prepared for His work. The movement of knowledge and the gospel along trade routes like the Silk Road shows how the Lord ‘prepares a way’ to spread truth and blessings, much as He did for His ancient servants.
t01.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have discovered coins, sculptures, ancient texts, and even the remains of caravans and inns along the route. Painted caves in China and ruins of old cities in Central Asia show what life was like for traders and travelers. Ancient Roman and Chinese records mention the exchange of silk and strange products, confirming much of what we know. DNA and artifact studies show that people and ideas truly mixed along these routes. Modern research continues to fill in our picture of how the Silk Road worked and how important it was for connecting continents.
t01.learn: From the Silk Road, we learn that sharing with others can bless all involved. The things we create, discover, or believe can travel farther and help more people than we might ever guess. Just as Heavenly Father helped people long ago cross great distances to share knowledge and truth, He can use us and the tools we have today—like technology, kindness, and our testimonies—to help His work go forward.
t01.child: Long ago, people carried silk and spices a very long way from China to Rome. Along these big roads, they also shared stories and learned new things about God. The Silk Road helped people become friends, even if they lived far apart.
t01.talk: What special thing from our life would you want to share if you traveled to another country?

t03.happened: Between the first and fourth centuries AD, the Roman Empire created one of the largest and most effective trade networks the world had ever seen. Spanning from the heart of Rome itself, these routes stretched westward through Europe, looped eastward into India and even reached the far-off lands of China. Ships full of goods sailed the Mediterranean Sea, while caravans crossed long, dusty desert roads. Precious items like silk from China, spices from India, gold and ivory from Africa, and glassware, wine, and olive oil from Rome moved along these paths. Roman merchants exchanged goods, stories, and even ideas with traders from many nations. Along with traders, Christian missionaries traveled these paved roads and safe sea lanes, spreading the teachings of Jesus Christ far beyond the borders of Judea. The famous Roman roads—built strong for armies—now carried the hopes and messages of regular people, merchants, and believers alike. By the year 150 AD, this wide web of roads and sea routes bustling with travelers was among the greatest highways for both commerce and communication in ancient history.
t03.background: Before Rome's greatest reach, much trade was local, and travel between faraway nations was hard and dangerous. The people of Rome lived in cities filled with noise and activity. Most people were farmers, but there were also builders, soldiers, merchants, and teachers. Rome itself was the center of a huge empire, touching many lands, peoples, and languages. Daily life for many involved work and family, with markets offering goods from every part of the known world. Romans ate bread and olives, wore colorful fabrics, and looked up at stone buildings. The government was strong, and its armies protected long roads and busy ports, making travel and trade remarkably safe—for the time. The empire connected Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, making the world seem smaller and more possible to cross than ever before.
t03.matters: The Roman trade network made the world feel connected in ways that had never happened before. People could experience new foods, colors, and ideas from faraway lands. For a family of faith, this mattered because the same roads and ships that carried silk and spices also made it possible for the message of Jesus Christ to travel quickly beyond its tiny beginning. The Apostle Paul and many missionaries could reach towns across the empire with relative ease. Today, we can see this as something Heavenly Father allowed—even planned for—so that the gospel could spread to all His children in those days. The ability for ideas to travel matters deeply in how faith grows and communities change.
t03.scripture: Several scriptures touch on the principle that Heavenly Father prepares people and circumstances to help His work move forward. In the Bible, Acts 9-28 tells about Paul's journeys using Roman roads to spread the gospel. Paul often traveled safely and could teach about Jesus in faraway cities because of this network. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:73, the Lord promises to 'hasten [His] work in its time,' showing that when the moment is right, the right means and paths are made ready. These passages remind us that God can use even government and trade systems, planned for other reasons, to bless His children.
t03.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found strong evidence of the Roman trade network. The remains of stone roads with mile markers show just how far Roman construction reached. Ancient shipwrecks carrying Roman and Indian goods have been found in the Mediterranean and Indian Oceans, providing proof of trade. Old Roman coins have been discovered in India and even as far as China, showing that trade reached these distant places. Written sources from Rome, Egypt, and India describe goods, merchants, and sometimes missionaries traveling these routes. Modern studies using satellite images have even traced lost roads and busy ports that once made this global exchange possible. While not every single journey can be traced, the overall picture is strongly supported by physical and written evidence.
t03.learn: From the Roman trade network, we learn that the Lord can use anything—even old roads or ship routes designed for business—to help people find truth and share it with others. We see that technology and travel, when used well, can bless many lives. Families can talk about how being connected with others is good, but it also means being wise about what we share and learn. As we use today’s technology, we can ask ourselves how we can use it to do good, just as early Christians did along the Roman roads.

t02.happened: Between the 11th and 16th centuries, the spice trade flourished as a vast network of maritime and overland routes connected Southeast Asia's spice-producing regions to Europe. Spices like pepper, cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg were highly prized in Europe for their ability to flavor and preserve food, as well as for medicinal uses. These valuable commodities were transported from the Moluccas (Spice Islands) in Indonesia, through the Indian Ocean, and onward via the Red Sea or Persian Gulf to Mediterranean ports. Arab and Persian merchants played key roles in this trade, controlling the flow of spices and maintaining high prices by keeping their sources secret. European demand for these exotic goods grew, leading to significant economic and cultural exchanges between the East and West. The desire to find direct sea routes to the spice-producing regions eventually spurred the Age of Exploration, with navigators like Christopher Columbus seeking new paths to these lucrative markets.
t02.background: In the medieval world, spices were not just culinary luxuries but essential commodities. They were used to enhance the flavor of food, preserve meats, and in various medicinal remedies. The high value of spices made them a form of currency and a symbol of wealth. The overland Silk Road and maritime routes facilitated the movement of these goods, but the journey was long and fraught with challenges, including taxing intermediaries and political conflicts. The fall of Constantinople in 1453 to the Ottoman Turks further complicated overland trade, prompting European nations to seek alternative routes to the East. This quest for direct access to spices led to significant advancements in navigation and shipbuilding, setting the stage for global exploration.
t02.matters: The spice trade was a catalyst for global exploration and the eventual European colonization of various parts of the world. For families of faith, this period underscores how commercial pursuits can lead to unintended, yet divinely significant, outcomes. The search for spices led to the discovery of new lands, including the Americas, which would later become a haven for religious freedom and the birthplace of the Restoration. It serves as a reminder that Heavenly Father can use worldly endeavors to fulfill His greater purposes, guiding individuals and nations toward paths that align with His divine plan.
t02.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention the spice trade, they do speak to the principle of seeking and finding. In Matthew 7:7, the Savior teaches, "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." This principle can be applied to the explorers' quests, where their search for spices led to the discovery of new lands and opportunities. Additionally, 2 Nephi 1:5 in the Book of Mormon speaks of a "land of promise" prepared by the Lord, which can be seen as a foreshadowing of the Americas becoming a land of religious freedom and restoration.
t02.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings provide substantial evidence of the extensive spice trade routes that connected Southeast Asia to Europe. Ancient texts from various cultures document the high value placed on spices and the lengths to which traders would go to obtain them. Maritime archaeology has uncovered shipwrecks along these routes, revealing cargoes of spices and other goods, confirming the scale and significance of this trade. The establishment of European trading posts and colonies in spice-producing regions further attests to the lengths nations went to secure direct access to these valuable commodities.
t02.learn: The history of the spice trade teaches us about the interconnectedness of the world and how economic pursuits can lead to significant cultural and spiritual developments. It reminds us that our efforts, even when driven by temporal goals, can be guided by Heavenly Father to fulfill His greater purposes. This encourages us to seek His guidance in all our endeavors, trusting that He can lead us to outcomes that align with His divine plan.
t02.child: Long ago, people loved spices like cinnamon and pepper because they made food taste better and helped keep it fresh. Traders traveled across oceans and lands to bring these spices from faraway places to Europe. Their journeys led to the discovery of new lands, including America.
t02.talk: How did the search for spices lead explorers to discover new lands?

lg01.happened: Around 3500 BC, in the land we now call Iraq, something amazing happened: people began to write things down for the very first time. The Sumerians, who lived in cities like Uruk, invented a system called cuneiform. Instead of using letters like we do, they pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay tablets using a reed. At first, this writing was mostly for counting things in temples—grain, sheep, and other supplies. Priests and temple workers needed to keep track of offerings and taxes, making sure everyone got their fair share. But it didn’t stop there. Soon, writing was used for stories, laws, and even prayers. The most famous story written in this script is the Epic of Gilgamesh, which tells about a great king, his adventures, and even talks about a big flood that sounds a lot like the story of Noah. This first writing system changed everything, letting people share ideas not just with their neighbors, but with generations who would come long after them.
lg01.background: Before Sumerians invented writing, people had to remember everything: stories, family history, and deals made in the market. Pictures and spoken words were all they had. Life in Sumer was busy and organized—families farmed wheat and barley, raised animals, and built homes from mud bricks along the rivers. Their cities grew large, with temples at the center where priests watched the skies and cared for statues of their gods. Sumerians made impressive inventions: wheels for carts, plows for farming, and boats for the rivers. Yet without writing, much of this knowledge was fragile, easily lost if memories failed. So, creating a way to write things down was like discovering a powerful tool the world had never seen before.
lg01.matters: The beginning of writing matters deeply for families of faith. Before words could be saved on a page, God’s messages depended on memory and retelling; they might be changed or forgotten. But once writing began, it became possible to record sacred teachings, prophecies, and spiritual experiences. For everyone, not just those in Sumer, this transformed the way stories, laws, and history could pass from parent to child, from one town to the next, and even over thousands of years. Today, we read scriptures and trust what was written long ago, all thanks to those first writers in ancient Mesopotamia.
lg01.scripture: While the Bible and Latter-day Saint scriptures don’t mention Sumerians or cuneiform directly, they teach us the importance of written records. The Book of Mormon tells how Nephi was commanded to make and keep records (1 Nephi 6:5–6, 9:2–6). The Lord said, 'For behold, I shall speak unto the Jews and they shall write it' (2 Nephi 29:4, 10–11). In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord often reminds His people of the importance of writing down what He reveals (D&C 21:1; D&C 47:1–4). This principle—that writing helps preserve truth—is woven throughout scripture.
lg01.evidence: Archaeologists have found thousands of clay tablets from ancient Sumer, many more than 5,000 years old. These tablets show simple pictographs at first, then more complex cuneiform signs as time went on. The oldest were mostly records of trade and temple offerings, but later tablets contain some of the earliest known stories and poems. The Epic of Gilgamesh, written on several tablets, was discovered in the ruins of Nineveh in the 1800s. Scholars can read these ancient symbols and confirm that Sumerian is the oldest known written language, with real objects you can visit in museums today. New tablets are still being uncovered, adding to our understanding of how writing began in Mesopotamia.
lg01.learn: From the story of Sumerian writing, we learn that Heavenly Father can use even the smallest inventions to help His children. Writing began as a simple way to count grain, but soon carried words that spoke of faith, hope, and courage—and even stories like the flood, echoing truths found in scripture. When we honor and keep records in our own lives, whether that’s a journal, a letter, or family scripture study, we’re continuing an important tradition that stretches back to the world’s first writers.

lg01.talk: Why do you think it is important to write things down, like in your journal or the scriptures?

lg02.happened: Around 3100 BC, the ancient Egyptians developed a writing system known as hieroglyphics. This intricate script combined pictorial symbols representing objects, ideas, and sounds. Hieroglyphics were primarily used for monumental inscriptions on temple walls, tombs, and other significant structures, as well as on papyrus for religious texts and administrative documents. The system comprised hundreds of symbols, each with specific meanings and phonetic values. Over time, hieroglyphics evolved, incorporating more symbols and becoming increasingly complex. This writing system remained in use for over 3,000 years, serving as a cornerstone of Egyptian culture and administration. The Merneptah Stele, dating to around 1208 BC, is a notable example of hieroglyphic inscription. This stone slab commemorates Pharaoh Merneptah's military victories and contains the earliest known external reference to Israel, stating, "Israel is laid waste, his seed is no more." This inscription provides valuable insight into the interactions between ancient Egypt and neighboring peoples.
lg02.background: In the late fourth millennium BC, ancient Egypt was emerging as a unified state along the Nile River. The development of hieroglyphics coincided with the consolidation of political power and the establishment of a centralized administration. The Nile's annual flooding created fertile lands, supporting agriculture and enabling the growth of a prosperous civilization. Daily life in ancient Egypt was deeply intertwined with religious beliefs, and the afterlife was of particular importance. Hieroglyphics played a crucial role in religious practices, as they were used to inscribe prayers, spells, and funerary texts intended to guide the deceased in the afterlife. The ability to read and write hieroglyphics was limited to a select group of scribes and priests, who underwent extensive training. This literacy was essential for maintaining records, conducting trade, and performing religious rituals, making scribes highly respected members of society.
lg02.matters: The development of hieroglyphics was a monumental achievement that laid the foundation for written communication in ancient Egypt. This writing system enabled the recording of history, religious beliefs, and administrative activities, preserving the culture and knowledge of one of the world's earliest civilizations. For families of faith, the existence of hieroglyphics underscores the importance of written records in preserving sacred teachings and historical events. The mention of Israel in the Merneptah Stele provides external validation of biblical narratives, offering tangible evidence of the Israelites' presence in ancient times. This connection highlights the enduring significance of written language in documenting and affirming faith traditions.
lg02.scripture: The Bible mentions that Moses was "learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22). This suggests that Moses, raised in Pharaoh's household, would have been educated in reading and writing hieroglyphics. His ability to communicate in both Egyptian and Hebrew would have been instrumental in leading the Israelites and recording their experiences. The scriptures emphasize the importance of preserving God's teachings through written records, as seen in passages like Deuteronomy 6:9, which instructs believers to write God's commandments on the doorposts of their houses. This principle underscores the value of written language in maintaining and transmitting faith across generations.
lg02.evidence: Archaeological discoveries, such as the Merneptah Stele, provide concrete evidence of the use of hieroglyphics in ancient Egypt. The stele, discovered in 1896 by Flinders Petrie, is housed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. It contains inscriptions detailing Pharaoh Merneptah's military campaigns and includes the earliest known reference to Israel. The decipherment of hieroglyphics was made possible by the Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799. This artifact features the same text in Greek, Demotic, and hieroglyphic scripts, allowing scholars to unlock the meaning of hieroglyphics. The successful translation of these texts has provided invaluable insights into ancient Egyptian history, culture, and interactions with neighboring civilizations.
lg02.learn: The development and use of hieroglyphics teach us the profound impact of written language on civilization. It enables the recording and preservation of knowledge, culture, and religious beliefs. For families of faith, this underscores the importance of maintaining written records of spiritual experiences and teachings. Just as ancient Egyptians used hieroglyphics to document their history and beliefs, we can use writing to preserve our faith and pass it on to future generations. This practice ensures that sacred teachings and personal testimonies remain accessible and influential over time.
lg02.child: Long ago, the Egyptians created a special way of writing called hieroglyphics, using pictures to tell stories and record important events. This writing helped them remember their history and share their beliefs with others.
lg02.talk: Why do you think it's important to write down our family stories and experiences?

lg03.happened: Around 2000 BC, Hebrew began to emerge as the language of the Israelites in Canaan, the area now known as Israel. This language became central to their identity and faith, serving as the medium through which they communicated with each other and with God. The entire Old Testament, including the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings, was composed in Hebrew. This language was not only a tool for daily communication but also a sacred vessel for conveying divine laws, prophecies, and poetry. Over time, Hebrew's use as a spoken language diminished, especially after the Babylonian exile in the 6th century BC, when Aramaic became more prevalent. However, Hebrew continued to be used in religious contexts and scholarly writings. Remarkably, after approximately 1,700 years of limited use as a spoken language, Hebrew was revived in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, becoming the national language of modern Israel. This revival is unique in human history, as no other language has been successfully restored to such widespread daily use after such a long period of dormancy.
lg03.background: In the ancient Near East, around 2000 BC, Canaan was a land of diverse cultures and languages. The inhabitants engaged in agriculture, herding, and trade. The Israelites, a group that settled in Canaan, developed Hebrew as their distinct language. Daily life for the Israelites involved farming, tending livestock, and participating in community and religious activities. Their language, Hebrew, was integral to their culture and religious practices, enabling them to record their laws, histories, and spiritual experiences. As time progressed, external influences, such as the Babylonian exile, introduced other languages like Aramaic into their daily lives. Despite these influences, Hebrew remained the language of their sacred texts and religious ceremonies, preserving their unique identity through centuries of change.
lg03.matters: The emergence and preservation of Hebrew are significant for both historical and spiritual reasons. For the world, Hebrew's development provides insight into the ancient Near East's linguistic and cultural dynamics. For families of faith, Hebrew holds profound importance as the language through which God communicated His laws and teachings to the prophets. The revival of Hebrew in modern times serves as a testament to the resilience of a people and the enduring power of language to unite and preserve cultural and religious identity. It also fulfills the prophecy in Zephaniah 3:9, which speaks of a 'pure language' being restored, allowing people to serve God with one accord.
lg03.scripture: The scriptures highlight the significance of Hebrew as the language of divine communication. In Zephaniah 3:9, it is prophesied: 'For then I will restore to the peoples a pure language, that they all may call on the name of the Lord, to serve Him with one accord.' This passage is often interpreted as foretelling the revival of Hebrew, enabling people to worship God collectively. Additionally, the Book of Mormon was written in 'reformed Egyptian,' a scriptural language related to ancient writing traditions, underscoring the importance of sacred languages in preserving and conveying divine teachings.
lg03.evidence: Historical and archaeological evidence supports the development and use of Hebrew among the ancient Israelites. Inscriptions dating back to the 10th century BC, such as the Gezer Calendar, demonstrate the early use of Hebrew script. The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered in the mid-20th century, contain extensive Hebrew texts from the Second Temple period, affirming the language's continued use in religious and communal life. The revival of Hebrew in the modern era is well-documented, with Eliezer Ben-Yehuda playing a pivotal role in its restoration as a spoken language. His efforts, along with those of the Language Committee he established, led to the creation of new vocabulary and the adaptation of Hebrew for contemporary use, culminating in its adoption as the official language of Israel.
lg03.learn: The story of Hebrew teaches us about the resilience of language and culture. It shows that with dedication and faith, it is possible to revive and preserve important aspects of our heritage. This revival also reminds us of the power of language to unite people and serve as a foundation for shared identity and purpose.
lg03.child: Long ago, people in Israel spoke Hebrew, the language of the Bible. After many years, people stopped speaking it every day. But about 100 years ago, they started speaking Hebrew again, and now it's the main language in Israel.
lg03.talk: Why do you think it's important to keep a language alive?

lg04.happened: Between approximately 500 and 300 BC, the Greek language underwent significant changes, leading to the development of Koine Greek, a common dialect that became widely spoken across the Mediterranean region. This transformation was largely influenced by the conquests of Alexander the Great, who, in the late 4th century BC, expanded his empire from Greece through Asia Minor, Egypt, and into parts of India. As Alexander's armies moved through these regions, they established Greek as the lingua franca, facilitating communication and administration across diverse cultures. This widespread adoption of Greek laid the groundwork for its use in various domains, including trade, governance, and literature. Notably, around 250 BC, Jewish scholars in Alexandria translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, producing the Septuagint. This translation made the sacred texts accessible to Greek-speaking Jews throughout the diaspora. Later, the entire New Testament was composed in Koine Greek, ensuring that the teachings of Jesus Christ and the apostles could reach a broad audience across the Hellenistic world.
lg04.background: Before the rise of Koine Greek, the Mediterranean world was a mosaic of languages and dialects. Classical Greek, with its various regional forms, was predominant in Greece, while other languages like Persian, Egyptian, and various Semitic tongues were spoken in neighboring regions. Daily life was characterized by localized cultures and limited interaction between distant communities. However, the conquests of Alexander the Great in the late 4th century BC dramatically altered this landscape. By establishing Greek-speaking cities and promoting Greek culture throughout his empire, Alexander facilitated a cultural and linguistic unification. This period, known as the Hellenistic era, saw increased trade, cultural exchange, and the spread of Greek education and philosophy, creating a more interconnected Mediterranean world.
lg04.matters: The adoption of Koine Greek as a common language had profound implications for the spread of Christianity. The precision and richness of Greek vocabulary allowed for the clear articulation of complex theological concepts. Terms like 'grace' (charis), 'repentance' (metanoia), 'baptism' (baptizo), 'gospel' (euangelion), and 'word' (logos) carried nuanced meanings that shaped Christian doctrine for centuries. For families of faith, understanding the linguistic context of the New Testament enhances comprehension of its teachings and underscores the importance of language in conveying divine truths. The widespread use of Greek ensured that the message of the Gospel could be disseminated effectively across diverse populations, fulfilling the command to teach all nations.
lg04.scripture: The scriptures highlight the significance of language in conveying divine messages. In John 1:1, it is written, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' The term 'Word' translates to 'Logos' in Greek, a concept rich with philosophical meaning, indicating reason and order. This usage demonstrates how the Greek language provided a framework for expressing profound theological ideas. Additionally, the Great Commission in Matthew 28:19-20 instructs believers to 'go and make disciples of all nations,' a task facilitated by the common language of Koine Greek, enabling the apostles to communicate effectively across different cultures.
lg04.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings support the widespread use of Koine Greek during the Hellenistic period. Inscriptions, papyri, and manuscripts from this era are predominantly in Greek, indicating its role as the common language of administration and daily life. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, serves as a tangible example of this linguistic shift. Early Christian writings, including the New Testament manuscripts, are also in Koine Greek, reflecting its accessibility to the general populace. These pieces of evidence collectively demonstrate the centrality of Greek in the cultural and religious developments of the time.
lg04.learn: From this historical development, we learn the importance of language in unifying diverse peoples and facilitating the spread of ideas. The adoption of a common language can bridge cultural gaps and promote understanding. For believers, it underscores the role of divine providence in preparing the world for the dissemination of the Gospel. Recognizing the significance of Koine Greek in early Christianity encourages us to appreciate the tools and means provided to share faith and knowledge effectively.
lg04.child: Long ago, people spoke many different languages. But when Alexander the Great traveled to many lands, he helped make Greek a common language. This made it easier for people to share stories, including the teachings of Jesus.
lg04.talk: Why do you think having a common language like Greek helped people learn about Jesus?

lg05.happened: Latin, originally the language of the Romans, became the dominant language of the Roman Empire, especially in the western provinces. As the empire expanded, Latin spread across Europe, becoming the common tongue for administration, law, and military affairs. In the late 4th century, Saint Jerome was commissioned by Pope Damasus I to translate the Bible into Latin, resulting in the Vulgate. This translation became the standard Bible for the Western Church, solidifying Latin's role in Christian liturgy and theology. For over a millennium, Latin remained the language of the Catholic Church, used in all official documents, theological writings, and liturgical services. This widespread use of Latin unified Western Christianity, providing a common language for scholars and clergy across different regions.
lg05.background: Before Latin's dominance, the Roman Empire was a mosaic of languages and cultures. Greek was widely spoken, especially in the eastern provinces, due to the influence of Alexander the Great's conquests. Local languages like Aramaic, Coptic, and various Celtic tongues were prevalent in different regions. Daily life varied greatly across the empire, with urban centers bustling with trade and cultural exchange, while rural areas maintained traditional practices. The spread of Latin was not enforced but occurred organically as people adopted it for its practical benefits in commerce, governance, and military service. Over time, Latin evolved into various dialects, eventually giving rise to the Romance languages such as Italian, French, Spanish, and Portuguese.
lg05.matters: Latin's role as the universal language of the Church had profound implications. It facilitated the spread of Christian doctrine and unified diverse peoples under a common religious framework. However, this exclusivity also created barriers, as ordinary people who did not understand Latin were unable to access the scriptures directly. The Reformation challenged this monopoly, with figures like Martin Luther and William Tyndale translating the Bible into vernacular languages, making it accessible to the general populace. This democratization of scripture paved the way for greater personal engagement with the word of God, aligning with the belief that Heavenly Father desires all His children to understand His teachings.
lg05.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of understanding God's word. In 2 Nephi 31:3, it states, "For the Lord God giveth light unto the understanding; for he speaketh unto men according to their language, unto their understanding." This principle underscores the significance of having the scriptures available in one's own language, ensuring that all can comprehend and apply divine teachings in their lives.
lg05.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings confirm Latin's widespread use in the Roman Empire and its enduring influence. Inscriptions, official documents, and literary works from the period are predominantly in Latin, illustrating its role in administration and daily life. The Vulgate, completed by Jerome between 382 and 405 AD, became the definitive Bible of Western Christianity for over a thousand years. Manuscripts of the Vulgate have been preserved and studied, providing insight into its textual history and variations. The Council of Trent (1545–1563) affirmed the Vulgate as the official Latin Bible of the Catholic Church, further cementing its authority and widespread use.
lg05.learn: The history of Latin's role in the Church teaches us the importance of accessibility in spiritual matters. While a common language can unify, it can also exclude those who do not understand it. Ensuring that sacred texts are available in the languages of the people promotes inclusivity and personal connection to divine teachings. This principle aligns with the belief that Heavenly Father desires all His children to have direct access to His word, fostering a personal relationship with Him.

lg06.happened: Between the 7th and 13th centuries, the Arabic language spread across the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of Europe, accompanying the expansion of Islam. During this period, Arabic-speaking scholars undertook the significant task of translating and preserving the works of ancient Greek philosophers and scientists, including Aristotle, Plato, Euclid, and Ptolemy. This effort was particularly concentrated in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, established around 800 AD, which became a renowned center for learning and scholarship. Here, scholars not only translated Greek texts but also made original contributions to fields such as mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and philosophy. Their work ensured that the knowledge of the ancient Greeks was not lost during the tumultuous times following the fall of the Roman Empire but was instead preserved and expanded upon within the Islamic world.
lg06.background: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century, much of Europe entered a period often referred to as the Dark Ages, characterized by political instability and a decline in scholarly activity. In contrast, the Islamic world experienced a flourishing of culture and learning. The Arabian Peninsula, the birthplace of Islam in the 7th century, became a hub for trade and intellectual exchange. Cities like Baghdad emerged as centers of learning, where scholars from various backgrounds gathered to study and translate texts from different cultures. Daily life in these regions was marked by a strong emphasis on education and the pursuit of knowledge, supported by the patronage of caliphs and wealthy individuals who valued scholarly endeavors.
lg06.matters: The preservation and expansion of Greek knowledge by Arabic-speaking scholars had a profound impact on the world. Their translations and commentaries were later transmitted to Europe, playing a crucial role in sparking the Renaissance—a period of renewed interest in science, art, and philosophy. For families of faith, this history illustrates how Heavenly Father can use diverse cultures and peoples to preserve and disseminate knowledge that benefits all of humanity. It serves as a reminder that the pursuit of knowledge and understanding is a divine endeavor that transcends cultural and religious boundaries.
lg06.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly reference the preservation of Greek knowledge by Arabic scholars, they do emphasize the importance of seeking wisdom and understanding. Proverbs 4:7 states, "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." This principle aligns with the efforts of scholars throughout history who have sought to preserve and expand human knowledge.
lg06.evidence: Historical records and surviving manuscripts provide substantial evidence of the translation movement undertaken by Arabic-speaking scholars. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad is well-documented as a center for these activities. Manuscripts from this period, many of which are preserved in libraries and museums around the world, showcase the Arabic translations of Greek texts. Additionally, the works of scholars like Al-Khwarizmi, who wrote on mathematics and introduced concepts that would later influence European scholars, further attest to the significant contributions made during this era.
lg06.learn: This historical episode teaches us the value of preserving and sharing knowledge across cultures. It highlights the importance of education and the pursuit of wisdom as means to uplift societies and foster understanding among diverse peoples. It also reminds us that Heavenly Father can work through various civilizations to accomplish His purposes, including the preservation and dissemination of knowledge.
lg06.child: Long ago, people who spoke Arabic saved many important books from ancient Greece. They translated these books so others could learn from them. Because of their work, we still know about these old ideas today.
lg06.talk: Why is it important to keep and share knowledge from the past?

lg07.happened: In 1382, John Wycliffe, a scholar from Oxford, completed the first full translation of the Bible into English. Before Wycliffe, the Bible was mostly read in Latin, a language that common people could not understand. Wycliffe believed that everyone should have access to God’s word directly, not just priests and scholars. With the help of other scholars and his followers, called Lollards, he worked from the Latin Vulgate Bible to translate every book, carefully hand-writing copies since the printing press had not yet been invented. The Lollards risked their lives to distribute these English Bibles around England, hiding them from authorities who saw this translation as dangerous. Religious leaders were angry, saying only the church should interpret scripture, and Wycliffe faced serious threats. Even after his death, church officials were so upset that they dug up his body forty-four years later and burned his remains. But his work could not be undone: people across England began reading the Bible for themselves, sparking new questions and faith.
lg07.background: In Wycliffe’s time, Europe was filled with castles and cathedrals, and life in England was hard for most people. Most were farmers, tied to the land, working long hours for wealthy landlords. Education was rare, and most people couldn’t read. Any education went to priests or monks, who learned Latin so they could read church texts. The church was very powerful and often the center of community life. Most people went to church but never heard the Bible in their own tongue. English was spoken at home and in the fields, but Latin ruled in the church and at university. The idea that a farmhand or a housewife could read God’s word was new and strange to many, yet deep within the human heart was a longing to hear God’s voice plain and clear.
lg07.matters: Wycliffe’s translation started a chain reaction that changed the world. By giving ordinary people a chance to read God’s words, he planted the seeds of the Reformation. Later translators like William Tyndale and Bible versions like the King James built directly on what he began. For families of faith, his work tells us that Heavenly Father wants all His children to know Him, using language they understand. Without Wycliffe’s courage and faith, Joseph Smith’s family might not have owned an English Bible, and the Restoration of the gospel could have unfolded differently.
lg07.scripture: The Bible itself speaks of the importance of understanding God’s word: 'So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God' (Romans 10:17). When Nephi and his brothers returned to Jerusalem for the brass plates (1 Nephi 3–5), it was because 'scriptures are laid up for a wise purpose' (1 Nephi 5:19-21). The Doctrine and Covenants gives a principle: 'And as all have not faith, seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom; yea, seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith' (Doctrine and Covenants 88:118). All point to the blessing of having God’s words in a form we can read and understand.
lg07.evidence: Historians are certain Wycliffe led the translation effort, and several handwritten copies, known as Wycliffe Bibles, still exist in museums and libraries. These ancient volumes are written in Middle English, matching the language people spoke and wrote at the time. Researchers have compared the handwriting, spelling, and notes and traced them to Wycliffe’s circle at Oxford. There is also a wide record of church trials and writings against Wycliffe and the Lollards, confirming how threatening authorities found these English Bibles. Chroniclers from the 1300s to the 1400s describe both the translation’s spread and the fierce attempts to stop it. Even the story of burning Wycliffe’s bones is confirmed in church history documents, showing how powerful his work remained long after his death.
lg07.learn: From Wycliffe’s story, we learn that courage in doing what is right can change many lives, even if things are hard or dangerous. We see that Heavenly Father’s words are meant for everyone, not just a few people. By giving families the scriptures, Wycliffe helped open a path for faith, learning, and personal prayer that still blesses us today. His life reminds us to value being able to read the scriptures and to share truth kindly and bravely.
lg07.child: Long ago, a man named Wycliffe helped write the whole Bible in English so normal people could read it. He was brave because others wanted to stop him, but he knew God wanted everyone to have His words. Now we can read the Bible in our own language because of people like him.
lg07.talk: Why do you think it was important for everyone to have the Bible in their own language?

lg08.happened: In 1534, Martin Luther finished a complete translation of the Bible into German so that everyday people could read the word of God for themselves. Before this, most Bibles in Western Europe were in Latin—a language few regular people could understand. Luther worked in the city of Wittenberg, Germany, where he studied old Hebrew and Greek texts carefully to make his German Bible as accurate as possible. He wanted the language to be clear, lively, and similar to how families spoke at home or in the marketplace, not stiff and scholarly. Luther’s Bible came out in printed form, just as the printing press was making books more available than ever. Soon, German families who could afford a Bible had one, reading it together and shaping the way they spoke. The language Luther chose helped to form a common German language, making it easier for people from different regions to understand each other. The Luther Bible changed not just how people read scripture, but how they spoke and learned.
lg08.background: In the early 1500s, most people in Europe were part of the Catholic Church, and church services were in Latin. Only those trained in universities—usually priests—could read and explain the Bible. Most Germans spoke regional dialects, sometimes barely understandable to those from a different town. Printing had only recently been invented, so books were rare and costly. Martin Luther, once a monk and scholar, felt that everyone should be able to read God’s word directly. His beliefs came at a dangerous time, as questioning church practice could lead to punishment. Yet Luther’s drive for ordinary people to connect with scripture grew, and others also began to write and speak plainly so families could understand important truths.
lg08.matters: Luther’s translation did more than share the Bible—it set a standard for making scripture understandable to all people, in their own language. This idea has shaped missionary work ever since: the gospel is for everyone, and Heavenly Father wants His word in every language and every home. For families of faith, this means that the words of scripture are meant to be heard by mothers, fathers, and children in the language they know best, making it easier to learn and feel the Spirit. Luther’s Bible inspired many future efforts to translate holy books, including those by early Latter-day Saints.
lg08.scripture: The principle that God's word belongs to all people is woven through the scriptures. In the Bible, Acts 2:6-8 tells how at Pentecost, the apostles spoke so that people from many lands heard the gospel in their own language. The Book of Mormon also teaches that God speaks to people in their language so they can understand (2 Nephi 31:3). Doctrine and Covenants 90:11 says all people will hear the gospel in their own tongue. These passages show how important it is for families to hear Heavenly Father's words in the language of their hearts.
lg08.evidence: Historical records confirm that Luther’s Bible was published in 1534, with copies surviving in museums today. Experts on language study old letters and books to show how Luther’s translation helped set the form of modern German, making it more unified. Printing records and church writings from Luther’s time show that once the translation spread, more families than ever could own and read the Bible. Many historians agree that this was a turning point for both Reformation churches and the German language itself. Few events are better documented: original copies, Luther’s own notes, and reactions from the time all still exist.
lg08.learn: Luther’s German Bible reminds us that Heavenly Father wants every family to have access to His word. Each time we read scripture together in our own language, we follow a tradition stretching back centuries. We learn that making sacred things understandable and close to home matters deeply. This event encourages us to value and seek out scripture in our own language, and to welcome truth spoken clearly, simply, and kindly.
lg08.child: A long time ago, Martin Luther put the Bible into German so even regular families could read it. Before that, only special church teachers could understand the Bible. Thanks to him, more people could learn about Jesus at home.
lg08.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants everyone to hear His word in their own language?

lg09.happened: In 1611, a new English translation of the Bible was published in London, England. This project was started by King James I, who wanted a version of the Bible that everyone in his country could read and trust. He gathered 47 scholars—some of the best language experts, ministers, and professors of that day—to do the work. Over several years, they divided into groups, each responsible for different parts of the Bible, carefully translating from Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. They compared their work with earlier translations and checked the meaning with great care. The final book was called the King James Version, and its language was meant to sound beautiful, respectful, and holy, like God’s word should. It became the main Bible used in churches, homes, and schools, and was passed from parent to child for generations. Over time, its words and phrases shaped the ways English speakers pray, talk about right and wrong, and even write stories or argue about ideas. Some phrases people say every day come straight from this Bible, even if they don’t realize it.
lg09.background: Before the King James Bible, English-speaking Christians used several different Bibles. Some of these were translated secretly, as translating the Bible into English was dangerous just a few decades earlier. The most popular earlier Bibles included William Tyndale’s translation and the Geneva Bible, which many early settlers in America also used. Life in England at that time was filled with change: new rulers, arguments over religion, and people learning to read in greater numbers. Books were becoming easier to print, but most people still depended on what their church leaders read aloud. The desire for a single, trustworthy, and beautiful translation grew out of these times of change. The people who worked on the King James Bible lived in cities and colleges, and their days were spent in reading, prayer, and careful word-by-word translation, hoping to give everyone God’s words in a way that felt sacred and true.
lg09.matters: The King James Bible matters so much because it shaped not just religion, but the entire English language and how people think about faith. For Latter-day Saint families, its words became the way many learned about Jesus Christ and Heavenly Father. Joseph Smith, the Prophet who began the Restoration, read from the King James Bible when he searched for truth and later translated the Book of Mormon using the same sacred-sounding language. Even now, reading this Bible helps us feel connected to generations who have loved and trusted these words. Its influence can be felt in prayers, church meetings, and even in the way we speak and write today.
lg09.scripture: One of the most important moments in Latter-day Saint history connects to James 1:5 from the King James Bible, where it says, "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God." This encouraged young Joseph Smith to pray, leading to the First Vision and the Restoration. The Book of Mormon, when translated, also uses the sacred register of King James English throughout, making scriptures feel familiar and holy. Although the Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price also use this style, the principle at work is to seek truth from God through prayer and scripture study, as taught in Matthew 7:7 and 2 Nephi 32:3.
lg09.evidence: Historians and language experts have many records showing exactly how the King James Bible was created. Letters, meeting minutes, drafts, and even earlier translations used as references are still kept in libraries and museums. These documents tell us who the translators were, how the work was divided, and how carefully they checked their words. Thousands of copies have survived from those early years, and the text has changed very little. Scholars can compare the King James Version to earlier and later translations, showing its great influence on English. Experts agree it is a careful, well-documented historical event with a deep impact on language and faith. Many academic and church sources study its history and how it shaped society.
lg09.learn: We learn that God can work through many people, even scholars in distant times, to make His word known to more of His children. We also see how the words we choose can shape hearts and minds for centuries. This event teaches us to value good, careful work, to help others understand truth, and to remember that the way we say things can make them feel more sacred.
lg09.child: A king in England asked smart people to make a Bible everyone could read. Their book became so special that many families still read it today. Even Joseph Smith used this Bible when he prayed to Heavenly Father.
lg09.talk: What is your favorite verse in the Bible, and how does it make you feel when you read it?

lg10.happened: Since the early 19th century, scholars have identified approximately 7,168 living languages worldwide. This linguistic diversity reflects the rich tapestry of human cultures and histories. In the realm of faith, the Bible has been translated into over 3,500 languages, making it accessible to a vast majority of the global population. The Book of Mormon, another testament of Jesus Christ, has been translated into 113 languages—92 full translations and 21 selections—allowing many to read its teachings in their native tongues. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints conducts meetings in 188 languages, emphasizing the importance of worship in one's own language. Organizations like Wycliffe Bible Translators continue to work diligently to translate scriptures into the remaining languages that still lack them, striving to ensure that every individual can access sacred texts in their mother tongue.
lg10.background: Before the 19th century, the world was a mosaic of languages, many of which were spoken by small, localized communities. The spread of major world religions, colonialism, and trade led to the dominance of certain languages, but countless others remained confined to specific regions or groups. Daily life for many involved oral traditions, with stories, laws, and histories passed down verbally. The advent of the printing press and increased global communication in the 19th century spurred efforts to document and translate languages, preserving them and making religious texts more widely available.
lg10.matters: Understanding and preserving the world's languages is crucial for maintaining cultural heritage and diversity. For families of faith, having access to scriptures in their native language deepens understanding and personal connection to spiritual teachings. It allows individuals to worship and study in a language that resonates with their hearts, fostering a more intimate relationship with their faith. Moreover, the translation of sacred texts into various languages fulfills the divine mandate to spread the gospel to all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people.
lg10.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of sharing the gospel with all people, regardless of language. In Acts 2:6, during Pentecost, it is recorded that "every man heard them speak in his own language," symbolizing the universal nature of the gospel message. Doctrine and Covenants 90:11 states, "For it shall come to pass in that day, that every man shall hear the fulness of the gospel in his own tongue, and in his own language." These passages highlight the divine desire for all individuals to receive His word in a language they understand.
lg10.evidence: Linguistic studies have documented the existence of approximately 7,168 living languages as of 2024. The translation of religious texts has been a significant endeavor; for instance, the Bible has been translated into over 3,500 languages, making it one of the most widely translated books in history. The Book of Mormon has been translated into 113 languages, with 92 full translations and 21 selections, reflecting ongoing efforts to make sacred texts accessible to diverse populations. These translations are the result of meticulous work by linguists, scholars, and missionaries dedicated to spreading religious teachings across linguistic boundaries.
lg10.learn: We learn the importance of linguistic diversity and the need to preserve and respect all languages. For families of faith, this underscores the value of making spiritual teachings accessible to everyone in their native tongue, fostering inclusivity and deeper understanding. It also reminds us of the ongoing responsibility to share messages of faith and hope with all people, regardless of linguistic differences.
lg10.child: There are many languages spoken around the world, and it's important for everyone to hear about Jesus in their own language. People work hard to translate the scriptures so everyone can understand them.
lg10.talk: Why do you think it's important for people to read the scriptures in their own language?

pp01.happened: Around 50,000 BC, the number of humans living on Earth is believed to have been very small — some scientists say there may have been as few as 10,000 to 100,000 people total. At this time, our ancestors were living in Africa and had begun to slowly spread into other parts of the world. These people lived in small groups or families, moving from place to place to find food, shelter, and water. Life was not easy; people depended on hunting animals, gathering fruits or seeds, using simple stone tools, and working together to survive. Because there were so few people, every family and birth was deeply important. Over thousands of years, their children and grandchildren would travel out of Africa and fill the earth, eventually giving rise to all the families and nations we know today. This was the beginning of our shared human journey — millions of years after the first humans appeared, and long before cities or written records, humans began to multiply and spread across the world.
pp01.background: Before this time, earth was home to many types of early humans and close relatives, but not all survived into the present. Most people living around 50,000 BC were Homo sapiens, the species to which all humans today belong. They lived in a world shaped by wild animals, dramatic climates, and untouched landscapes. Daily life centered on staying alive — finding food, caring for families, and working together to make shelters. Fire offered warmth and protection, while shared stories or knowledge helped each group learn from the past. Everything they needed came from nature, and their lives were shaped by the rhythms of the land and sky.
pp01.matters: This moment matters because it marks a very real point when all humans were part of a small, close-knit family. For families of faith, understanding our shared ancestry can bring a sense of unity and love for all people, as every person living now is connected to those early families. It shows that God’s children, though once few, were watched over and preserved so His purposes on earth could unfold — leading to the wide, beautiful family we see today.
pp01.scripture: The scriptures do not tell us exactly about this time in history, but the Bible teaches in Genesis 1:27 and Acts 17:26 that all people are made in God's image and are of “one blood.” The Book of Mormon and other scripture often speak of remembering that all are children of God (Mosiah 4:19). Doctrine and Covenants 18:10-12 reminds us of each person's worth to Heavenly Father. These principles echo the idea that every person on earth is part of one great family, each precious to God.
pp01.evidence: Modern genetics tells us that all living humans today share a common ancestry, and that at one point, our ancestors were few in number. Scientists find this evidence by studying differences and similarities in DNA from people all over the world. Archaeological finds, such as ancient tools and bones, support the idea that humans started in Africa and then spread outwards. Genetics research supports a population bottleneck and a shared recent ancestry for all people living today. While exact numbers are still debated, there is strong agreement that our history includes a time when humans were few and carried forward the family tree for all of us.
pp01.learn: We can learn that even small beginnings can lead to great things, and that every family is important in God’s plan. Remembering that everyone is part of one human family helps us treat others with kindness and respect, no matter where they come from. We are all connected, and our choices matter to the generations who come after us.
pp01.child: A long, long time ago, there were not many people in the whole world—maybe only enough to fill a big stadium. They were all part of one big family, just like we are all part of God’s family today. Every person you meet is part of that family, too.
pp01.talk: How does it feel to know that every person on earth is related to you in God’s family?

pp02.happened: Around 2350 BC, the world was a very different place from today. This was the time many traditions speak of Noah, his family, and the great flood. According to the Bible, Noah was asked by God to build an ark to save his family and two of every kind of animal from a flood that would cover the earth. After the flood, Noah’s family began again, and people slowly spread across the lands. Scholars today estimate that the total number of people living at that time could have been about ten million—mostly in regions like the Fertile Crescent, along the Nile in Egypt, and near the Indus River. Life was mostly focused on farming, raising animals, and small trade between villages. The story goes on to say that Noah had three sons, and from their descendants came the many peoples and languages of the earth, as listed in Genesis 10, a chapter often called the “Table of Nations.” This account is not just about survival, but about the beginning of human families who would fill and bless the world.
pp02.background: Before Noah’s time, the earth saw families and small groups develop skills in farming, building shelters, and making simple tools. People lived close to rivers where the land was rich and water was plentiful. Most worked as farmers, herders, or craftsmen, and lived in mud-brick homes in small villages. Trade was starting to grow, with simple goods like grain, cloth, and pottery moving between close communities. The Fertile Crescent, stretching from Egypt through Mesopotamia, was especially rich. Ancient stories from different cultures also speak of great floods, making the memory of such an event important to many people living in this part of the world.
pp02.matters: This event is meaningful for faith and family because it teaches us about new beginnings and the unity of all people as family. From the story of Noah and his descendants grows the idea that every person on earth is related, a message that echoes through scripture and connects us to all of God’s children. For families, it offers a time to talk about starting fresh after hard times and being part of a bigger family stretching all the way back to the first people. These lessons can help us see everyone as a brother or sister and remind us of our shared hopes and duties.
pp02.scripture: Genesis chapters 6 through 10 tell the story of Noah, the great flood, and the Table of Nations, which lists the families who spread across the earth afterwards. Genesis 10 is especially important for seeing how people are connected to Noah. The Book of Mormon (Ether 1:3, 33) and the Doctrine and Covenants (D&C 138:41) also mention Noah, showing his importance in God’s plan. These passages teach us that all people are part of God’s family and that there is purpose and order in how the earth was populated after Noah’s time.
pp02.evidence: Modern scholars try to estimate ancient world populations using evidence from archaeology, ancient city sizes, and farming technology. No exact numbers are possible, but respected estimates for the world’s population at the time of Noah range from five to twenty million people. Most people would have lived in river valleys where farming could support larger numbers. Archaeology has found towns and trade networks in the Fertile Crescent, Egypt, and the Indus Valley. There are many ancient flood stories, but evidence for a single worldwide flood remains debated. The earliest genealogies in the Bible, and similar stories from other cultures, show a real human desire to understand where people come from and how families relate to each other.
pp02.learn: From this event we learn about resilience, the value of families, and the belief that we are all connected. Even though the details may be hard to prove, the lessons about caring for each other and trusting in a new beginning after trial are powerful. It also helps us remember that God’s love and plan cover all people and ages, no matter where they live or when they were born.
pp02.child: Long ago, there may have been about ten million people on earth when Noah lived. The Bible tells us everyone comes from one family after a great flood. This teaches us we are all connected and can start again with faith.
pp02.talk: What does it mean to you to know that everyone in the world is part of one big family?

pp03.happened: Around the year 1000 BC, about 50 million people lived on the earth. This was a time when some of the oldest and most powerful civilizations were flourishing. Egypt, with its mighty pharaohs and great pyramids, was still a center of learning and power. In Mesopotamia, along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, people built cities with walls and ziggurats, and kings ruled over their lands. In China, the Zhou Dynasty brought order and traditions that would last for centuries. The Indus Valley was home to skilled traders and builders. Most people lived in villages or farming communities, growing plants and raising animals for food. In the middle of all this, the Israelites were living in the land of Canaan. King David and then his son Solomon ruled over Israel, making it strong and wealthy. Solomon even built a beautiful temple in Jerusalem where the people could worship God. Travel, trade, and messages moved along river valleys and roads that ran through the land of Israel.
pp03.background: Before 1000 BC, people had begun to build cities and learn to farm. Families would plant crops, raise animals, and trade goods like grain, goats, and cloth with their neighbors. Writing was already an important tool in places like Egypt and Mesopotamia, using clay tablets or papyrus to record stories and keep track of supplies. People faced hard work each day but also had times for music, stories, and celebrations. Kingdoms often fought wars over land and water. Long before the Israelites had kings, their ancestors wandered with herds, moving from place to place as the Bible tells us. Over time, groups settled down, and the world slowly filled with more people, each group with its own language and way of life.
pp03.matters: Knowing that there were about 50 million people on the earth puts the Bible story into a real-world setting. God placed His covenant people, Israel, right where many roads and travelers passed by. This helped His teachings, and eventually the teachings of Jesus, spread to many lands. For a family of faith, remembering this helps us see that God uses ordinary places and people to do extraordinary things. Today, just as then, He often puts us where we can share goodness with those around us, blessing many through small and simple acts.
pp03.scripture: The Bible tells us about the time of kings David and Solomon in 2 Samuel and 1 Kings. These chapters describe how Israel grew strong and was known by its neighbors. In Deuteronomy 7:6-8, God explains that Israel is His 'chosen people,’ not because they were the biggest nation, but because of His love and promises. Acts 17:26 reminds us that God 'hath made of one blood all nations of men,' showing that He cares for all His children, wherever they live. The Book of Mormon, in Alma 37:6-7, teaches that by small and simple things, great things can come to pass.
pp03.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have looked at ancient records, pottery, buildings, and burials to estimate the world population at this time. While it is not possible to know the exact number, most modern studies suggest that between 30 and 70 million people lived on earth around 1000 BC. Civilizations along great rivers left behind many clues showing city life, trade, and even early science and writing. Israel’s location is well-documented as a crossroads between Africa, Asia, and Europe, making it a key place for trade and communication in the ancient world.
pp03.learn: We learn that even when the world was much smaller and simpler, God cared about where His people lived and the work they could do. Our families are placed in neighborhoods, schools, and towns where we can also shine our light. Just like the Israelites, we are part of a bigger story, and Heavenly Father invites us to make a difference right where we are.
pp03.child: A long time ago, when there were about 50 million people on earth, God put the Israelites where many people traveled. He wanted them to share His love and teachings with others. We can help too, right where we live.
pp03.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wanted His people to live in a place where so many people passed by?

pp04.happened: Around the time of Jesus Christ's birth, the world was home to an estimated 200 to 300 million people. The Roman Empire, a vast and powerful entity, likely had a population of about 50 to 60 million. In the East, the Han Dynasty in China governed a similarly large populace. Other regions, including the Indian subcontinent, the Americas, the Pacific Islands, and sub-Saharan Africa, were inhabited by smaller, diverse communities. This era was marked by significant connectivity, especially within the Roman Empire, where an extensive network of roads and sea routes facilitated trade and communication across the Mediterranean and beyond.
pp04.background: Before this period, human societies had transitioned from nomadic lifestyles to settled agricultural communities, leading to population growth and the development of complex civilizations. The Roman Empire, with its advanced infrastructure and governance, provided a relatively stable environment that encouraged economic and cultural exchanges. Daily life varied widely: in Rome, citizens enjoyed urban amenities, while rural populations engaged in farming. In China, the Han Dynasty's bureaucratic system and Confucian ideals shaped society, emphasizing family and social harmony. Despite regional differences, many societies experienced advancements in technology, art, and philosophy during this time.
pp04.matters: Understanding the world's population and interconnectedness at the time of Christ highlights the remarkable spread of the gospel in the first century. The extensive networks of the Roman Empire enabled the apostles to travel widely, sharing the teachings of Jesus. For families of faith, this underscores the importance of community and communication in spreading and nurturing beliefs. It also serves as a reminder of how divine guidance can work through existing structures to fulfill a greater purpose.
pp04.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the rapid spread of the gospel during the apostles' time. In Colossians 1:23, Paul speaks of the gospel "which was preached to every creature which is under heaven." Similarly, in Acts 1:8, Jesus instructs His disciples to be His witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth." These passages reflect the swift dissemination of Christ's teachings across the known world, facilitated by the era's connectivity.
pp04.evidence: Historical and archaeological studies provide insights into the world's population during this period. Estimates suggest that around the time of Christ, the global population was approximately 200 million, with the Roman Empire accounting for about 50 to 60 million inhabitants. These figures are derived from analyses of historical records, archaeological findings, and demographic modeling. While exact numbers are challenging to determine, the consensus among scholars supports these approximate figures.
pp04.learn: Reflecting on this period teaches us about the power of communication and infrastructure in spreading ideas and beliefs. It reminds us that even in times of limited technology, dedicated individuals can make a profound impact. For families, it highlights the importance of sharing values and teachings within our communities and beyond, trusting that sincere efforts can lead to meaningful change.
pp04.child: Long ago, when Jesus was born, there were about 200 million people in the world. The Roman Empire had many roads that helped people travel and share news quickly. This made it easier for Jesus' followers to tell others about His teachings.
pp04.talk: How do you think the roads and connections in the Roman Empire helped Jesus' followers share His message?
