pp05.happened: The Black Death was one of the most devastating events in human history. It was a terrible outbreak of plague that swept through Europe and Asia between 1347 and 1351. This disease, now known as the bubonic plague, was carried by fleas on rats and could spread quickly from person to person. It arrived in Europe through trading ships, bringing sudden sickness that would touch nearly every family. People would get sick very fast, with fevers, painful swellings, and sometimes dark patches on their skin. Most people who caught it died within days. By 1400, Europe’s population had fallen by about a third. Entire villages disappeared, and cities shrank. The death and suffering left people deeply shaken and changed the way they saw the world, their families, and their faith. It was a time of great fear, but also reflection, as survivors wondered why it had happened and what life meant afterward.
pp05.background: Before the Black Death, Europe and Asia were home to bustling towns, growing cities, and busy trade routes. Many people were farmers, working the land from dawn to dusk, while others crafted goods, traded, or served in churches. Life was ruled by tradition and the church, and most people expected things to remain the same generation after generation. The plague arrived in a world already hungry: poor harvests and wars made daily life hard for many families. People often lived close together in crowded towns, which made it easier for diseases to spread. Ideas about sickness were simple, and people did not understand germs or how to stop the plague. Faith was a huge part of life, and priests and monks were trusted guides through every joy and sorrow. But nothing had prepared people for disaster on the scale of the Black Death.
pp05.matters: The Black Death matters because it reshaped both the map and the heart of Europe. With so many people gone, families, communities, and traditions had to change. Labor became more valued, and old ways of working and ruling were questioned. Most importantly, it drove people to look for answers about life, suffering, and God. Many began to seek a more personal faith, setting the stage for the Reformation and, centuries later, the Restoration of the gospel. For families of faith, the Black Death shows how even in dark times, the Lord can prepare the world for future blessings and help hearts become ready for His truth.
pp05.scripture: While the Bible doesn’t mention the Black Death, it includes stories of plagues and suffering, such as in Exodus 12 or Amos 4:10, where plagues led people to remember God and seek Him earnestly. The Book of Mormon also teaches about times when societies faced great destruction but were given new opportunities to turn toward the Lord (3 Nephi 8–10). These scriptures remind us that Heavenly Father can use even terrible events to help people come closer to Him and prepare for times of renewal.
pp05.evidence: Historians and scientists have found many records of the Black Death through church documents, town records, and even layers of mass graves that show its sudden, devastating impact. DNA studies on old plague victims have proven the bacteria Yersinia pestis caused it. Archaeologists have uncovered signs of abandoned villages and shifts in farming, showing how population collapse changed the land. Writings from the time—letters, diaries, and chronicles—describe deep sorrow and confusion but also spiritual searching. There is wide agreement among experts that the Black Death was a turning point in world history, bringing a real and lasting change to populations and to how faith was understood and practiced.
pp05.learn: From this event, we learn that upheaval can lead to new growth. Just as a forest changes after a fire, societies can change after tragedy, sometimes in ways that make room for more light and growth. Trials often invite us to ask hard questions and seek God more sincerely. Families can remember that hardship never means Heavenly Father has abandoned His children. Instead, He works through every age and challenge to prepare His children for blessings ahead.
pp05.child: A sickness called the Black Death spread very quickly and made many people sad and scared. Even though so many families lost loved ones, people began to think more deeply about God and how to live better lives. Later, these changes helped prepare the world for good things to come.
pp05.talk: Why do you think hard things sometimes help people get closer to Heavenly Father?

pp06.happened: In the year 1804, something special happened on our planet: Earth’s population reached 1 billion people for the very first time. For thousands of years, the number of people in the world had grown slowly, but around this time, everything changed. New inventions like the steam engine, better farming equipment, and the spread of books allowed more people to live longer, healthier lives. Big cities in Europe and America became busier as people left farms for jobs in factories. Families sometimes had many children, and most people worked hard every day. Everywhere, people began to feel more connected. Letters could travel faster, news could spread further, and new ideas moved across oceans. This was also the time when the world was opening up—people wondered about far-off places and how life might change. The timing is important: this new, bigger, and more connected world was the same world the Prophet Joseph Smith lived in. Just a few years after the population hit this milestone, the Restoration began. It was a moment when new tools and new numbers of people were lining up, almost as if the world was getting ready for a new message to reach every land.
pp06.background: Before 1804, the world was much quieter and less crowded than today. Most people lived in small villages or on farms, doing what their families had done for generations. Travel was slow and most people never left their hometowns. The biggest countries were places like China, India, and European nations, with their own kings and traditions. Many people could not read or write, and books were treasures. Life was often hard—disease and hunger were common, and families depended on the weather for their food. But inventions were beginning to change things. The spinning jenny, steam engine, and printing press were making work faster and spreading ideas further. People started to believe that life could be better and that important changes were possible. These changes set the stage for both the population milestone and the Restoration of the gospel.
pp06.matters: Reaching 1 billion people matters because it shows how much Heavenly Father cares for every family and every individual. When the world became big and connected enough, Heavenly Father began the Restoration and gathered tools so that everyone, someday, could hear the gospel. For families of faith, it is a reminder that the Lord prepares the world carefully. He does not forget anyone, and He arranges history so His message can reach every corner of the earth, just as He promised. It teaches us to watch for how technology and humanity work together in Heavenly Father’s plan.
pp06.scripture: In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord told Joseph Smith that the gospel should be preached to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people (Doctrine and Covenants 1:2; 133:37). The Bible also speaks of a time when 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea' (Isaiah 11:9). While no scripture says exactly when the world would reach a billion people, these passages help us see that a growing, connected world is part of God’s plan to spread His truth to all of His children.
pp06.evidence: Historians and scientists agree that it was around 1804 when Earth’s population crossed the 1 billion mark. They base this on church records, old census counts, and studies of how families grew over time. While earlier counts are only rough guesses, records from the late 1700s and early 1800s became more careful. Scholars look at birth, marriage, and death records, and compare them with what we know about food, health, and farming from those days. No one knows the exact day or month, but the year 1804 is widely accepted as the best estimate. Population experts at the United Nations and history projects like Our World in Data use these records to explain how quickly the world began to grow after this time.
pp06.learn: From this milestone, we learn that great changes take time, but Heavenly Father is always working in history. When new hopes and inventions arrive, we can look for how they might help us serve others and share what we believe. It also reminds us to care about the world’s people, because each person matters to God and, like the Restoration, big changes often come when the world is ready to receive them.
pp06.child: A long time ago, there were not as many people on earth as there are now. In 1804, there were finally 1 billion people living all over the world. It’s like our family, but with many, many more people—everyone is important to Heavenly Father.
pp06.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father waited until the world was so big before He started the Restoration?

pp07.happened: In 1927, the world reached a significant milestone as its population hit 2 billion people. This marked a substantial increase from the 1 billion recorded in 1804, taking 123 years to double. This growth was largely due to advancements in medicine, agriculture, and sanitation, which reduced death rates and improved life expectancy. During this period, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints also experienced notable growth. From its humble beginnings with six members in 1830, the Church expanded to approximately 644,745 members by 1927, establishing a presence in North America, Europe, and the Pacific Islands. This era also saw technological innovations like the automobile and radio, which transformed communication and information dissemination worldwide.
pp07.background: The early 20th century was a time of rapid change and development. The aftermath of World War I led to significant political and social shifts. Technological advancements, such as the widespread adoption of automobiles and the advent of radio broadcasting, began to shrink the world, making communication faster and more efficient. In the realm of religion, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was expanding its missionary efforts, reaching new regions and cultures. Daily life was becoming more interconnected, with people gaining access to information and ideas from distant places, fostering a sense of a global community.
pp07.matters: The doubling of the world's population to 2 billion in 1927 highlights the rapid pace of human growth and the challenges and opportunities that come with it. For families of faith, this period underscores the importance of adapting to a changing world while holding onto core values. The growth of the Church during this time demonstrates the resilience and dedication of its members in spreading their message. The technological advancements of the era, such as radio, provided new avenues for sharing faith and connecting with a broader audience, illustrating how innovation can serve as a tool for fulfilling spiritual missions.
pp07.scripture: The scriptures teach about the importance of spreading the gospel to all nations. In Matthew 28:19-20, Jesus instructs His disciples to "go ye therefore, and teach all nations." Similarly, in Doctrine and Covenants 88:81, members are reminded of their duty to warn their neighbors. These passages emphasize the responsibility to share faith widely, a task that became increasingly feasible with the technological advancements of the early 20th century.
pp07.evidence: Historical records confirm that the world population reached 2 billion in 1927, a milestone that took 123 years to achieve after reaching 1 billion in 1804. This growth is well-documented in demographic studies and historical analyses. Church records from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints indicate a membership of approximately 644,745 by 1927, reflecting steady growth since its establishment in 1830. The expansion of radio broadcasting during this period is also well-documented, with stations beginning to transmit voices and music over long distances, revolutionizing communication.
pp07.learn: This event teaches us about the rapid pace of change in the world and the importance of adapting to new circumstances. It highlights how technological advancements can be harnessed to spread messages and connect with others. For families of faith, it serves as a reminder of the ongoing responsibility to share beliefs and values, using the tools and opportunities available in each era.
pp07.child: Long ago, there were 2 billion people in the world. That's a lot of people! During that time, the Church grew too, reaching many new places and helping more people learn about Jesus.
pp07.talk: How do you think new inventions like the radio helped people learn about the Church back then?

pp08.happened: In 1960, the world’s population reached 3 billion people, only a short 33 years after it had reached 2 billion in 1927. This rapid growth was partly due to better medicine, which meant more babies and mothers survived, and people lived longer. Around this time, families in many countries—especially after World War II—had more children than before, a time called the 'baby boom.' At the same time, technology was changing daily life quickly. Televisions became common in homes, and people around the world could watch news and events as they happened, making the world feel both larger and smaller at once. That year, members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints numbered about 1.7 million, spread across dozens of nations, and the Church was preparing to reach even more people. The 1960s also saw the rise of airplanes and faster travel, along with important changes inside the Church—like the start of the correlation program, which aimed to help every member study and learn the gospel in a united, organized way, no matter where they lived. These changes meant the restored gospel could reach more of Heavenly Father's children as the earth became ever more full.
pp08.background: Before 1960, the world had been through tough years—two world wars, a great depression, and many changes in how people lived. The 1950s were years of rebuilding and hope, especially in places like the United States, where families grew bigger and new inventions like the television brought news, entertainment, and learning into the home. Vaccines and better sanitation made childhood diseases less deadly, and life expectancies grew. Most families still got their news from newspapers or radio, but television was becoming the new way to learn about the world. Many parts of Asia, Africa, and Latin America saw their populations grow as health and food supplies improved, even as many still lived in poverty. For Latter-day Saints, the Church was moving into more countries, and members were learning to connect with others across languages and cultures, often for the first time in their lives.
pp08.matters: This moment matters because it marked a turning point in human history—a world suddenly busy with more people than ever. Larger families meant new challenges, like making sure everyone had enough to eat or a place to live. But it also meant more chances to learn, to serve, and to share the blessings of the gospel. For families who have faith in God, it’s a reminder that our world is big, full of children of Heavenly Father, each precious to Him, and that technology and organization can be used to reach for goodness. The Church’s focus on reaching members everywhere reflects a desire to care for all Heavenly Father’s children as the world grows busier.
pp08.scripture: One principle found in the scriptures is that of gathering: the Lord desires that all His children have the chance to hear the gospel (Matthew 24:14; Doctrine and Covenants 1:2). In 3 Nephi 27:21, Jesus says, 'This is my gospel... and ye know the things that ye must do in my church.' The rapid growth of the earth’s population and the Church’s efforts to organize and teach reflect these scriptural purposes—to reach every nation, kindred, and tongue. Doctrine and Covenants 90:11 teaches that every person will hear the gospel in his or her own language. The spread of technology, translation, and organized teaching all help fulfill these promises.
pp08.evidence: Historical records from the United Nations and national governments confirm that the world population reached roughly 3 billion in 1960, and it has continued to climb ever since. Increases in life expectancy and decreases in child mortality during the 1940s and 1950s are well documented by health agencies and historians. The term 'baby boom' is supported by census data, showing a sharp rise in births in the United States and other nations after WWII. Church records likewise show a steady increase in international membership during this period, and official histories include information on the worldwide introduction of Church curriculum and correlation efforts. The expansion of television news and air travel is also well supported by contemporary reports and photographs.
pp08.learn: We can learn that when the world changes rapidly, Heavenly Father prepares tools and ways for His work to grow too. Just as families and societies adapt to care for more people, the Lord’s Church can organize and find new ways to serve and teach. This teaches us to welcome change, look for how it can be used for good, and trust that God is aware of all His children, even in a busy world.
pp08.child: A long time ago, there were only about 3 billion people in the whole world, and families were growing fast. The Church found new ways to teach and help everyone, even far away, because Heavenly Father loves all His children.
pp08.talk: How do you think Heavenly Father feels about every person on earth, now that there are so many more people?

pp09.happened: On July 11, 1987, the world reached a significant milestone as the global population was estimated to have surpassed five billion people. This event, known as the "Day of Five Billion," was recognized by the United Nations to highlight the rapid growth of the human population. To commemorate this occasion, the UN Secretary-General at the time, Javier Pérez de Cuéllar, traveled to Zagreb, Croatia, to meet Matej Gašpar, who was symbolically chosen as the five-billionth person. This milestone underscored the accelerating pace of population growth; it had taken only 12 years to add the fifth billion, compared to the 15 years it took to reach four billion. The rapid increase raised awareness about the challenges and opportunities associated with a growing global population, including resource management, economic development, and environmental sustainability.
pp09.background: The late 20th century was a period of significant change and development. Advances in medicine and agriculture had led to lower mortality rates and increased life expectancy, contributing to rapid population growth. In 1987, the world was also experiencing the early stages of the digital revolution. Personal computers were becoming more common, and the foundations for the internet were being laid, setting the stage for unprecedented global connectivity. Politically, the Cold War was nearing its end, with the Berlin Wall set to fall just two years later, leading to the opening of Eastern Europe. For The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, this era was marked by expansion. By the end of 1987, the Church reported a membership of approximately 6.44 million, with 34,750 full-time missionaries serving in 205 missions worldwide. The Church was establishing a presence in more countries than ever before, reflecting its commitment to spreading the gospel globally.
pp09.matters: The Day of Five Billion serves as a reminder of the rapid growth of the human family and the accompanying responsibilities. For families of faith, this milestone highlights the importance of sharing the gospel message with an ever-increasing population. The Church's growth during this period demonstrates the fulfillment of the divine commission to take the gospel to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people. However, the expanding population also presents challenges, such as ensuring that resources are used wisely and that all individuals have the opportunity to hear the gospel message. It emphasizes the need for continued missionary work and the use of emerging technologies to reach a broader audience.
pp09.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of sharing the gospel with all people. In Matthew 28:19-20, Jesus instructs His disciples to "go ye therefore, and teach all nations." Similarly, in Doctrine and Covenants 133:37, the Lord commands that the gospel be preached "unto every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people." These passages underscore the divine mandate to spread the gospel message to the entire world, a task that becomes increasingly significant as the global population grows.
pp09.evidence: Historical records from the United Nations and other reputable sources confirm that the global population reached approximately five billion in 1987. The United Nations designated July 11, 1987, as the "Day of Five Billion" to mark this milestone. Additionally, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' official statistical reports indicate that by the end of 1987, Church membership had grown to approximately 6.44 million, with significant increases in the number of missionaries and missions worldwide. These records provide clear evidence of both global population growth and the Church's expansion during this period.
pp09.learn: This event teaches us about the rapid growth of the human family and the importance of adapting our efforts to share the gospel accordingly. It reminds us to be mindful stewards of the earth's resources and to use technological advancements to further the Lord's work. As the population continues to grow, we are encouraged to find innovative ways to reach out to others and share the message of the gospel.
pp09.child: In 1987, the world had five billion people! That's a lot of people, like filling up many, many big stadiums. The Church was also growing, with more members and missionaries sharing the gospel everywhere.

pp10.happened: On October 31, 2011, the United Nations estimated that the world's population reached seven billion people. This milestone was marked by symbolic celebrations worldwide, including the birth of babies representing the seven-billionth person. For instance, in the Philippines, a baby girl named Danica May Camacho was welcomed with festivities. This rapid population growth highlighted both the advancements in healthcare and the challenges of resource distribution. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reported approximately 14 million members at that time, representing about 0.2% of the global population. Additionally, social media platforms like Facebook had around 800 million users, and movements such as the Arab Spring were utilizing these platforms to advocate for change in the Middle East. The world was becoming more interconnected than ever before, fostering both unity and a collective search for meaning.
pp10.background: Before reaching the seven-billion mark, the world experienced significant demographic changes. It took humanity until 1804 to reach one billion people, but the pace accelerated dramatically in the 20th century due to medical advancements and improved living conditions. The population doubled from three billion in 1959 to six billion by 1999. This rapid growth was uneven, with developing countries experiencing higher birth rates compared to developed nations. The early 21st century also saw a surge in digital connectivity. Social media platforms emerged as powerful tools for communication and organization, playing pivotal roles in global events like the Arab Spring. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints continued its missionary efforts, utilizing new technologies to share its message worldwide.
pp10.matters: Reaching a population of seven billion underscored the pressing need to address global challenges such as resource distribution, environmental sustainability, and social equity. For families of faith, this milestone served as a reminder of the vastness of God's children and the importance of sharing the gospel message. The Church's membership of 14 million highlighted the immense potential for missionary work. The proliferation of digital tools and social media platforms provided unprecedented opportunities to connect with individuals across the globe, making it easier to spread messages of faith and hope.
pp10.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of sharing the gospel with all nations. In Matthew 28:19-20, Jesus instructs His disciples to "go ye therefore, and teach all nations." Similarly, Doctrine and Covenants 88:81 states, "Behold, I sent you out to testify and warn the people." These passages underscore the responsibility to reach out to the growing global population with messages of faith and salvation.
pp10.evidence: Demographic data from the United Nations and the U.S. Census Bureau confirm the rapid population growth leading up to 2011. The UN's "Day of Seven Billion" was set for October 31, 2011, while the U.S. Census Bureau estimated the milestone would be reached in March 2012. Despite slight differences in projections, both organizations acknowledged the significant population increase. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reported a membership of approximately 14 million in 2011, reflecting steady growth. The rise of social media platforms like Facebook, which had around 800 million users by 2011, played a crucial role in global events such as the Arab Spring, demonstrating the power of digital connectivity in shaping societal movements.
pp10.learn: This event teaches us about the rapid changes in our world and the importance of adapting to new challenges. It highlights the need for responsible stewardship of Earth's resources and the opportunities presented by technological advancements to connect and share messages of faith. As the global population grows, so does the responsibility to reach out with compassion and understanding.
pp10.child: In 2011, there were seven billion people in the world. That's a lot of people! It reminds us to be kind and share with everyone.
